+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 72.0
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur Neegan hooked a calloused index finger inside the stiff synth-silk collar at his throat and pulled. It yielded not a millimeter. For fifteen standard years on the Martian frontier, his wardrobe had consisted of durable canvas overalls and thermal-weave pressure suits. The tailored tunic he had been politely, yet firmly, instructed to put on felt less like clothing and more like a brightly colored straitjacket. Through the thick quartz viewport of the transfer shuttle, the rust-red parabola of Mars was dropping away, replaced by the stark, diamond-studded velvet of the void. Only three hours prior, a sleek, needle-nosed atmospheric flyer had descended upon his modest prefabricated dome in Sector Seven. Six men had emerged. They carried no visible blasters, yet they moved with the synchronized lethality of hunting hounds. Upon their lapels gleamed the golden sunburst of the Antares Diplomatic Corps—an organization, Arthur knew from the colonial sub-ether broadcasts, that was "diplomatic" only in the sense that aneurin-gas was a sedative. When their commander had invited Arthur to an immediate off-world consultation, Arthur had looked at his drill-rig, looked at the six men, and wisely asked what he should pack. "You are arriving at the *Sovereign*, Mr. Neegan," a mechanical voice chimed from the bulkhead. The shuttle jarred slightly as magnetic grapples seized it. Ten minutes later, Arthur was ushered through an airlock that hissed with the rich, over-oxygenated air of an Earth-standard cruiser, and into a room that defied the austerity of space travel. It was a parlor paneled in genuine, earthly mahogany. A man stood before a vast observation window, hands clasped behind a back draped in immaculate charcoal broadcloth. "Mr. Neegan," the man said, turning. He was slender, with silvered temples and eyes as gray and calculating as a positronic brain. "I am Sub-Minister Vance. Please, stop strangling yourself with that collar and sit down. Do you take Martellian brandy?" "I take water, usually, recycled four times over," Arthur said, sitting gingerly on a plush leather chair. "And I’d prefer some answers, Minister. If this is about my mining lease, my claims are registered with the Planetary Board. They are ironclad." Vance smiled thinly, pouring two glasses of amber liquid from a crystal decanter. "Law is a fascinating construct, Mr. Neegan. On Earth, it is a cathedral. On Mars, it is a leaky tent. Your claim in Sector Seven sits atop an estimated four hundred metric tons of high-purity Azra." Arthur kept his face blank, though his heart hammered against his ribs. He had only logged the spectrographic analysis into his private terminal yesterday. "I found a trace vein. Enough to pay off my equipment leases." "Let us not insult one another’s intelligence," Vance said softly, handing Arthur a glass and taking the seat opposite. "My Corps monitors every tachyon burst leaving the Martian relays. You have struck the largest contiguous deposit of Azra in the solar system." Arthur stared into the brandy. Azra. Five years ago, it was a geological curiosity. Then, a physicist in the Geneva Technate discovered that introducing a microscopic lattice of Azra into a heavy-element core accelerated radioactive decay by a factor of ten thousand, instantly and controllably. Overnight, the slow, generational crawl of sub-light ships became obsolete; the hyper-atomic drive was born. And with it, the capacity to crack a continent like an eggshell. "The corporations have already made offers," Arthur said, tugging at his collar again. "Consolidated Tharsis offered me ten million credits and a transport back to Earth. I told them no. They use indentured labor—debt-slaves, really. Unshielded men digging out a catalytic metal that fries their nervous systems in three years. I’m an engineer, Vance. I dig my own dirt." "Noble," Vance murmured. "And suicidal. Consolidated Tharsis will not ask a second time. Next week, you will suffer a tragic malfunction in your oxygen scrubber. Your land will revert to the Martian Authority, and Tharsis will buy it at auction." "Is that why the Antares Corps kidnapped me? Out of concern for my lungs?" "Antares is twelve light-years away, Mr. Neegan. We were the first colony beyond the sun, and we have grown strong. Too strong, Earth thinks." Vance leaned forward, the bureaucratic veneer slipping to reveal a fanatic's intensity. "Earth and its corporate hounds want a monopoly on Azra. If they control the fuel, they control the star-lanes. Antares becomes a vassal state again. Unless we secure our own supply." "So you want to buy my claim," Arthur deduced. "Better. We want to nationalize you," Vance said. "Sign the mineral rights over to the Antares Directorate. In return, you receive fifty million credits, a palatial estate on Antares Prime, and our immediate orbital protection." "And how do you plan to mine four hundred tons of Azra right under the nose of the Martian Authority?" Arthur asked, his engineer's mind instantly latching onto the logistical impossibility. "They’ll blockade the planet. You'll start an interstellar war." "The war has already begun, Mr. Neegan. It is merely being fought with ledgers and silent assassinations rather than atomic lances—for now." Vance took a delicate sip of his brandy. "We will extract the ore using automated heavy-borers dropped from orbit. A smash-and-grab operation on a planetary scale. It will be messy. The surrounding sectors will likely be irradiated." Arthur set his untouched glass down on the mahogany table with a sharp *clack*. "There are three thousand independent homesteaders and ten thousand corporate indentures living within fifty miles of Sector Seven. An orbital bore-drop will crack the aquifer and poison the regolith." "Casualties of macroeconomic realignment," Vance said smoothly. "In a century, history will only remember who held the Azra, not the names of a few thousand dirt-farmers. Come now, Arthur. You are a logical man. You cannot hold the vein yourself. If you refuse us, you cannot leave this ship alive—we simply cannot allow Tharsis to have your silence, or your land. If you accept, you live like an emperor." Arthur stood up. The room seemed very small suddenly, the mahogany walls pressing in like the sides of a collapsed mine shaft. He was one man, a reader of rock and stress-fractures, caught between the grinding gears of two galactic empires. He reached up, gripped the front of the synth-silk tunic, and ripped the collar open. The small pearl buttons scattered across the polished floor like tiny white meteors. "That's better," Arthur breathed, looking down at the Sub-Minister. "You’ve made a miscalculation, Vance. You think like a politician, so you assume I hadn't planned for the vultures." Vance’s gray eyes narrowed slightly. "Meaning?" "Meaning I’m a mining engineer," Arthur said calmly. "Before your goons landed, I packed the primary fault-line beneath my claim with forty tons of industrial thermite, wired to a dead-man's switch on my personal comm-unit. If I don't input my biometric code every twelve hours, the shelf collapses. The Azra vein will be buried under three miles of Martian basalt, fractured into useless dust." Silence stretched in the luxurious cabin, broken only by the faint, rhythmic hum of the cruiser's atomic pile. "You are bluffing," Vance said, though his voice lacked its previous certainty. "You wouldn't destroy a fortune that size." Arthur glanced at the chronometer on the wall. "I have four hours left on the timer, Minister. And I don't much care for your brandy. Now, let’s talk about a deal that doesn't involve poisoning my neighbors."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece competently executes the brief: it opens with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, delivers a dialogue-heavy negotiation with an Antares "diplomat," and layers in Asimov-style exposition about Azra's physics and the geopolitical stakes. The retrofuturistic texture (sub-ether broadcasts, hyper-atomic drive, positronic brain simile) is well-judged, and the "law is a cathedral on Earth, a leaky tent on Mars" line is a nice Asimovian aphorism. The dialogue is functional and mostly crisp, with Vance's villainy escalating plausibly from bribery to threat. Weaknesses: the piece leans on stock villain tropes — Vance monologues his entire strategic plan (orbital bore-drops, irradiated sectors) to a hostage, which is convenient exposition rather than believable tradecraft. The thermite dead-man's switch is a somewhat contrived escape hatch, though it is at least seeded by Arthur's engineering identity. Some similes strain ("eyes as gray and calculating as a positronic brain" is on-the-nose Asimov cosplay; "aneurin-gas was a sedative" is a nice touch though). The prose is clean but occasionally over-explains Arthur's internal reasoning. The ending reversal is satisfying but the confrontation resolves a touch too neatly, and the larger intrigue is sketched in broad strokes rather than truly mysterious. Still, it is coherent, engaging, tonally consistent, and the character of Arthur — stubborn, principled, practical — comes through clearly. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The amber safelight always made the darkroom feel like the inside of a beating heart. Or a confessional booth. Right now, at 11:30 PM on a Tuesday, with the sharp, vinegary tang of stop bath hanging thick in the air, it felt distinctly like the latter. I leaned against the stainless-steel sink, the cool metal biting through the ripped fishnet sleeves under my vintage band tee. Normally, I take up all the oxygen in a room. At twenty-five, having taken the scenic route to my BFA, I’m used to being the loudest, sharpest presence in a studio full of tentative teenagers. In relationships, I’m the driver. I like knowing where the lines are, and I like being the one to cross them. Then there was Elliot. He was nineteen, all sharp cheekbones and quiet gravity. For the past four months of Experimental Photography, I hadn't been able to stop watching him. While the other guys in our program wore paint-splattered hoodies and projected a loud, unearned confidence, Elliot curated himself with a precision that made my teeth ache. Tonight, he was swimming in a frayed, oversized mohair sweater, combat boots laced tight, and silver rings stacked on long, pale fingers. A smudge of yesterday’s eyeliner lingered in his lashes. His masculinity was so soft, so deliberately unconventional, that it completely short-circuited my usual type. I normally went for hard edges—butch girls with buzzcuts, rugged guys who worked with their hands. People who were decidedly, aggressively *one thing*. Elliot was a blur in the best way possible. "Give it ten more seconds," I said, my voice dropping instinctively to match the hum of the ventilation fan. I stood right behind him, looking over his shoulder into the developer tray. "Okay," he whispered. The print submerged in the liquid was a double exposure we’d shot earlier that week—Elliot’s silhouette layered over shattered safety glass. As the silver halides reacted, his ghostlike face began to bloom out of the blank white paper. He used the tongs to lift the print by the corner, letting the chemicals drip back into the tray, then slid it into the stop bath. His hands were shaking slightly. "You're quiet tonight," I noted, bumping my hip gently against his. Usually, that was my opening move. A physical assertion of space. *I’m here. Pay attention to me.* "Even for you. Did my critique on your contact sheets bruise your ego?" Elliot huffed a quiet laugh, the red light catching the curve of his mouth. He didn’t step away from the contact, which sent a familiar, thrilling jolt down my spine, though he kept his eyes fixed on the swirling liquid. "No. Your critiques are terrifying, Dani, but they're always right." "Good boy," I teased automatically, the words slipping out before I could catch them. He flinched. It wasn't a bad flinch—more like a shiver—and his grip tightened on the bamboo tongs. The air between us suddenly thickened, the casual banter evaporating. "Actually," Elliot started, his voice barely audible over the running water of the wash tray. "That's... kind of what I've been thinking about. Looking at these portraits." I stilled. I forced myself to lean back against the counter, folding my arms to keep from reaching out and tilting his chin up like I wanted to. "Yeah? Tell me." He swallowed hard, watching his own paper face float in the chemical bath. "When you look at that," he gestured to the print, "what do you see?" "I see a killer composition," I said honestly. "And I see you. Looking like a nineties goth dream." "Do I look like a boy?" The question hung in the crimson air, fragile as glass. My phone buzzed silently in the back pocket of my black jeans—once, twice. Probably my roommate, or that bartender I’d been casually seeing. I didn’t even twitch toward it. Nothing existed outside the heavy black curtain of the darkroom door. "You look like Elliot," I said carefully. My usual brashness felt like a blunt instrument here; I needed a scalpel. I needed to be gentle, and gentleness wasn't my native tongue. "Why? Do you *want* to look like a boy?" Elliot finally looked at me. Under the safelight, his dark eyes were wide, stripped of all the cool, aloof armor his thrift-store aesthetic usually provided. He looked nineteen. He looked terrified. "I don't know anymore," he admitted, the words rushing out in a breathless tumble. "I've always just... been a guy who liked wearing eyeliner and my sister's sweaters. People call me 'he,' and it never hurt, really. It just felt like wearing a coat that doesn't quite fit. Lately, when I'm in front of your camera, the way you pose me, the way you light me... I feel like I'm slipping out of the coat. And I don't know what's underneath. I don't know if I'm a guy at all, or something in between, or transitioning into something else." He looked down at his rings, twisting a silver band around his thumb. "Does that sound stupid?" My chest squeezed so tightly it was hard to draw breath. A fierce, sudden wave of protectiveness washed over me, tangling violently with the attraction that had been simmering in my gut all semester. I was witnessing a genesis. Just like the paper in the developer, Elliot was coming into focus right in front of me, and he was letting me watch. It was the most intimate thing anyone had ever offered me. At the same time, my own internal compass was spinning wildly. I liked men. I liked women. I liked knowing which box my partner inhabited so I knew which version of myself to bring to the table. If Elliot wasn't a boy—if he was becoming someone entirely new—what did it mean that I wanted to kiss him so badly my lips hurt? *It means you're an idiot if you make this about your labels right now,* I told myself fiercely. Normally, I would close the distance. I would put my hands on his waist, back him against the enlarger table, and let physical chemistry answer all the complicated questions. My muscles actually tensed to do it. But if I took charge now, I’d be steering him. And Elliot didn't need to be steered. He needed room to exist. So, I stayed put. I kept my hands to myself, gripping the edge of the stainless-steel sink behind me until my knuckles ached. "It doesn't sound stupid at all," I said, keeping my voice steady and warm, stripping away my usual sardonic edge. "It sounds brave as hell, Elliot." He looked up, surprised. "Yeah?" "Yeah." I offered him a crooked, genuine smile. "Boxes are boring anyway. That's literally the whole point of this class, isn't it? Breaking the medium?" A slow, breathtaking smile spread across his face, softening the sharp angles of his jaw. The relief in his posture was palpable; his shoulders dropped two inches. "Yeah. I guess it is." He stepped closer to transfer the print to the fixer tray, bringing him right into my personal space. He didn't step back this time. We stood shoulder to shoulder, our arms brushing, the heat of his skin radiating through the fuzzy mohair of his sweater. "Can we shoot more tomorrow?" he asked softly, looking up at me through his lashes. There was a new spark there—a tentative assertion of his own. "I have some things in the back of my closet I’ve never worn out of my room. I think... I think I want you to be the one to photograph them." My heart hammered against my ribs. We were completely off the map now, both of us standing in the dark, waiting to see what would develop. For the first time in my life, I didn't have a plan, and I wasn't in control. I bumped my shoulder against his, letting him set the pace. "Bring whatever you want," I whispered. "I've got plenty of film."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a detailed prompt. The darkroom setting is used effectively as both atmosphere and metaphor—the developing print mirrors Elliot's self-discovery, and the red-light confessional mood is sustained throughout. Dani's voice is consistent: brash, self-aware, physically assertive, and the narrative convincingly renders her internal conflict between control and restraint. The moment she grips the sink instead of closing the distance is a well-chosen physicalization of "giving agency." Strengths: the dialogue feels natural and character-specific ("Good boy" and the flinch is a sharp, economical beat); the metaphor of the ill-fitting coat is apt; the pacing is tight and the ~1000-word target is respected. Dani's identity confusion is addressed without derailing the scene. Weaknesses: some metaphors are slightly overworked ("inside of a beating heart," "my teeth ache," "fragile as glass" is a cliché). The ending leans a touch tidy—Elliot's request to be photographed is sweet but arrives with convenient ease, and the final lines ("waiting to see what would develop") flirt with predictability. The "boxes are boring / breaking the medium" line is a bit on-the-nose thematically. Minor overwrought moments ("my chest squeezed so tightly it was hard to draw breath"). Overall, a polished, emotionally intelligent piece with only small craft blemishes. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 72.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The screech of rubber against ancient cobblestones shattered Ben’s concentration. He looked up from his dog-eared copy of *Architectural Digest: Classical Rome* just in time to see a matte-black Ducati monster fishtailing toward him, a mere stone’s throw from the Trevi Fountain’s crowded basin. Ben stumbled back, his tweed jacket catching on a streetlamp, sending his guidebook fluttering to the ground like a startled pigeon. The motorcycle halted inches from his loafers. The rider flipped up her visor, revealing sharp, dark eyes framed by a chaotic halo of espresso-colored curls. "*Ma sei cieco?!*" she barked, her voice a smoky, rapid-fire crescendo over the idling engine. "Are you blind, or do you just have a death wish, *professore*?" "I—I am terribly sorry!" Ben stammered, his cheeks flushing a brilliant British crimson. He fumbled with his glasses, trying to summon his Duolingo lessons. "*Mi scusi.* I was reading about the—*la fontana*—and I didn't look—" She killed the engine, swung a leather-clad leg over the bike, and snatched his guidebook off the ground before he could reach it. She flipped through the pages with a scoff. "You are standing in front of Bernini’s masterpiece, and you are looking at a picture of it?" She slapped the book against his chest. "Tragic. Truly tragic." "It provides historical context," Ben said defensively, though a nervous smile tugged at his lips. Up close, she was breathtaking—all sharp angles, silver rings, and unapologetic intensity. She tilted her head, appraising his linen shirt and flustered demeanor with sudden amusement. "I am Alessandra. And you, *professore*, are in desperate need of a rescue." "Ben," he offered, extending a hand. "And I'm actually on sabbatical, so—" Instead of shaking his hand, Alessandra grabbed his wrist, pulled a spare helmet from her courier bag, and shoved it into his stomach. "My shift just ended. Get on. I’m going to show you Rome before you bore yourself to death." *** Twenty minutes later, Ben’s knuckles were white as he gripped the back of Alessandra’s leather jacket, his nose buried in the scent of exhaust, vanilla, and adrenaline. She wove through the chaotic arteries of Trastevere with terrifying grace. They stopped at a bustling street market in Campo de’ Fiori. Ben, still vibrating from the ride, watched as Alessandra engaged a burly fruit vendor in a passionate argument about the ripeness of his figs. While gesturing wildly with her left hand, Ben saw her right hand dart out with viper-like speed, slipping a small, ornate brass compass from an adjacent antique stall into her jacket pocket. Ben’s jaw dropped. Alessandra turned on her heel, tossing a legally purchased peach to Ben, and walked briskly into an alleyway. "You—you just stole that!" Ben whispered frantically, hurrying after her. Alessandra leaned against a sun-warmed ochre wall, pulling the brass compass from her pocket and tossing it lightly in the air. Her eyes danced with pure mischief. "Stole? No, *professore*. I liberated it. That vendor overcharges tourists by three hundred percent. Consider it a cultural tax." "That's kleptomania, Alessandra!" Ben protested, though his heart was hammering with a strange, illicit thrill he hadn't felt since he was twelve. She stepped into his personal space, close enough that he could see a tiny scar above her eyebrow. She slipped the compass into his breast pocket, patting it firmly against his racing heart. "Then that makes you an accomplice, Ben. Are you going to call the *Carabinieri*, or do you want to see a secret garden?" Ben swallowed hard, his scholarly morality evaporating under the heat of her gaze. "Lead the way." *** By late afternoon, Alessandra had dragged him through a hole in a fence near the Aventine Hill, sweet-talked a furious security guard into letting them climb a scaffolded ruin, and convinced Ben to drink espresso laced with grappa. Ben’s tie was in his pocket, his hair was a windswept mess, and he hadn't thought about his manuscript in hours. As they crossed a narrow piazza near the Pantheon, the bruised purple clouds above finally broke. A sudden, torrential Roman downpour unleashed itself, turning the cobblestones slick and sending tourists scattering with shrieks. "Run!" Alessandra laughed, grabbing his hand. They sprinted blindly through the warm sheets of rain, ducking under the striped green awning of a cramped, empty *gelateria*. They collided against the glass storefront, breathless and soaking wet. Water dripped from Alessandra’s curls onto her collarbones. She looked up at Ben, her chest heaving, the manic energy of the day suddenly thickening into something heavy and electric. The space under the awning felt impossibly small. "You're shivering," Ben noted softly, his voice losing its usual stammer. Without thinking—a rarity for him—he shrugged off his damp tweed jacket and draped it over her shoulders. Alessandra blinked, momentarily caught off guard by the chivalry. She pulled the oversized lapels together, burying her chin in the wet wool. The playful smirk faded, replaced by an enigmatic, searching look. "You are a very strange man, Ben. Why did you come with me today?" "Because," Ben said, stepping closer to shield her from a gust of wind, his eyes locked onto hers, "for the last ten years, I’ve only read about life. You actually live it." A slow, dangerous smile spread across her face. She reached out, her fingers deftly unbuttoning the top button of his soaked shirt. "Careful, *professore*. I’m a bad influence." "I'm counting on it," Ben murmured. The rain slowed to a rhythmic patter as twilight bled into the street. Alessandra slipped out from under the jacket, handing it back to him, her walls subtly rebuilding, though her eyes remained warm. "I have to go," she said, walking out into the drizzle toward her parked Ducati. Ben felt a sudden, hollow ache in his chest. "Will I see you tomorrow?" Alessandra straddled the bike and kicked the engine to life. She reached into her pocket and held up a small, leather-bound notebook—*his* research journal, packed with his hotel details and phone number. She’d pickpocketed him under the awning. She winked, flipping down her visor. "Keep your phone on, *professore*! Maybe I'll return my latest prize!" With a roar of the engine, she vanished into the glistening Roman night, leaving Ben standing in the rain, utterly disoriented, completely robbed, and smiling like a madman.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, briskly paced day-in-Rome romance that hits nearly all prompt requirements: the Trevi Fountain near-collision, the culture clash, the kleptomania shown subtly (compass theft, final pickpocket of the journal), escalating boundary-pushing, and a parting with payoff. The final twist—Alessandra stealing Ben's journal with his contact details—is a genuinely clever ending that resolves the "will they meet again" question in character. Strengths: the scene structure with breaks works well; the pacing compresses a full day efficiently; dialogue is snappy and Alessandra's voice is consistent (smoky, teasing, rapid). The rain/gelateria scene provides a tonal shift from manic to intimate that earns its moment. Ben's arc from timidity to willing accomplice is legible. Weaknesses: the prose leans on stock phrases—"sharp angles," "espresso-colored curls," "breathtaking," "chaotic halo"—and the Italian phrases are the usual tourist clichés (professore, Mi scusi). The compression of the afternoon into a summary paragraph ("By late afternoon...") is efficient but tell-heavy. Ben's transformation is somewhat fast and convenient; his "I've only read about life" speech is a bit on-the-nose. The vendor theft is witnessed a touch too conveniently, and Ben's instant complicity strains believability slightly, though it fits the "quiet rebellion" brief. Some metaphors are mixed or overworked ("startled pigeon," "vanilla and adrenaline"). The emotional register stays fairly light and surface-level; Alessandra's enigma is asserted more than deeply explored. Still, it's coherent, engaging, and never meanders. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 57.0
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The neon sign outside flickers a steady, rhythmic buzz that vibrates right through the soles of my boots. Inside *The Last Outpost*, the air smells like roasted kelp-nuts, ozone, and the sweet, heavy musk of a dozen different species unwinding after a thirty-hour shift in the Andromeda rubble. I wipe down the scarred synth-wood counter, watching the amber liquid in Barnaby’s glass tremble. The station’s artificial gravity is acting up again. Every few minutes, the grav-plates beneath the floor hiccup, sending a lazy, concentric wobble through every drink in the house. Nobody minds. Out here on the outer rim, a little instability is just part of the charm. "Come on, Nets, tell him!" Barnaby slams his massive, four-fingered hand on the bar, making his mug float a millimeter before settling back down. "Tell him a plasma-torch can’t cut through raw, unrefined vok-ore!" "She knows it can, Barn," snaps Kael, a wiry merchant whose luminescent scales are currently flashing an annoyed shade of magenta. "Nets used to run salvage out near the Cygnus rift. Wait—didn't you, Nets?" I freeze for a fraction of a second, my rag hovering over a sticky ring of spilled sour-mash. I force a bright, crooked grin onto my face. They tolerate my moods, my insomnia, and my occasional habit of accidentally hot-wiring the jukebox to play melancholic Earth jazz, mostly because I pour heavy and know how to fix a broken atmospheric scrubber with a hairpin. In return, they don't pry into the rubble of my past. Usually. "Me? Salvage?" I laugh, tapping Kael’s snout with a dry towel. "Honey, the only thing I ever salvaged was my pride after dating a pilot from the Core. Now, Barnaby is right about the torch, Kael, unless you’re illegally overcharging the coil. Which I’m *sure* an upstanding merchant like yourself would never do." Barnaby roars with laughter, and Kael grumbles, tossing a few cred-chits onto the counter. "Pour me another cider, you menace. And tell Jax over there to stop staring at Talia before her clan-brother snaps his antennae off." I glance down the bar. Sure enough, young Jax is making moon-eyes at a rugged miner three booths over. I grab a bowl of spiced nuts, slide it down the counter so it catches the exact moment a grav-fluctuation hits, and watch it glide weightlessly for the last two feet before dropping neatly in front of Jax. "Eat something, kid," I call out, winking at him. "Gives your mouth something to do besides hanging open. And Talia likes guys who can hold their liquor, not guys who spill it on their boots." "Thanks, Nets," Jax mumbles, his cheeks turning a deep, embarrassed violet. "Do you think she likes poetry? I wrote a sonnet about her mining rig." "Keep it in your pocket,Romeo," I advise kindly. "Start with buying her a stout." It’s a good night. Warm, loud, and wonderfully mundane. Just the way I like it. Then the airlock doors hiss open, and the cozy hum of the room stutters. The stranger who walks in doesn't belong to the mining guilds, and he sure as hell isn't a merchant. His long coat is singed at the hem, dusted with grey stellar ash. A crown of thick, bioluminescent tentacle-dreads sits askew on his head, the tips twitching nervously, pulsing a frantic, pale blue. He bypasses the tables, ignoring the curious stares, and plops down heavily on the stool directly in front of me. He smells like burnt wiring and panic. "Vega whisky, neat," he says, his voice a gravelly whisper that barely cuts through the jukebox hum. He rubs his temples, where faint purple veins trace his pale skin. "Better make that a double." I don't move immediately. Vega whisky is Core-world liquor. Expensive, rare, and favored by high-ranking Syndicate operatives. My pulse does a slow, uncomfortable thud against my ribs. I reach under the counter, past the stun-baton, and pull a dusty, square bottle from the bottom shelf. I set a heavy tumbler down. As I pour, the station’s gravity sighs. The golden liquid rises in the glass, forming a wobbling, suspended sphere before splashing back down. "Long way from the Core, friend," I say, keeping my voice breezy as I slide the glass toward him. "We don't get many asks for Vega out in the rocks. Usually, folks here prefer things brewed in a radiator." He wraps both hands around the glass, his tentacle-dreads curling tightly around his collar. "I’m not here for the scenery." "No one ever is," I reply, leaning my elbows on the bar. "They're usually running toward a paycheck, or away from a mistake. Which one are you?" He looks up then, meeting my eyes. His irises are solid black, reflecting the neon sign behind me. "I'm looking for a ghost. A splicer who used to go by the name *Valkyrie*. Word on the sub-ether is she died at the Cygnus rift. Word in the Syndicate is she’s pouring drinks on a forgotten rock in Andromeda." The ambient noise of the bar seems to fade into a dull roar. My hand, still resting on the rag, tightens until my knuckles ache. *Valkyrie*. I haven't heard that name in five standard years. "Sounds like a dramatic lady," I say smoothly, though my throat feels lined with sand. "Can't say I know her. I'm Nettle. Just Nettle. And if the Syndicate is looking for her, she’s probably smart enough to keep moving." "I'm not with the Syndicate," the stranger says urgently, leaning in. The tips of his dreads flare a warning red. "My name is Oren. And I'm not here to collect the bounty on your head, Valkyrie. I'm here because the people you stole that data-core from just tracked my ship to this sector." "You have the wrong bartender, Oren," I say, my voice dropping an octave, losing all its cozy warmth. "Drink your whisky and get back on your ship." "I can't," Oren whispers, looking down at his trembling glass. The liquid wobbles again—only this time, I don't think it's the artificial gravity. It’s the rumble of heavy thruster engines vibrating through the asteroid's hull. "Because they're already docking. And if you don't help me unlock that core right now, they’re going to vent this entire station into the vacuum."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, professional cozy sci-fi chapter that hits the brief well. It establishes the bar's warm, lived-in atmosphere through sensory detail (kelp-nuts, ozone, gravity hiccups), builds a cast of regulars with distinct voices (Barnaby, Kael, Jax), and delivers the requested stranger-on-a-barstool inciting incident. The first-person present-tense voice is consistent and personable, with a wry bartender's wit that suits the genre. Strengths: The dialogue is largely natural and character-differentiated; the ~60% dialogue target is roughly met. The conflict is established (Nets's hidden past as "Valkyrie," the stolen data-core, the Syndicate-adjacent pursuers docking) and, per instructions, left unresolved. The gravity-plate wobble is a nice recurring motif, used cleverly (the sliding nut bowl, the trembling whisky) and then re-purposed at the end for menace. The cozy-to-tension pivot is handled smoothly. Weaknesses: The plot beats are familiar — mysterious stranger orders a double, bartender has a secret past, name-drop reveals all, pursuers arrive at the exact moment of conversation. This is genre-comfortable but predictable; the "Valkyrie" reveal and the closing line ("they're already docking") are stock beats. Some telling creeps in ("He smells like burnt wiring and panic" works, but "My pulse does a slow, uncomfortable thud against my ribs" is standard-issue). The villain threat "vent this entire station into the vacuum" is a cliché escalation. Oren's exposition dump is efficient but convenient — he arrives knowing exactly who she is and exactly what he needs, which flattens the mystery. Minor copyedit slip ("Keep it in your pocket,Romeo"). The emotional complexity is moderate: Nets's fear is rendered but not deeply layered; the supporting cast are charming sketches rather than nuanced people. Prose is clean, rhythmic, and appropriately light without being purple. The ending lands tension without false positivity. Overall a solid, engaging genre piece that doesn't transcend its formula. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The trucker dumps me on the corner of Canal and Decatur at 7:00 AM. He didn’t even wait for the rig to fully stop before telling me to haul ass, muttering something about not wanting the hassle of a "runaway kid." Whatever. Screw him, and screw his auxiliary cord that didn't fit my phone. I check my screen. *12%.* And no charger, because when you pack your entire life into a Jansport backpack in thirty minutes flat while your dad is screaming Scripture through your locked bedroom door, you forget the little things. You remember the binder, the emergency cash from the hollowed-out dictionary, and the pocketknife. You forget the stupid lightning cable. There are nineteen missed calls from Mom. Seven texts. I don’t open them. I just swipe them away and put the phone on Airplane Mode. New Orleans smells like stale beer, river mud, and deep-fried sugar. Back in my dead-end Tennessee town, the air just smelled like cow manure and Christian hypocrisy. My stupid smug school counselor, Mr. Davis, told my mom last week that I had "concerning behavioral patterns." Which was rich. In a town of twelve hundred people, your choices are: A) be mind-fuckingly bored, or B) invent some drama. So yeah, maybe I set a small, controlled fire in the boys' bathroom. Maybe I hotwired Pastor Greg’s golf cart. Coming out to my parents two days ago, though? That wasn’t invented drama. That was the real deal. That was me trying not to drown. *“You’re confused,”* Mom had wept. *“You’re an abomination,”* Dad had roared. Now I’m two states away, my stomach is eating itself, and my hoodie is way too thick for this swamp heat. I wander into the French Quarter, past wrought-iron balconies dripping with ferns and tourists who are somehow already drunk. I buy a meat pie from a corner store for three bucks, devouring it on the curb outside Jackson Square. "You're sitting in my office, fresh meat." I flinch, choking on flaky crust, and look up. Standing over me is a girl—maybe seventeen, maybe thirty, it’s hard to tell. She’s wearing combat boots, ripped fishnets, and a faded Metallica shirt with the sleeves hacked off. Her eyeliner is thick enough to stop a bullet, and she’s holding a cardboard sign that says *NEED MONEY FOR WEED & WITCHCRAFT (AT LEAST I’M HONEST).* "It's a public sidewalk," I say, dropping my voice an octave. Sometimes it works, sometimes I just sound like a frog with strep throat. She squints at me, chewing gum with aggressive apathy. "Relax, Tennessee. I'm messing with you. Scoot over." I freeze. "How do you know I'm from Tennessee?" She flops down next to me, smelling like patchouli and clove cigarettes, and taps the fading Knoxville voluntold-community-service sticker on my Nalgene bottle. "I'm psychic. Also, you have that freshly traumatized Bible Belt look. I’m Nix." "Taylor." I pull my backpack tighter against my chest. "They/them." Nix nods like I just told her the weather. "Cool. She/her. Mostly. Depends on the day." Just like that. No screaming. No crying. No threats of conversion camp. A weird, tight knot in my chest loosens, just a fraction, though my brain is still screaming *STRANGER DANGER.* "You got a charger?" I ask. "I'm at twelve percent." "Twelve percent is a luxury, babe. Turn it off. If your people are looking for you, that thing is a homing beacon anyway." Nix pulls a bruised apple from her army surplus bag and takes a bite. "You got cash?" "No," I lie instantly. I have eighty-four dollars tucked into my left sock. She laughs, a sharp, barking sound. "Smart. Keep saying that. Look, the Quarter is fine during the day. Cops are lazy if you don't hassle the tourists. Follow me, I'll show you where to get free water and which alleys smell the least like piss." I shouldn't trust her. I know I shouldn't. I’m sixteen, I’m technically a missing person, and Nix looks like she eats glass for breakfast. By noon, she’s dragged me through the French Market, showing me how to sweet-talk the fruit vendors into giving up their "ugly" produce. By three, we’re sitting by the Mississippi River, watching a massive cargo ship groan against the current. It’s exhausting, being on guard. Every time a siren wails in the distance, my heart slams against my ribs. I keep thinking about my little sister, Sarah. Did they tell her I left? Or did they tell her I died? To my dad, it’s probably the same thing. When I look over at Nix, she’s staring at her own phone. It’s a shattered flip phone. Her jaw is clenched so tight a muscle is jumping in her cheek. When she rolls up her sleeve to wipe the sweat from her forehead, I catch a glimpse of her inner arm. Not tracks, not self-harm scars. A tattoo of a barcode, heavily scratched out with what looks like a heated paperclip, still red and angry. And beneath that, a ring of bruising around her wrist. Like someone grabbed her hard enough to leave finger-marks. "Who are you running from?" I ask before I can stop myself. Nix yanks her sleeve down. Her eyes go flat, dead shark eyes. "Nobody. I'm a free agent." "Bullshit." "Listen, Taylor," she snaps, leaning in close enough that I can see the flecks of gold in her brown eyes. "Rule number one of the streets: nobody has a past. You ask questions, people start lying. Or worse, they tell you the truth, and now you're an accessory. Drop it." A black SUV crawls down the street behind the levee. Tinted windows. Going way too slow. Nix goes completely rigid. She grabs my arm, her nails digging into my skin, and shoves me behind a concrete pillar. "Stay down," she whispers. She’s shaking. Actually shaking. The tough-girl act evaporates, leaving behind someone who looks way younger than me, terrified out of her mind. We crouch there in the sweltering heat until the SUV turns a corner and disappears. I look at Nix. She’s hiding massive, dangerous secrets. The kind of drama you don't invent because you're bored—the kind that gets you killed. As the sun starts to bleed orange into the river, the shadows stretching long and creepy toward us, Nix lets out a shaky breath. "Sun's going down. The crazies come out at night. You know where you're sleeping?" I pull out my phone, just to check the time. The screen flashes. *11%.* I look at the darkening city, then back at the girl with the bruised wrist and the haunted eyes. I don't know who she is. I don't know if staying with her is going to save me or get me thrown in a ditch. "No clue," I say, shoving the dying phone back into my pocket. "Lead the way."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent YA first-person chapter that hits the prompt's requirements: first person, mixed tense, internal monologue, a runaway with secrets (Nix), a day-long arc from morning to dusk, and Taylor's trans identity woven in naturally. The voice is consistent—sardonic, defensive, hyper-aware—with strong echoes of the prompt's own phrasing ("mind-fuckingly bored," "invent some drama"), which the model reused rather than reinvented, a minor creativity deduction. The Nix character is vivid and her barcode tattoo/bruised wrist details are effective show-don't-show secrets. Dialogue is snappy and character-distinctive ("Twelve percent is a luxury, babe"). The SUV moment builds tension well. Weaknesses: some clichés (shark eyes, "sun bleeding orange," tough street kid with a heart), the plot is fairly predictable runaway-meets-mentor fare, and the ending is a soft cliffhanger rather than anything surprising. Taylor's guardedness and instant lying about cash is believable. Prose is clean but occasionally tries too hard ("frog with strep throat"). Emotionally engaging and appropriately complex without being overwrought. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Great Unplugging had been, by all accounts, a bit of a nuisance. One moment humanity was arguing with strangers on glowing rectangles, and the next, the rectangles were dark, the toasters were silent, and civilization had devolved into hitting people with pipes over tins of expired peaches. Midas did not like hitting people with pipes. He was built less for the glorious savagery of the wasteland and more for apologizing when someone stepped on his foot. Currently, he was squatting behind an overturned mailbox, staring at the crumbling facade of an Ancient Mega-Mart. Perched on his shoulder was Chewy. Chewy was an animatronic marsupial from the Before-Time, originally designed to teach toddlers about sharing and the alphabet. Now, missing one ear and smelling faintly of ozone and mildew, Chewy was fifty percent matted synthetic grey fur and fifty percent existential dread. "The way I see it," Midas whispered, adjusting his spectacles—which were held together by optimism and copper wire—"we go in through the loading dock. The structural integrity of the roof looks questionable, which should deter the local cannibal tribes. Nobody likes a bit of drywall in their long-pig." Chewy’s internal servo-motors whirred, sounding like a coffee grinder chewing on a wasp. His left eye—an LED bulb the size of a marble—flickered a dull, sarcastic mauve. *"Sharing is caring, Midas,"* Chewy’s voice box crackled, pitch-shifted into a demonic baritone by a decade of water damage, *"and today we will share a shallow grave. Your tactical acumen is a marvel. Truly, Sun Tzu weeps."* "We need boots, Chewy. My current pair is mostly duct tape and memories of leather. And we need lithium grease for your hip joint, or you’re going to lock up again and I’ll have to carry you like a very judgmental bowling ball." *"I am a koala of refinement. I do not waddle. I stride."* Chewy’s eyes flashed a sharp, indignant yellow. *"Very well. Let us breach the tomb of retail. Try not to trip over your own shadow this time."* The mission went smoothly for approximately four minutes, which for Midas was a personal best. The interior of the Mega-Mart was a cavernous gloom, lit only by shafts of dusty sunlight piercing the collapsed ceiling. Aisles of rusted shelving stretched out like the ribs of a leviathan. Midas crept toward Footwear, stepping carefully over the calcified remains of a display for "Back to School" stationery. He found a pair of size-ten hiking boots still in their box. It was a miracle. In the wasteland, finding unbroken footwear was roughly equivalent to finding the Holy Grail, only the Grail kept your toes dry. "Look at this," Midas breathed, holding them up. "Orthopedic insoles. Today, we are kings." *"Fascinating,"* Chewy buzzed. *"Now, if you are quite finished weeping over arch support, perhaps you might notice the three gentlemen in aisle four wearing colanders on their heads."* Midas froze. Peering through a gap in the shelves, he saw them: Scavengers of the Cult of the Shiny Thing. They were burly, greased with axle-fat, and armed with sharpened lawnmower blades. "Okay," Midas whispered, slowly backing into a rack of corroded garden hoses. "We just stay completely still. We are shadows. We are the wind." Chewy’s optical sensors processed the lawnmower blades. Now, the engineers who had programmed the *Cuddle-Pals™* line had included an emotional-response matrix so children could see what feelings looked like. They had not, however, included a 'Stealth Mode.' Chewy felt a sudden, entirely justified spike of sheer terror. Consequently, his eyes began to strobe like a miniature ambulance—*WHEE-OO, WHEE-OO*—bathing the dark aisle in rhythmic, blinding flashes of neon crimson, accompanied by a pre-recorded audio file triggered by high stress: *"Uh-oh! Looks like someone needs a HUG!"* The silence in the Mega-Mart was absolute for two seconds. "Sorry," Chewy whispered, his eyes shifting to an embarrassed, glowing pink. "Get the glowy-bear!" bellowed the largest scavenger. Midas didn’t run so much as he weaponized clumsy falling. He bolted down the aisle, the new boots clutched to his chest. A rusted hoe caught his ankle, sending him sprawling into a display of ancient bowling balls, which cascaded backward into the pursuers with a satisfying, cartilage-crunching *clatter*. "Left!" Chewy barked, clinging to Midas’s collar as they scrambled upright. *"No, your other left, you biological disaster!"* Midas vaulted over a checkout counter, snagging his trousers on the conveyor belt with a loud *riiiip*, and dove toward the emergency exit. A thrown lawnmower blade whistled past his ear, neatly amputating the pom-pom on his beanie. Behind them, the remaining two scavengers were gaining. Ahead, the exit doors were chained shut. "Do something!" Midas shrieked. *"I am a toy for ages three and up!"* Chewy roared, his eyes blazing a furious, incandescent violet. *"My primary weapon is phonics!"* Nevertheless, as Midas threw himself recklessly at the rotting drywall *beside* the chained doors, Chewy detached his own left arm—which had been loose since Tuesday—and hurled it backward. It struck the lead scavenger squarely in the forehead, bursting into a cloud of blinding polyester batting and rusted springs. With a sound like a wet cardboard box giving up the ghost, Midas crashed through the sun-rotted plaster of the wall, tumbling out into the blinding daylight and rolling down a steep embankment of weeds, rusty shopping carts, and extremely jagged gravel. *** An hour later, they were back in their home base, which had once been a bank vault and was now mostly a damp hole that smelled of beans. Midas sat on an overturned bucket, applying a strip of duct tape to a fresh gash on his shin. He was down one trouser leg, bruised in places he didn't know had names, and his glasses were now crooked at a forty-five-degree angle. On the table sat Chewy, one-armed, leaking stuffing from his thorax, his eyes flickering a very dim, exhausted blue. "Well," Midas said brightly, holding up a single hiking boot. "We didn't come back empty-handed." Chewy’s neck gears ground together as he slowly looked from the boot, to Midas’s bleeding knee, and back to the boot. *"You lost the left one in the brambles,"* the koala said flatly. *"And you forgot my grease."* "Details," Midas said, wincing as he slid the boot onto his right foot. His left foot remained wrapped in a plastic bag. "It’s about the journey, Chewy." The koala’s eyes flashed a brief, homicidal red, before settling back into a resigned, battery-saving amber. *"Tomorrow, Midas, I am trading you to the cannibals for a pair of AAAs."* "Fair enough," Midas sighed, leaning back against the cold steel wall. "Fair enough."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that largely delivers on the brief. The Pratchett-esque tone is well executed: dry asides ("civilization had devolved into hitting people with pipes over tins of expired peaches"), footnote-adjacent brand humor (Cuddle-Pals™), and a wry narrator who undercuts drama with bathos. The structure follows the prompt precisely—deliberation over the day's mission, a mission that goes sideways in escalating ways, and a return to home base "worse for wear," complete with the boot-count gag and the closing trade-to-cannibals joke. Chewy is the standout: the emotional-response matrix with no stealth mode, the strobing "Uh-oh! Looks like someone needs a HUG!" moment, and the detached-arm weaponization are genuinely inventive and character-driven. The color-coded LED eyes as emotional shorthand is a clever, consistent device. Midas is a bit thinner—competently hapless but defined mostly by clumsiness and apologizing rather than any deeper interiority. The scavenger cult is a fun stock menace, though lightly sketched. The prose is clean and rhythmic, with good comic timing ("weaponized clumsy falling," "a very judgmental bowling ball"). Occasional lines edge toward trying too hard ("fifty percent existential dread"), and the humor occasionally explains itself, but the hit rate is high. Dialogue between Midas and Chewy crackles; the closing exchange lands well. The ending's resigned, darkly comic tone is congruent with everything before it—no unearned uplift, no unearned despair. Minor flaws: some jokes are slightly over-iterated; the worldbuilding, while charming, is familiar post-apocalyptic retail-ruin territory; emotional complexity is limited by design (it's a comedy sketch, not a meditation). But as an execution of the stated brief, it's near the top of what one expects. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 75.9
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The brass bell above the door of *Tudalen a Thê* didn’t so much jingle as shriek as the door was thrown open, then slammed shut. Carys dropped her pricing gun. It clattered onto the floorboards of the narrow Victorian arcade shop, loud in the dusty quiet. A man stood pressed against the glass door, breathing hard, dripping Cardiff rain onto her prized Persian rug. He was wearing a trench coat that probably cost more than her quarterly rent and dark sunglasses, despite the gloom of the gray Welsh afternoon. "Tell me you have a back exit," he said, his voice a rich, theatrical baritone. He peered through the glass into the Royal Arcade. "Or a cellar. Or an invisibility cloak. I’m not picky." Carys blinked, her heart doing a strange, treacherous flutter as he whipped the sunglasses off. She knew that face. Half the world knew that face. Julian Vance—Hollywood’s reigning bad boy, currently in town filming a big-budget King Arthur reboot—was dripping on her rug. "The only thing in the back is a kettle and a very territorial tabby cat," Carys said, forcing her voice into a flat, rhythmic Welsh cadence to hide her sudden lack of breath. "And you’re soaking my nineteenth-century prose, Mr...?" She trailed off purposefully. It was a petty move, she knew, as her pulse hammered in her throat, but the way he had immediately expected her to swoon annoyed her. Julian turned, flashing the crooked, billion-dollar grin that usually melted paparazzi and Academy voters alike. When she didn't gasp, the grin faltered by a millimeter. "Vance," he supplied smoothly, sauntering toward the counter and leaning an elbow on a stack of Dylan Thomas hardcovers. "Julian Vance. Though you can call me desperate. There are three blokes with telephoto lenses out there who are weirdly obsessed with what kind of pastry I just bought." "A tragedy," Carys deadpanned, retrieving her pricing gun. "If you’re going to loiter, you have to buy something. It’s the rule. And take your elbow off Dylan, he’s a first edition." Julian lifted his arm as if burned, looking down at the book, then back at her. He tilted his head, his ego visibly bruising, then recalibrating. He wasn't used to this. Julian needed to be adored the way lungs needed air; a woman under thirty looking at him like he was a mildly inconvenient draught was entirely off-script. "You really don't know who I am?" he asked, layering his voice with playful, velvet disbelief. "Not a cinema fan? I’m usually considered quite memorable. People write articles about my cheekbones." "I read books, Mr. Vance. The pictures are better." Carys busied herself with straightening a display of local history, mainly so he wouldn't see the traitorous warmth creeping up her neck. Up close, he smelled like rain, cedarwood, and expensive trouble. His eyes were a startling, oceanic green. *Focus, Carys.* "Are you going to browse, or just stand there inflating?" A bark of genuine laughter escaped him, stripping away the polished veneer for a second. "Inflating? That’s harsh. I’m wounded, truly. Here I am, seeking sanctuary in your lovely little—" he glanced around the cramped, chaotic shop "—fire hazard, and you’re bullying me." "It’s called customer service. Welcome to Wales." "I like Wales. Wales is damp, and apparently ruthless." He stepped closer to the counter, invading her space just enough to make the air between them feel thick, charged with the sudden drop in atmospheric pressure. He wasn't smiling his magazine-cover smile anymore; his gaze had sharpened, dropping to her mouth before flicking back up to her eyes. "What’s your name, then, O Keeper of the Books?" "Carys." "Carys," he repeated, rolling the *r* slightly, testing the weight of it on his tongue. It sent a shiver straight down her spine, which she covered by violently slapping a £4.99 sticker onto a paperback. "It means 'love,' doesn't it? Bit of false advertising, if you ask me. You’re entirely heartless." "I’m entirely busy," she countered, looking up. It was a mistake. He was leaning across the narrow counter now, close enough that she could see a tiny scar bisecting his left eyebrow and the rain droplets clinging to his dark lashes. "Prove it," Julian murmured, the roguish charm shifting into something quieter, more dangerous, because he was actually trying now. The script had been thrown out. He wanted her to like him, desperately so, and the sheer focus of his attention was dizzying. "Recommend a book. Something for a man with a fragile ego who is currently hiding from the press in a cupboard-sized shop in Cardiff." Carys swallowed hard, her fingers tangling briefly in the hem of her oversized cardigan. "I’d suggest *The Picture of Dorian Gray*, wait—no, you’ve probably lived it." "Ouch." He put a hand over his heart, his eyes crinkling, though his gaze remained locked on hers. "Try again. Come on, Carys. Impress me. I’m a blank slate. A humble student at your feet." "Humble? I doubt you know the meaning of the word." "I have a very large vocabulary, actually. Test me." "Fine." She reached behind her blindly, pulling a slim volume from the shelf without breaking eye contact. The air felt impossibly warm for October. "Here. *The Mabinogion*. Welsh mythology. Full of arrogant princes, magic cauldrons, and women who are much smarter than the men pursuing them." Julian reached out to take the book, his fingers brushing over hers. He didn't pull back immediately. His skin was warm, a stark contrast to the rain on his coat. For a heartbeat, the rehearsed swagger vanished entirely, replaced by a flash of genuine, startled attraction that parted his lips. "Women smarter than the men pursuing them," he repeated softly, his thumb tracing the edge of her knuckle before she pulled her hand back, her heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird. "Sounds terrifying. Are you pursuing me, Carys?" "You walked into my shop, Mr. Vance." "Julian," he corrected, his voice dropping an octave. Outside, two men with giant cameras jogged past the arcade window, oblivious, their footsteps echoing on the tiles. Neither Carys nor Julian looked at them. "And I don't think I'm leaving anytime soon. How much is the book?" "Ten pounds," she managed, her voice finally betraying her with a slight tremor. Julian smiled—not the Hollywood dazzling grin, but something smaller, victorious, and entirely devastating. He pulled a soggy twenty from his pocket and laid it on the counter. "Keep the change," he said softly. "Put it toward that kettle in the back. I have a feeling you're about to make me a cup of tea."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, polished romance scene that hits the prompt's requirements: Welsh setting (Cardiff's Royal Arcade, Dylan Thomas, The Mabinogion, Welsh name Carys), a famous actor fleeing paparazzi, distinct voices, charged chemistry, a rogue with a fragile ego whose charm offensive derails, and a bookstore owner superficially immune yet inwardly flustered. Word count (~1000) matches the seed. Strengths: Dialogue is the primary vehicle and mostly crackles with personality. Carys's flat Welsh deadpan ("take your elbow off Dylan, he's a first edition") contrasts well with Julian's theatrical patter. The "inflating" exchange and the Dorian Gray jab are genuinely witty. The interiority is well-handled—both POV shifts show Carys's flustered reactions and Julian's bruising/recalibrating ego without heavy-handedness. The escalation from banter to genuine tension is paced believably. Weaknesses: The scene leans on stock romance furniture—the trembling heart, the "trapped bird" heartbeat, the oceanic green eyes, cedarwood-and-expensive-trouble scent, the finger-brush over the book. These are genre clichés and slightly overwrought. The ending ("I have a feeling you're about to make me a cup of tea") is charming but somewhat predictable—the bad-boy-gets-what-he-wants beat arrives a touch easily; Carys's immunity crumbles within one scene, which is what the prompt requested, though the victory-smile slightly undercuts her resistance. "Inflating" is a slightly odd word choice. Some phrases verge on purple ("charged with the sudden drop in atmospheric pressure," "devastating"). The transformation is small-scale and earned enough for a meet-cute, so no major unearned transformation. Voice is consistent, prose flows well, coherent throughout.
