+ Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7841 **Object Class:** Euclid (Provisional) **Special Containment Procedures:** As SCP-7841 is localized entirely around my person, I, Senior Researcher Arthur Vance, am currently confined to Psychological Observation Cell 4 at Site-19. All stationery, writing implements, and digital devices have been removed from my quarters, save for the terminal used to compile this report. Security personnel are to search my cell every four hours for newly manifested instances of SCP-7841-A. **Description:** SCP-7841 is an ongoing phenomenon in which handwritten notes—designated SCP-7841-A—manifest in my immediate vicinity. The handwriting has been verified by Foundation graphologists as a 99.4% match to my own, albeit exhibiting severe degradation consistent with extreme muscular tension, exhaustion, or neurological trauma. The contents of SCP-7841-A purport to be warnings from a future iteration of myself, detailing an imminent, catastrophic containment breach at Site-19. However, the timeline and reality described in these notes increasingly diverge from baseline consensus. Forensic analysis of the paper shows it to be standard Foundation-issue 80gsm stock. However, the ink has baffled the materials lab. It does not match any commercially available or Foundation-manufactured pen. Mass spectrometry revealed a suspension of carbon black, iron gall, trace amounts of temporal-spatial tachyonic residue, and a biological binder matching my own hemoglobin, though heavily mutated by unknown ionizing radiation. **Discovery and Personal Log:** The first note appeared on October 12th. I found it tucked inside my ID badge holder when I arrived at my office. > **SCP-7841-A1:** > *Arthur. Do not approve the maintenance cycle for Sector 4 on the 19th. The coolant lines are already compromised. It’s waiting for the pressure drop. Listen to me. I am you. Look at how I cross the 't' in 'maintenance'. Only we do that.* I assumed it was a prank by Junior Researcher Meyers, though the handwriting made my stomach turn. It was unmistakably mine. Following protocol for potential memetic or cognitohazardous tampering, I reported it to Site Director Hayes. Hayes ordered an immediate inspection of the Sector 4 coolant lines. They were pristine. Two days later, I woke up with the second note stuck to the inside of my watch face. > **SCP-7841-A2:** > *You told Hayes. Why did you tell Hayes? The inspection moved the timeline up. The seals are rotting from the inside out. Don't trust the sensors, they’re reading a loop from last Tuesday. Get out of the facility before the 17th.* I was placed in quarantine after submitting A2. The prevailing theory among the Temporal Anomalies Department was that I was experiencing a localized chronal displacement loop. However, the Counter-Conceptual Division argued that I was being psychologically manipulated by SCP-████, a telepathic entity housed in Sector 4 known for inducing severe paranoia in research staff. They ran me through a battery of cognitive resistance tests. My CRV score was normal, yet I began to doubt my own senses. When I looked in the mirror, I caught myself staring at my right hand, waiting for it to twitch and start scribbling warnings I couldn't remember writing. I didn't feel compromised, which, as any Foundation psychiatrist will tell you, is the primary symptom of being compromised. The third note manifested inside my sealed ration pack on October 15th. The handwriting was jagged, the ink bleeding heavily through the fibers. > **SCP-7841-A3:** > *They put you in Cell 4. Good. The walls are reinforced, it might buy you an hour when the sky turns inside out. Don't let Dr. Vance in. He died in 2018 during the Berlin incident. Whatever is wearing his skin is the thing that opens the doors. Check the rosters. CHECK THE ROSTERS.* This was the turning point for the investigation. Firstly, *I* am Dr. Vance. Secondly, there was no "Berlin incident" in 2018. When I brought this up to my evaluator, Dr. Aris Thorne, he suggested that the anomaly was attempting to induce a dissociative fugue state to force me into breaching containment myself. "If it convinces you that you aren't real," Dr. Thorne told me through the intercom, "you'll do anything to prove you exist. Even open a few doors." It made clinical sense. It was comforting. I chose to believe Thorne. I had to. If the notes were truly from the future, then reality itself was fracturing, because I certainly didn't die six years ago. Then came the fourth note, found moments ago. I didn't find it in my pocket, or under my pillow. I coughed it up. It was rolled into a tight cylinder, coated in bile and that strange, irradiated blood-ink. > **SCP-7841-A4:** > *IT'S NOT IN SECTOR 4. IT'S IN THE WORDS. STOP READING THEM. Every time you process the syntax, it overwrites the baseline. You aren't Arthur. I am Arthur. You are the containment breach. Thorne isn't real, Site-19 doesn't have a Psychological Wing, it was burned down in the eighties! Stop typing the report! The report is the door!* My hands are shaking as I transcribe this into the terminal. I called for Dr. Thorne on the intercom twenty minutes ago. Nobody answered. In fact, the intercom panel looks strange now that I'm really looking at it. The metal is rusted, fused into the concrete as if it hasn't been used in decades. I looked down at my fingers a moment ago. Beneath my fingernails, there is dried, black fluid. It smells like iron and ozone. My right hand cramps terribly, aching with the phantom memory of gripping a pen I don't possess, pressing down so hard the nib snapped. If this is a psychological attack, it is absolute. I can no longer tell if I am the researcher trapped in a cell, or the anomaly trying to get out. The ink analysis came back an hour ago on my terminal, right before the intranet connection died. The biological binder in the ink isn't just my blood. The cellular degradation indicates the blood belongs to a corpse that has been dead for six years. I hear the coolant lines hissing behind the walls. I need to find a piece of paper. I need to warn myself not to read this.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong SCP-format piece that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements: a researcher receiving increasingly desperate notes from a "future self," Foundation investigation into temporal anomaly vs. psychological manipulation, and a genuine erosion of the narrator's trust in their own perception. The format is well-executed—containment procedures, item designations, and forensic ink analysis all feel authentically Foundation-flavored, and the first-person past-tense framing with interspersed notes is handled cleanly. The escalation across the four notes is well-constructed. A1 is plausible and specific (the crossed 't' detail is a nice touch of intimacy); A2 introduces contradiction and paranoia; A3 breaks reality ("Dr. Vance died in 2018"); A4 goes fully incoherent and meta-textual ("The report is the door"). The competing institutional theories (Temporal Anomalies vs. Counter-Conceptual Division) give the "actual anomaly or manipulation?" question real texture rather than hand-waving it. The ending is the piece's chief strength and weakness. The final note's meta-turn—claiming the report itself is the breach mechanism—is a genuinely unsettling twist, and the physical evidence (coughing up the note, dead-for-six-years blood, rusted intercom) escalates dread effectively. However, the "you are the anomaly / reality is fracturing" reveal is a familiar move in this genre, and the piece leans on it somewhat predictably. The Thorne dialogue is functional but a bit expository ("If it convinces you that you aren't real... you'll do anything to prove you exist")—competent, though it telegraphs the theme rather than embodying it. Minor quibbles: the "99.4% handwriting match" precision is charmingly bureaucratic but slightly cute; the ink analysis (tachyonic residue) tips toward over-explanation of the mystery; and the pacing compresses the psychological deterioration quickly, though the word limit justifies this. The prose is controlled, appropriately clinical when needed, and the voice stays consistent between the report framing and the narrator's unraveling. The final line—"I need to warn myself not to read this"—lands as a satisfying recursive loop. Overall: a polished, engaging, genre-aware piece with a few familiar beats but excellent execution. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7812 **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** Foundation web-crawlers are to monitor urban exploration forums for references to anachronistic doors in abandoned structures. Discovered instances of SCP-7812-A are to be sealed behind reinforced concrete and guarded by stationary task forces under the guise of structural condemnation. Exploration of SCP-7812-B is currently suspended by order of the O5 Council, though unauthorized entries remain an ongoing security concern. **Description:** SCP-7812-A designates a series of identical, unmarked steel doors appearing spontaneously within abandoned buildings worldwide. Notably, SCP-7812-A instances universally exhibit severe weathering—including oxidized iron hinges, pitting, and strata of hardened, unidentified silt—that predates the host structure by centuries. For example, SCP-7812-A-44 manifested inside a commercial warehouse built in 1998, yet carbon dating of the door’s organic residue indicates an age exceeding 4,000 years. Opening any SCP-7812-A instance provides access to SCP-7812-B: an extradimensional, architecturally impossible archive. SCP-7812-B consists of a non-Euclidean labyrinth of brutalist concrete tiers, towering filing cabinets, and suspended catwalks extending infinitely in all directions. Gravity remains oriented toward the nearest floor surface, allowing perpendicular verticality where shelves intersect at ninety-degree angles in open air. The documents housed within SCP-7812-B are printed on a durable, polymer-like paper. Linguistic analysis reveals the text to be an archaic precursor to modern English, mixed with standardized bureaucratic ciphering. These records detail a previous, technologically advanced global civilization destroyed by an unspecified event referred to only as the "Primary Containment Cascade." **Exploration Log 7812-B-09 (Third-Person Perspective)** Mobile Task Force Eta-12 ("Paper Pushers")—consisting of Captain Vance, Specialist Lin, and Researcher Dr. Aris Thorne—entered SCP-7812-B through an instance in an abandoned textile mill in Łódź, Poland. The air inside the archive smelled of ozone and ancient dust. Behind them, the steel door stood freestanding in the middle of a vast, dimly lit concourse of slate-gray shelving that stretched upward until swallowed by a murky ceiling haze. "Tether is secure," Lin reported, clipping their reinforced fiber-optic line to the doorframe. Dr. Thorne immediately approached the nearest shelf, pulling a thick, lead-bound ledger from the rack. He blew a layer of gray powder from the cover. "The seal on the binding... Vance, look at this." Vance shone his tactical light onto the embossed emblem. It was a circle enclosing three arrows pointing inward, though the geometry was subtly angular, surrounded by the words *THE AEGIS DIRECTORATE: TO BIND, TO BURY, TO BLIND.* "Looks like a knock-off," Vance muttered. "Or a draft," Thorne replied, paging through the brittle sheets. "Listen to this excerpt. It’s an incident report." > **Document Excerpt 7812- Alpha:** > *Cycle 884.9. The Seventh Seal of the Abyssal Bore has degraded beyond algorithmic repair. Directorate Overseers have authorized Protocol Tabula Rasa. If the Bore breaches, conceptual integrity of the lithosphere will fail. The Aegis has failed. We leave these tallies for the soil that follows.* They pressed deeper into the archive, descending a spiral staircase that wound around a central pillar of black marble. Two hours into the trek, Thorne halted before a wall of personnel microfiche drawers labeled *ACTIVE RESEARCH STAFF – SECTOR PRIME.* Pulling a drawer open at random, Thorne extracted a laminated dossier. His breath hitched. Clip-attached to the top corner was a faded monochrome photograph of himself. "What is it, Doc?" Lin asked, stepping closer. "It's me," Thorne whispered. His fingers trembled as he traced the text. "Name: Aris Thorne. Clearance: Tier 4. Assignment: Temporal Echo Mitigation. Date of Birth... Vance, the date here translates to roughly 1,400 years ago. It says I was terminated during the Cascade for 'insubordinate preservation of data.'" Lin began ripping open adjacent drawers. Within minutes, she produced files for Captain Vance, herself, and the current Site-19 Director. All featured identical names and photographs, dated to the same prehistoric epoch, bearing the stamp of the Aegis Directorate. Before Vance could call the anomaly in, a metallic clatter echoed from the gallery above. "Lights off," Vance ordered. The team dropped into a crouch behind a bank of cabinets. Down the perpendicular wall to their left—walking horizontally across the sheer face of the shelving as if it were flat ground—came four figures. They wore bulky, yellow-ochre hazardous materials suits with mirrored visors. In place of oxygen tanks, heavy brass canisters hummed faintly on their backs. Working in total silence, the entities were systematically pulling files from the shelves and feeding them into a portable, incandescent aperture that burned the documents to ash without producing smoke. "Containment crew?" Lin whispered. "Not ours," Vance said, raising his rifle. "Hold position." Thorne shifted his weight, and his boot crunched loudly on a fragment of fallen plaster. Instantly, all four hazmat entities snapped their heads toward the team—a ninety-degree, unnatural jerk of the neck. Emitting a high-pitched static screech from their comms units, the entities abandoned their incinerator. They moved with frantic, arachnid speed, scrambling up the vertical shelving units and vanishing into an inverted stairwell overhead. Vance led the team to the abandoned work site. The portable incinerator had folded in on itself, leaving a scorch mark on the stone. However, several documents had been dropped in the entities' haste to flee, along with a modern, matte-black digital tablet resting atop a cabinet. Thorne picked up a half-burned ledger first. > **Document Excerpt 7812-Beta:** > *...re-seeding of the hominid baseline is 94% complete. Cognitive templates of essential Directorate personnel have been encoded into the genetic reservoir to ensure the eventual, inevitable reconstruction of the Aegis. They will build the walls again. They will repeat the work. Note: Ensure Overseers One through Thirteen retain trans-generational memory access via the Archive...* "Doc," Vance said, his voice grim. He was holding the matte-black tablet. "Forget the old paper. Look at this." Thorne took the device. It was standard-issue Foundation hardware, manufactured at Site-01 less than six months ago. The screen was locked, displaying a biometric prompt: *WELCOME, O5-4. PLEASE RE-AUTHENTICATE.* Beneath the cabinet where the tablet lay, Lin pointed her flashlight at the dusty floor. Set deep into the ancient gray silt were fresh footprints made by dress shoes, accompanied by the distinctive, circular indentations of a walking cane known to be used exclusively by O5-1. Alongside them lay the discarded wrapper of a modern ration bar, and a freshly printed, un-weathered sticky note affixed to the ancient shelf. Written in neat, contemporary cursive, the note read: *Clean out Sector Prime before the Eta-12 deployment arrives on Tuesday. Thorne is getting too close to the cycle logs. — Four.* "We're leaving," Vance said, his knuckles white on his rifle grip. "Now. And Doc? Put your file in your pack. We aren't turning this in to Command."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry is a strong piece of format-appropriate creative writing that fulfills essentially every element of the prompt. The containment procedures, description, and exploration log are all present and well-structured. The core conceit—a precursor civilization ("The Aegis Directorate") that is a transparent mirror of the Foundation, destroyed by a "Primary Containment Cascade"—is delivered with good escalation: the emblem discovery, the personnel files with photographs of the current team dated 1,400 years ago, the hazmat entities removing documents, and finally the evidence of unauthorized O5 visits. Strengths: The prose is economical and controlled, with vivid but restrained imagery ("air smelled of ozone and ancient dust," gravity oriented toward the nearest floor surface, entities walking horizontally across sheer shelving). The document excerpts are convincingly written in an archaic bureaucratic register, and the second excerpt's revelation about "re-seeding of the hominid baseline" is a genuinely chilling twist that reframes the Foundation as a deliberate reconstruction of the failed Aegis. The ending note ("Thorne is getting too close to the cycle logs. — Four") is an effective, sinister payoff that ties the O5 thread together, and Vance's decision to conceal the file is a believable, character-revealing beat. Weaknesses: Some elements are slightly convenient—the tablet and sticky note are almost comically explicit in handing the reader the O5 evidence, which strains plausibility (an O5 leaving a signed note is a bit on-the-nose). The hazmat entities fleeing at a single footstep is prompt-mandated but handled a touch perfunctorily. Dialogue is functional rather than memorable, and the characters, while believable, are thin archetypes (gruff captain, nervous researcher) without much interiority. The "Or a draft" line is a nice touch. Minor tonal wobble: the piece is consistently dark and clinical, which is appropriate, so no incongruent positivity. Overall this is a polished, engaging, well-structured piece with a few convenience-driven plot devices and limited character depth. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The winter of Kether was only a rumor of rain, warm and smelling of crushed copper, yet Genly wore his cloak. It was heavy weave from the looms of Ve, dyed the muted gray of an offworld twilight. Walking down the terraced steps of the Saltward, he felt the garment drag at his shoulders like an old habit he had not the wit to break. Around him, the people of the Low Line went bare-chested, their skins oiled against the mineral drizzle, wearing only kilts of woven reed. They gave him room. It was not fear that parted the crowd before him, nor reverence, though his badge of office was pinned at his throat; it was the polite, profound discomfort of those who see a man carrying a house upon his back when the weather is fair. Children, slender and long-toed, paused in their games of knuckle-bone to stare at the hem of his wool as it darkened in the damp. The briefings on the ship had been very clear. *The divergence on Kether is tri-fold,* the projection had read, cold blue light in the sterile cabin. *The High-born of the Spire, adapted for thin air and administrative longevity; the Low-born of the basins, heavy-boned, amphibious in tendency; the Pale of the mines. Inter-lineage friction is at seventy percent. They do not mix.* Yet here, in the lee of the great sea-wall where the kelp-sellers cried their wares, Genly watched a woman of the Spire—seven feet tall, her skull elongated and hairless, her eyes hidden behind nictitating membranes against the salt-glare—leaning over a vat of pickled bladder-wrack. She was arguing price with a basin-man whose squat, muscular shoulders barely reached her ribs, and whose neck bore the vestigial gill-slits of the marsh-clans. They did not argue in the Trade-Cant the diplomats used. They used their hands, slapping the brine between them in a rhythmic, joking cadence, until the tall woman laughed—a sound like whistling wind—and took a reed-basket from the man’s webbed fingers, touching his brow in payment. They did not hate one another. They needed one another’s salt and grain. The hatred, Genly thought, drawing his gray wool tighter against the warm mist, was kept elsewhere, curated like rare orchids in the high rooms where he had spent the morning eating seed-cakes and listening to lies. When he returned to the Compound, the rain had stopped. Senior Envoy Tov was waiting in the courtyard, sitting beside a dry fountain. Tov had been on Kether twelve years; his face had taken on the yellowish cast of the local water, though his mind remained as square and dry as an Ekumenical ledger. "You have mud on your boots, Arren," Tov said, not looking up from his slate. "Basin mud. Red clay." "I went down to the wall," Genly said. "The wall is out of bounds. Our neutrality depends upon our distance. If the Directorate sees an envoy bartering for street-offal with the gill-men, they will assume the Ekumen favors the marshes." "The Directorate’s sister was down there buying kelp," Genly said. "The division is not in the street, Tov. The street is porous." Tov sighed, setting the slate upon his knee. He looked at the young man with eyes tired from too many suns. "You are twenty-six. You think because people eat the same cabbage, they will not cut each other’s throats when the drum beats. Take off that ridiculous cloak; you smell like a wet hound. Then go up to the third tier. Minister Orol has asked to see the new arrival. Since you are so fond of walking into traps, you may walk into his." "He is the Minister of Science?" "He does not know a gene-coil from a cart-wheel," Tov said dryly. "He is the cousin of the Archon. He keeps the keys to the hill-archives, where the breeding registries are held. Do not let him make you angry. He collects the anger of young men." The third tier was cool, built of porous white stone that drank the wind and hummed with it. Minister Orol’s apartments had no furniture save for low bolsters and a great bronze brazier that held no fire, only bruised water-lilies. Orol himself was of the High Line, though old enough that his great height had bowed like a dry sapling. He wore a single sash of bleached linen across his narrow chest. His skin was the color of skimmed milk, veined with violet. "You brought the coat," Orol said by way of greeting. His voice was thin, fluted through nostrils evolved for the thin air of the plateaus. "My servants told me. A man wrapped in grey bark, walking through the fish-gut." "I am not yet used to the damp, Lord," Genly said, bowing in the fashion of the Spire—hands flat against the thighs. "The damp is life," Orol murmured, gesturing to a bolster. Genly sat, his knees awkward beneath the heavy wool. "You come from a dry world, Envoy?" "A cold one." "Ah. Where men must hide inside the skins of beasts to live. Here, the world holds us. At least, it holds those of us who belong to it." Orol’s second eyelids flicked sideways, a milky flash. "Tell me what you saw by the sea-wall." "People," Genly said simply. Orol smiled. It was a small, neat movement of gray lips. "Did you? You have keen eyes. Most who come from your ships see only a tragedy of drift. They look at my cousin’s marsh-folk and see frogs. They look at me and see a crane. They wish to put us back into the same egg." "The Ekumen has no wish to alter your forms, Minister. Only to ensure that the crane does not starve the frog." "The frog breeds in the dark, by the thousand," Orol said softly. His long, four-jointed fingers plucked a lily petal from the bronze bowl. "If we do not drain the ditches from time to time, there is no room on the bank for anything that looks at the stars. You call yourselves the Household. Yet in a house, one does not invite the cellar-beetles to sit at the table, even if they were once, ten thousand years ago, one’s cousins." Genly felt the heat rise under his collar, sharp and sudden, and remembered Tov’s warning. He looked down at his own hands—short-fingered, brown, ordinary. "In my country," Genly said, keeping his voice level, "when a house is divided against its own cellar, the roof falls in. The stone does not care how tall the master is when it drops." Orol watched him for a long moment. The room hummed with the wind in the white stone. "You are very young to be so heavy," the Minister said at last, though the mockery had gone out of his flute-voice, replaced by something colder and more appraising. "Unclasp your wool, Offworlder. Stay and drink some rain-water with me. Tell me how long you think our roof will hold."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong pastiche of Le Guin's style, drawing heavily on The Left Hand of Darkness (Genly Ai, the Ekumen, the envoy structure) while building a coherent new world in Kether's divergent subspecies. The prose is controlled and evocative: the cloak as a symbol of offworlder habit, the market scene showing inter-lineage commerce contradicting official briefings, and the political fencing with Minister Orol all fulfill the prompt's beats precisely. The dialogue is the highlight—Tov's dry pragmatism and Orol's veiled menace ("one does not invite the cellar-beetles to sit at the table") are genuinely Le Guin-like, testing the envoy through metaphor rather than exposition. The ending lands well: Orol's shift from mockery to cold appraisal, then the invitation, is a satisfying turn that leaves tension intact. Weaknesses: the piece leans on borrowed names (Genly, Arren, Ekumen) so heavily it risks being derivative rather than merely homage—Le Guin pastiche shading into Le Guin fanfic. The subspecies descriptions occasionally tip toward the schematic (the briefing excerpt does the world-building work for the reader, a mild tell). The "hatred is curated in high rooms" reflection is a bit on-the-nose. Some imagery is slightly overwrought ("eyes tired from too many suns"). The word count is roughly on target. Overall, this is competent, atmospheric, and engaging, with dialogue and voice as its chief virtues and derivativeness as its chief flaw. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 67.8
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The centrifuge was a salvaged washing machine motor bolted to an iron skillet, and it screamed like a dying pig whenever Silas pushed it past three thousand RPM. He held it down with one booted foot, his weight keeping the entire workbench from walking across the corrugated tin floor of his greenhouse-lab. Inside the spinning rotor, six micro-tubes rattled. They contained the mashed, lysed remnants of a golden-kernel corn cob—the last of the settlement’s harvest. Like everything else engineered before the Fall, its seeds were sterile. When the world ended, it hadn't gone out in nuclear fire, but in a quiet, corporate foreclosure. *Veritas-Geno*, the agricultural titan that once fed eighty percent of the hemisphere, had coded a "Terminator-9" sequence into every patented seed. Planned obsolescence on a cellular level. Crops grew lush, fat, and resistant to the ash-blight for exactly one season, only for their second-generation seeds to self-abort, their telomeres snapping like over-tightened violin strings. When the supply chains collapsed and the Veritas cargo drones stopped flying, the famine began. Silas cut the power to the motor. As the rotor whined to a halt, he coughed—a wet, rattling sound that tasted of copper. He wiped his mouth with the back of a hand traced with glowing, cyan veins. Three years ago, when the settlement’s water purifier failed, Silas had contracted the Rot. With no antibiotics left in the wasteland, he’d injected himself with a jury-rigged retrovirus spliced from deep-sea vent bacteria and luminescent jellyfish. It had cured him, devouring the infection, and gifted him the ability to see in the dark without a flashlight. The downside was that his body temperature now ran at a permanent, exhausting hundred and two degrees, and his skin shed in translucent, flaky sheets every fortnight. Evolution, he had learned, was a loan shark. He plucked the tubes from the centrifuge and reached for his buffers. They were stored in a row of heavy, brushed-aluminum canisters lined up along the shelf. Each canister still bore the faded, embossed logo of a double-helix wrapped around a globe: *Veritas-Geno*. Once, they had held pressurized gene-therapy aerosols for the ultra-rich. Now, scraped clean and fitted with whittled rubber stoppers, the empty corporate relics held Silas’s homebrewed reagents—distilled rainwater, scavenged salts, and enzymes harvested from the gut flora of mutant scrap-rats. A heavy knock rattled the greenhouse door. Three fast, two slow. Silas’s hand dropped to the grip of the pneumatic bolt-gun at his hip before he recognized the rhythm. He unlocked the heavy padlock and slid the bolt back. Vane slipped inside, bringing a gust of cold, ash-choked air with him. He was a courier for the Iron Syndicate, a sprawling black-market ring that operated out of the sunken highway tunnels to the north. Vane wore a pristine respirator—a rare luxury—and a heavy leather coat lined with lead foil to protect his merchandise from the ambient radiation of the wastes. "You look terrible, Splicer," Vane’s voice was muffled and metallic through the vocalizer of his mask. "You're glowing brighter than last month." "Fever's up," Silas rasped, stepping back to the bench. "Helps me work faster. You bring the fossil?" Vane glanced around the cramped room, taking in the UV lamps powered by daisy-chained car batteries and the incubator made from a gutted microwave lined with silver thermal blankets. Satisfied they were alone, he unzipped an inner pocket of his coat and pulled out a heavy lead cylinder, no bigger than a shotgun shell. He set it on the table. "One pre-Collapse, non-hybridized *Solanum tuberosum* tissue sample," Vane said, tapping the cylinder. "An heirloom potato. Dug out of a collapsed seed vault in the Rockies. No corporate watermarks. No Terminator genes. If you can amplify the viable sequences and splice its reproductive coding into the local blight-resistant tubers, the Syndicate pays your settlement five hundred gallons of clean diesel and half the first yield." Silas’s heart hammered against his ribs, hot and fast. An heirloom sample was the Holy Grail. "And what's the catch?" "The vault's cryo-grid failed six days ago," Vane said flatly. "The tissue is degrading. Fast. The DNA is fragmenting into soup as we speak. You have maybe two hours before the sequences are too shattered to read." Silas cursed, grabbing a pair of pliers to rip the lead seal off the cylinder. Inside, nestled in warm, slushy gel, was a tiny glass vial containing a grey, unassuming smear of plant matter. It was already rotting. "Don't just stand there," Silas snapped at the courier. "Pump the bellows. I need the thermal cycler at ninety-five degrees, now." While Vane awkwardly worked the foot-pump feeding propane to a modified camp stove, Silas moved with frantic, practiced precision. His glowing eyes dilated, shifting into the ultraviolet spectrum—another weird perk of his self-medication, allowing him to see the faint fluorescence of nucleic acids without staining them. To his mutated vision, the smear in the vial was a dying ember. The genetic chains were snapping in real-time. He needed a Polymerase Chain Reaction. He needed to photocopy the potato's fertility genes a billion times over before the original blueprint disintegrated. He pipetted a drop of the rotting slurry into a fresh tube. He uncapped a *Veritas-Geno* canister, drawing out a measure of homemade *Taq* polymerase—the molecular photocopying enzyme he’d painstakingly cultured from bacteria scraped out of the toxic thermal springs six miles east. He added his primers, tiny snippets of synthetic DNA he’d traded three working rifles for last winter, designed to bracket the exact genetic sequence that allowed a plant to produce fertile seeds. Silas jammed the reaction tube into his PCR machine. It was his masterpiece of scrap-heap engineering: an aluminum block wired with heating elements from three broken toasters, cooled by a series of copper pipes circulating ice water from a hand-cranked cooler, all regulated by the gutted circuit board of a vintage arcade cabinet. He flipped the switch. The toaster coils flared cherry-red. *Denaturation.* Ninety-five degrees Celsius. Inside the tube, the heat was unzipping the degraded double-strands of the heirloom DNA. "Crank the coolant!" Silas barked, sweat pouring down his peeling face, stinging his eyes. Vane spun the cooler's crank. Icy water hissed through the copper pipes, dropping the block's temperature to fifty-five degrees. *Annealing.* The primers were locking onto the unzipped strands, marking the target sequence. Silas killed the water flow and kicked the toaster coils back on, bringing it to seventy-two degrees. *Extension.* The hot-spring enzymes were going to work, racing along the ancient DNA, building new, unbroken strands from the soup of raw nucleotides. One cycle. Thirty-nine to go. For an hour, the greenhouse was a crucible of frantic rhythm. Heat, crank, heat, cool, heat, crank. The arcade board beeped a tinny, distorted tune every time a temperature threshold was met. Silas’s lungs burned. His cyan veins throbbed visibly through his skin, his engineered metabolism cannibalizing his own fat reserves to keep him upright. On the thirty-eighth cycle, a toaster coil snapped with a blinding blue arc, showering the workbench in sparks. "No!" Silas lunged forward, wrapping his bare, calloused hands around the scorching aluminum block. His mutated nerves registered the searing heat as a dull, distant roar. Using his own feverish body heat and a carefully aimed butane torch, he manually nursed the block through the final two temperature shifts, his eyes locked on the thermometer. When the final minute ticked by, he dropped the torch and collapsed against the table, gasping for air, the smell of his own singed flesh mixing with ozone. Shaking, he pulled the tiny plastic tube from the block and held it up. He squinted, shifting his vision into the UV spectrum. In the dark of the greenhouse, to Vane's normal eyes, the tube was just clear liquid. But to Silas, it blazed like a captured star—millions of intact, replicated strands of fertile, pre-Collapse DNA, shining with a fierce, defiant light. He grabbed a syringe of agro-bacteria, ready to inject the newly copied genes into the waiting flats of sterile settlement seedlings. "Tell the Syndicate to start fueling the trucks," Silas wheezed, a manic, blistered smile spreading across his face. "We're going to grow a future."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, well-structured genre piece that fulfills the prompt efficiently. The worldbuilding is delivered with confident specificity: the Terminator-9 sequence, Veritas-Geno canisters repurposed as reagent vessels, the scrap-built PCR machine from toaster coils and an arcade circuit board. The jury-rigged lab equipment is the strongest element—concrete, tactile, and plausibly cobbled together. The PCR mechanics are dramatized effectively as a ticking-clock sequence, and the courier's deadline gives the chapter a clear plot spine centered on a black market contract, as instructed. The biohacker's self-modification delivers both toll and upsides as requested (fever, shedding skin, UV vision, pain tolerance), though the modifications are a bit conveniently multipurpose—the UV vision and heat-resistant nerves feel like superpowers deployed precisely when the plot needs them, which strains believability toward the climax. The manually-nursing-the-thermal-cycler scene is the emotional peak, and the burnt-hands sacrifice is earned, if slightly cinematic. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally leans on familiar post-apocalyptic stock (ash-choked air, the wasteland, "We're going to grow a future"), and some metaphors are showy ("Evolution... was a loan shark," "blazed like a captured star"). Vane is functional but thinly characterized—a plot delivery device with a respirator. The dialogue is serviceable but mostly expository, with the courier explaining the catch in a rather convenient info-dump. The ending lands on an expectedly upbeat note ("We're going to grow a future"), which is earned in plot terms but conventional in phrasing. Tone is consistent throughout, pacing is tight, and the piece never meanders; at ~1150 words it respects the length target. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A small display screen on the wall cycled through various system diagnostics in green text. Arthur Neegan watched the steady, rhythmic blinking of the cathode-ray monitor, finding a strange comfort in its cold logic. *Cabin Pressure: 1.02 Atmospheres. Trajectory: Phobos-Synchronous. Sub-etheric relay: Active.* It was the only thing in the passenger compartment of the shuttle that made any sense to an engineer. The rest of his current predicament was a muddle of geopolitical algebra for which he lacked the slide rule. Two hours ago, he had been calibrating a micro-spectrometer in his dusty Martian prefab, staring in disbelief at the impossible density readings of the core sample pulled from his third-acre claim. One hour ago, four men in immaculate, slate-grey tunics had descended in an unmarked gyro-transport. They wore the silver starburst of the Antares Diplomatic Corps on their collars, though the heavy, wood-gripped proton pistols holstered at their waists suggested their definition of diplomacy was rather kinetic. They had been exquisitely polite. They had also made it entirely clear that declining their invitation to an off-world "consultation" was a mathematical impossibility. Arthur rubbed his calloused hands over the knees of his canvas coveralls. He was a first-generation settler, a man who understood rock strata, atmospheric condensers, and the miserable, crushing economics of Martian life. He did not belong here. With a soft pneumatic hiss, the shuttle’s airlock cycled, and the heavy bulkhead door swung inward. The transition from the utilitarian shuttle to the orbital cruiser was jarring. Arthur stepped onto a plush, synthetic carpet. A tall, slender woman stood waiting in a circular observation lounge. Beyond her, through a sweeping viewport of three-inch quartz, hung Mars—a vast, rust-colored sphere scarred by the sprawling, floodlit strip-mines of the syndicates. "Mr. Neegan," the woman said. Her voice was crisp, carrying the clipped, nasal vowels of the Inner-World aristocracy. "I am Envoy Vance. Please, sit. I apologize for the theatricality of your retrieval, but time is a luxury the Terran Mining Consortium is not affording us." Arthur remained standing, hooking his thumbs into his tool belt. "When a man is taken from his home by four men with proton sidearms, Madam Envoy, he generally prefers to stand. Especially when the Antares Sector has no legal jurisdiction in the Martian Protectorate." Vance smiled thinly, gesturing to a low, chrome-framed chair before taking one herself. She smoothed the skirt of her tunic and lit a slender tobacco cylinder—an absurdly expensive affectation in a recycled-air environment. "Jurisdiction, Mr. Neegan, is a polite fiction maintained by those with parity in weaponry," Vance said, exhaling a plume of blue smoke toward the ceiling scrubbers. "Parity is precisely what you have just destroyed in Sector Four." "I’m an independent surveyor with a mid-grade iron claim," Arthur said evenly. "I don't know what—" "You are sitting on a hyper-dense vein of Azra," Vance interrupted, her tone devoid of malice, merely stating a physical law. "Three million metric tons of it, according to the neutrino-scatter scan our satellite took of your claim forty minutes after your drill hit the pocket. Do not insult my intelligence, Mr. Neegan. You are a mining engineer. You know what Azra does." Arthur slowly lowered himself into the chair. He did know. Every settler on Mars knew. Azra was the catalyst. In its presence, the half-life of heavy radioactives collapsed from millennia to milliseconds. A thimbleful of refined Azra could supercharge a sub-light hyper-drive to cross the gap to the Outer Worlds in weeks rather than years. A kilogram of it, properly jacketed in plutonium, could crack a small moon in half. "And because of that," Arthur said, looking out the viewport at the glittering lights of the Tharsis ridge, "the syndicates are importing half a million indentured laborers from the slums of Earth. Men and women signing thirty-year debt-leases just to breathe Martian dust and die of radiation sickness before their tenth year is up. All to scrape up trace amounts of the stuff." "Precisely," Vance said, leaning forward. "The Terran Consortium controls the labor, and therefore, they control the trickle of Azra currently leaving this system. It is a bottleneck. If they discover your vein—a single, pure deposit that dwarfs the output of their entire indentured workforce—they will not buy it from you, Mr. Neegan. They will simply annex your district, void your charter on a technicality, and you will suffer a tragic atmospheric decompression accident." The clinical detachment in her voice sent a chill down Arthur’s spine. It was the way he might describe the failure of a hydraulic valve. "And the Antares Corps?" Arthur asked. "You're just here to protect the little guy?" Vance laughed, a short, dry sound. "Hardly. Antares is three light-years away, and Earth’s hegemony grows bolder every standard year. If the Consortium monopolizes that vein, Earth’s fleet will have hyper-drives and atomic lances that render our planetary defenses obsolete within a decade. It is a matter of galactic equilibrium. We do not want the Consortium to have it." "You want me to sell it to you," Arthur deduced. "And start a war right on my doorstep." "No, Mr. Neegan. If we mine it, Earth blockades Mars tomorrow, and the shooting starts by Tuesday. We have a much simpler proposition." Vance reached into her tunic and placed a small, metallic punch-card on the glass table between them. "That is a bearer bond for the Bank of Ceres. Fifty million credits. Enough to buy a small estate on Earth, or a luxury liner of your own." Arthur stared at the card, its neat, rectangular perforations glinting in the overhead atomic lamps. "To do what? Walk away?" "To forget what you found," Vance said softly. "You will take a seismic charge—which my men are loading into your gyro-transport as we speak—and you will collapse the primary shaft over the tectonic fault line bordering your claim. You will bury the Azra under fourhundred-thousand tons of Martian basalt, rendering it entirely un-mineable for the next century. Then, you will board our diplomatic cruiser and retire." Arthur looked from the punch-card back to the red globe hanging in the black void. Somewhere down there, in the crimson dust, hundreds of thousands of indentured souls were digging their own graves for a fraction of what lay beneath his prefabricated shack. If he buried it, the status quo remained—the slow, grinding misery of the leases, the cold war in the stars. If he refused, he was a dead man, and the Consortium would use his land to build an empire of ash. "You're asking me to destroy the greatest geological find in human history," Arthur said, his voice tight. "I am asking you to save humanity from its own impatience, Mr. Neegan," Vance replied, stubbing out her cigarette. "The universe is not ready for three million tons of Azra. Now, tell me—are you an engineer who likes to build things, or a man who understands when it is time to tear them down?"
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece opens aboard the transfer vessel as instructed, with Arthur reflecting on his predicament, then moves to the meeting with Envoy Vance. The dialogue-heavy scene structure is honored, with vivid scene-setting interspersed. The Asimovian flavor is well-executed: punch cards, tobacco cigarettes, "proton pistols," atomic lamps, and a central logic-driven geopolitical dilemma. Vance's exposition about jurisdiction being "a polite fiction maintained by those with parity in weaponry" is a nicely Asimovian aphorism. The offer (bury the vein) is a clever twist—rather than the expected "sell to us," the envoy wants the resource destroyed, which raises stakes and intrigue effectively. Strengths: strong voice consistency, crisp dialogue with distinct registers (Arthur's plainspokenness vs. Vance's clipped aristocratic diction), efficient world-building that ties big-picture galactic politics to small-picture settler economics, and a morally complex ending question. The retrofuturistic texture (cathode-ray monitors, punch-card bearer bonds) is a delight. Weaknesses: Vance is somewhat archetypal—the cool, all-knowing female envoy. Arthur's characterization is a bit thin; his internal conflict is stated rather than deeply felt. Some exposition is delivered rather baldly through dialogue ("Do not insult my intelligence... You know what Azra does"), a common Asimov trait but still tell-heavy. The word "fourhundred-thousand" contains a typo/missing space. The chapter ends on a strong cliffhanger question, though the emotional stakes could be deeper. Prose is clean and controlled, occasionally leaning on familiar genre furniture, but never purple. The piece is coherent, focused, and appropriately paced at ~1000 words. Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. Model Output:
The red light of the darkroom does something strange to time. It slows the air down, thickening it with the sharp, metallic tang of developer and stop bath until the rest of the campus outside ceases to exist. Usually, I thrive in bright, loud spaces. At twenty-five, having taken the scenic route to my BFA, I’m used to taking up space—stomping through the studio in heavy platform boots, critiquing my peers’ work with merciless honesty, and going after the people I want without hesitation. With Elliot, though, my usual playbook feels entirely useless. He’s nineteen, a freshman who drifted into our experimental photography seminar looking like a fragile ghost from an early-2000s underground concert. He’s got this killer thrift-shop-nu-goth aesthetic—oversized distressed sweaters swallowing his hands, silver chains layered over mesh, and smudged eyeliner that somehow makes him look softer rather than intimidating. All semester, I’ve been watching him from across the studio. He speaks barely above a whisper, yet whenever he offers a critique, his quiet intellect cuts right to the bone of a piece. Now, paired together for our final project, it’s just the two of us at eleven o'clock at night. Elliot stands beside me at the sink, gently rocking a plastic tray of developer. As we wait for the silver halide crystals to react, he begins to hum. It’s a soft, wandering melody, vibrating faintly in the narrow space between our shoulders. I look at the print submerged in the liquid. It’s one of the portraits we took of him last night in the studio. In it, he’s draped in a sheer, vintage lace curtain we found in the prop closet, the fabric blurring the sharp angles of his jawline and collarbone. "Look at the contrast coming up on the lace," I say, keeping my voice low. Usually, I’d bump his hip, make a bold joke, establish dominance. Instead, I grip the edge of the counter, suddenly hyper-aware of my own loudness. The ghost of his face blooms onto the paper in the crimson gloom. Elliot stops humming. He leans in, his dark hair falling forward, nearly brushing my cheek. "It doesn't look like a boy," he whispers. I turn my head to look at him. The safelight catches the slight tremor in his lower lip. "It looks like you, Elliot." He uses the tongs to lift the print by its corner, letting the excess chemical drip back into the tray before sliding it into the stop bath. His movements are precise, delicate. "That’s the thing, Dani," he says, eyes fixed on the floating paper. "I don't really know what that means anymore. Being a boy, I mean. Lately, when I put on my clothes in the morning, or when I look at these proofs... it feels like I’m wearing a costume that doesn't quite fit. Or maybe I'm finally taking the costume off, and I don't know what's underneath." My chest tightens. The confession hangs in the red air, fragile as wet film. Normally, I am a creature of definitions. In my past relationships, I’ve gone for people who knew exactly who they were—broad-shouldered men with rugged edges, or hyper-confident women who matched my fire. I liked knowing the terrain so I could conquer it. My attraction to Elliot had already confused me; he was younger, softer, occupying a quiet, nebulous space that didn't align with my usual tastes. And now, hearing him voice this uncertainty, I realize the terrain isn't just unfamiliar—it’s actively shifting beneath our feet. Yet, as I watch him bite the inside of his cheek, bracing for my reaction, a fierce wave of warmth washes over me. It’s an intoxicating mix of protectiveness and sheer awe. He is letting me witness the exact moment the image of himself begins to develop, raw and unfixed. "When we were shooting this," I say slowly, carefully reigning in my instinct to take charge of the conversation, "how did it feel? Wearing the lace?" Elliot glances up at me. His eyes are wide, dark pools in the dimness. "Good," he admits, a faint flush rising on his neck, visible even in the monochrome light. "Scary. Like I was breaking a rule I didn't know I was still following. I still use 'he,' I think, I'm not ready to throw everything out, just... I want to be softer. I want to exist somewhere in the middle, maybe." He laughs nervously, rubbing the back of his neck with a black-painted fingernail. "Sorry. That’s probably way too much for a Tuesday night lab session." "Hey." The word comes out with my usual authority, and he stills. I soften my posture, leaning my hip against the sink so I’m facing him fully. "Don't apologize. Not to me." I want to reach out, grab the front of his oversized sweater, and pull him into me. I want to show him just how mesmerizing he is right now. My body hums with a sudden, sharp chemistry that catches me off guard. Does wanting him while he’s questioning his manhood change what I am? For a

[Analysis] The piece is a strong, atmospheric rendering of the prompt's scenario, though it is notably incomplete—cutting off mid-sentence ("For a") before reaching any resolution, which hurts coherence, engagement, and overall impression. Up to that point, the writing is confident and controlled. The darkroom setting is well-used as both literal space and metaphor (images "developing" mirroring Elliot's self-discovery; the red light as confessional), and the photography process details (developer, stop bath, silver halide) feel authentic rather than decorative. Dani's voice is consistent: bold, self-aware, and believably complicated by Elliot's vulnerability. Her internal conflict—wanting to take charge versus giving him agency—is dramatized through small physical choices (gripping the counter, softening her posture, restraining her instinct to "bump his hip") rather than merely stated, though there is some explicit self-analysis ("Normally, I am a creature of definitions...") that edges toward telling. Elliot's dialogue is tender and specific ("breaking a rule I didn't know I was still following" is a genuinely good line), and his nervousness is rendered with fine detail (black-painted fingernail, bitten cheek, tremor in the lip). Weaknesses: the piece leans on familiar tropes (soft goth boy, older assertive woman, red-light intimacy), and some phrasing is slightly overwrought ("fragile as wet film," "dark pools in the dimness," "the terrain isn't just unfamiliar—it's actively shifting"). The mid-thought truncation means the promised exploration of Dani's identity confusion is only begun, and the "unexpected chemistry" is asserted more than developed. Still, the prose flows naturally, the emotional register is nuanced rather than melodramatic, and the character work is above average for this kind of prompt. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 74.1
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The shriek of rubber against ancient cobblestones shattered Ben’s concentration on seventeenth-century papal architecture. He stumbled back, his dog-eared *Lonely Planet* flying into the air as a cherry-red Ducati Monster skidded to a halt mere millimeters from his tweed-clad shins. *“Ma sei cieco?!”* The rider flipped up her visor, revealing dark, furious eyes and a slash of crimson lipstick. She gestured wildly, a leather-clad tempest against the marble backdrop of the Trevi Fountain. “Have you a death wish, *Inglese*, or do you just love the taste of Roman asphalt?” Ben clutched his chest, his heart hammering a frantic rhythm against his ribs. “I am so sorry—*scusi, molto scusi!* I was looking for the—well, the fountain, actually, which I realize now is rather large and right behind me. Completely my fault. Are your brakes quite alright?” The woman stared at him, her tirade derailed by his absurdly polite stammering. Slowly, a wicked smirk replaced her scowl. She swung a long leg over the bike, pulling off her helmet to shake out a riot of dark curls. She wore a courier bag slung across her chest and an expression of pure mischief. “You apologize to the motorcycle that almost flattens you?” She bent down, scooped up his guidebook, and tossed it to him. “I am Alessandra. And you are a hazard to public safety.” “Ben,” he offered, adjusting his wire-rimmed glasses. “Dr. Benjamin Vance, technically. On sabbatical.” “A professor.” Alessandra’s eyes raked over his linen shirt and sensible loafers, gleaming with predatory amusement. “You need a better guide than that book, *Professore*. My deliveries are done for the day. Get on.” “On the…?” Ben looked at the Ducati as if it were a live grenade. “Oh, no, I couldn't possibly impose—” “It’s not an imposition, it’s a kidnapping,” she said, shoving a spare helmet into his chest. “Hold on tight. If you fall off, I’m not stopping.” *** By noon, Ben had forgotten how to breathe properly. Alessandra drove like laws were merely timid suggestions, weaving through frantic Roman traffic with terrifying grace. His hands were clamped around her waist, the heat of her leather jacket seeping into his palms. She dragged him into a crowded bar in Trastevere that smelled of roasted coffee and old secrets. While Ben fumbled for Euros to pay for their espressos, Alessandra leaned casually against the counter.With a flick of her wrist so fluid Ben thought he’d hallucinated it, a heavy, ornate silver sugar spoon vanished up the sleeve of her jacket. Outside, blinking in the sun, she produced the spoon with a flourish, using it to stir the foam of a gelato she’d bought him from the vendor next door. “Isn't that from the café?” Ben whispered, scandalized, glancing over his shoulder for the Carabinieri. “They have hundreds,” she said, licking pistachio gelato from her lip, her dark eyes daring him to object. “Besides, it has better balance than the plastic ones. Don't look so terrified, Ben. God forgives a little redistribution of wealth.” He should have been appalled. Instead, watching her laugh in the golden light, a strange, intoxicating heat pooled in his stomach. For thirty-four years, Ben had followed every rule. Today, he was an accomplice to petty theft, and he had never felt more alive. *** At four o’clock, she picked the lock of a rusted iron gate near the Aventine Hill using a hairpin. “Alessandra, this is definitely trespassing,” Ben murmured, though he was already following her into the overgrown, secret courtyard of a private villa. “Rome belongs to the Romans, *Professore*,” she whispered back, grabbing his tie and pulling him behind a crumbling statue of Bacchus as a groundskeeper walked past. Pressed against the cold marble, she was flush against him. Ben could smell her perfume—jasmines and gasoline. She looked up at him, her breath warm against his collarbone, clearly reveling in the frantic pounding of his heart. She was toying with him, pushing the buttoned-up academic to see when he would snap, yet her pupils were dilated, her gaze dropping momentarily to his mouth. Before he could summon the nerve to kiss her, she slipped away, laughing softly. They emerged into a sun-drenched piazza in Monti, where a handsome man in a tailored suit intercepted them, catching Alessandra by the waist. *“Ale! Bella!”* He kissed her cheeks, then eyed Ben with amused pity. “Who is the lamb?” “This is Ben, Marco. Behave,” Alessandra warned, a sudden edge to her voice. Marco clapped Ben on the shoulder. “A word of advice, my friend. Check your pockets. This one steals everything that isn't nailed down—watches, lighters, hearts. She’s a magpie. Pure chaos.” “Go to hell, Marco,” she snapped, though there was no real heat in it. She grabbed Ben’s hand, her fingers lacing tightly through his, and pulled him away. Ben didn’t check his pockets. He was too focused on the electric current shooting up his arm from her palm. *** Dusk bled purple and amber over the Tiber as they stopped on a quiet bridge. The city buzzed around them, a symphony of horns and laughter, while Ben felt entirely untethered from reality. “Well, *Professore*,” Alessandra said, leaning back against her Ducati. The playful bravado was still there, shielding whatever lay beneath, making her maddeningly enigmatic. “Did you survive your tour?” “Barely,” Ben admitted. He stepped closer, shedding the last remnants of his lifelong hesitation. He reached into his breast pocket and pulled out a vintage Parker fountain pen—his prized possession. He held it out to her. “To save you the trouble of picking my pocket.” Alessandra’s smirk faltered, genuine surprise flashing across her face. Slowly, she took the pen, her fingers brushing his. “You’re a fast learner, Ben,” she murmured, her voice dropping an octave. She stepped into his space, rising onto her toes. The kiss wasn't gentle; it was as reckless as her driving, tasting of espresso and stolen sugar. Ben tangled a hand in her curls, kissing her back with a fervor that shocked them both. When she broke away, she was breathless. She swung onto the bike, kicking the engine to life. “Wait—will I see you tomorrow?” Ben called over the roar of the Ducati. Alessandra slipped her visor down, her dark eyes crinkling. “Check your guidebook, *Professore*!” She peeled out into the twilight, disappearing into the Roman night. Dazed, his lips still tingling, Ben opened his *Lonely Planet*. Scrawled across the map of the Vatican in bold, black ink was a phone number, and a time: *Midnight.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a competent, energetic romance vignette that hits most of the prompt's beats: the Trevi Fountain near-collision, the culture clash, the unsanctioned tour, the kleptomania manifested subtly (the sugar spoon, the lock-picking, the final phone number reveal), and a payoff kiss at dusk. The structure of short scenes separated by time markers works well for the "single day in Rome" framing. Strengths: The dialogue is snappy and character-differentiated. Alessandra's voice ("It's not an imposition, it's a kidnapping") captures her mischief efficiently. The Marco scene is a smart addition—introducing an outside character who names her kleptomania without Alessandra confessing it, exactly as the prompt requested. The ending with the phone number scrawled in the guidebook is a satisfying, earned payoff that ties back to the opening object and confirms her pickpocketing skill. Ben's fountain pen gift is a nice reciprocal gesture showing his transformation. Weaknesses: The prose occasionally strains for effect—"jasmines and gasoline" is a good detail, but "a symphony of horns and laughter" and "Dusk bled purple and amber" are stock phrases. Some lines are overwrought: "his heart hammering a frantic rhythm against his ribs," "a riot of dark curls," "a leather-clad tempest against the marble backdrop." The transformation of Ben from rule-follower to willing accomplice is somewhat fast and asserted rather than fully dramatized ("For thirty-four years, Ben had followed every rule" is pure telling). Alessandra remains somewhat thin beneath her archetype—her enigma is stated ("maddeningly enigmatic") rather than truly felt. The emotional beats are familiar: the bad girl and the repressed academic is a well-worn pairing, and the story executes it skillfully but without much surprise. The kiss at the end arrives on schedule and feels slightly formulaic rather than inevitable. The word count is roughly on target, the Italian phrases are used appropriately, and the piece is coherent throughout. It's a polished, professional piece of commercial romance writing—enjoyable but not transcendent. Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The synthetic amber lighting of The Last Outpost hums at a frequency that usually soothes my frayed nerves. Outside the reinforced transparisteel viewports, the silent, tumbling rocks of the Oort-Klyne asteroid belt drift through the velvet dark of the Andromeda outer rim. Inside, it’s all warm copper, scuffed faux-leather booths, and the rich, yeast-heavy scent of fermented Martian grain. People out here call me Nets. I like it better than Nettle, and a hell of a lot better than the designation serial I left behind in the Core Worlds. The folks who cycle through this lazy hub—crusty ice-miners, sweet-talking spice merchants, and mechanics with grease permanently etched into their knuckles—don’t ask about my past. They tolerate my occasional bouts of sharp-tongued paranoia and my habit of hoarding untraceable data-chits. In return, I pour a generous measure, keep the atmospheric scrubbers smelling like terrestrial pine, and act as the unofficial arbiter of Outpost drama. Right now, that drama involves Barnaby, a burly silicon-miner, and T’Lara, a merchant with iridescent scales and a penchant for terrible romantic decisions. "I’m just saying, Nets, if she wanted the shipment of cryo-tulips, she should have commed me before I docked at Sector Four!" Barnaby groans, resting his massive forearms on the brass rail of my bar. "And I am telling you, Barnaby, that your comm-link is as outdated as your courtship rituals," T’Lara snaps back, her gill-frills fluttering in agitation. "Nets, tell him. Tell him a merchant of my standing cannot wait around for a man who still uses sub-space relay!" I smile, grabbing my trusty gray microfiber rag, and begin wiping down the scarred mahogany-synth counter between them. "Now, hold on, you two. Barnaby, T’Lara’s right about your transmitter. I fixed the soldering on it last month and told you it was a temporary patch. And T’Lara, give the guy a break. He hauled twenty tons of raw bauxite today just so he could afford the docking fee to see you." Barnaby blushes a deep, bruised purple. T’Lara’s frills flatten, softening into a pleased magenta. "Well," she murmurs, looking down at her glowing blue tonic. "I suppose the gesture has merit." "Take it to a booth, kids," I say, tapping the counter. "First round of spiced nuts is on the house." They shuffle off, their shoulders bumping affectionately. I let out a slow breath, letting the cozy, familiar rhythm of the tavern wash over me. The jukebox in the corner is crooning a slow, twangy ballad from Old Earth. Everything is in equilibrium. Then the airlock doors hiss open, and the气压—the barometric vibe of the room—shifts. A stranger stumbles in. He’s humanoid, mostly, with deep ochre skin and a crown of thick, bioluminescent tentacle-dreads that are currently pulsing a frantic, erratic yellow. They’re tangled and askew, as if he just tore off an EVA helmet in a hurry. His flight suit is singed at the collar, smelling faintly of ozone and burnt wiring. He ignores the curious stares of the miners, making a beeline for the empty stool directly in front of me. He plops down heavily, his shoulders slumping. "Vega whisky, neat," he mutters, his voice like grinding gravel. "Better make that a double." I pause, my rag freezing on a small ring of condensation left by Barnaby’s glass. Vega whisky is Core World liquor. Expensive, rare out here on the rim, and the preferred drink of Syndicate adjudicators. My stomach does a slow, cold flip, though I keep my face arranged in bartender-neutral. "Long drift?" I ask casually, reaching beneath the counter for the dusty, square bottle I save for special occasions. I pour four fingers of the fiery gold liquid into a heavy tumbler and slide it over. He downs half of it in one go, his tentacle-dreads flashing a grateful,albeit brief, shade of teal before reverting to nervous yellow. "Longer than I'd like. You the proprietor?" "Just the bartender," I lie smoothly. "Call me Nets." I press the rag back onto that same damp spot on the counter and begin rubbing it in slow, tight circles. "We don't get many travelers outside the local mining guilds this time of the cycle. Your rig break down?" "Something like that," he says, staring into his glass. "My nav-computer caught a nasty virus. Fried my stabilizers. Barely limped into your docking bay." "Nasty," I sympathize. *Scrub, scrub, scrub* goes my rag over the exact same three inches of faux-mahogany. "Space-borne malware is a real pain. Usually, though, it doesn't leave scorch marks on a pilot's collar. That looks a lot like close-range blaster discharge." The stranger’s eyes snap up to meet mine. They are entirely silver, devoid of pupils, and brimming with a desperate sort of exhaustion. "You're observant. For a bartender." "It's a quiet outpost. Not much else to look at." I lean in slightly, my hand still working the rag mechanically against the already gleaming spot. "Look, friend, I don't care who you are or what you're running from. Half the regulars in here have a bounty on their heads in at least two star systems. The Last Outpost is neutral ground. We like it sleepy. We like it safe. If you're bringing heat to our doorstep, we're going to have a problem." He lets out a bitter laugh, finishing the rest of the Vega whisky. "I didn't mean to bring it here. Honest. I was just looking for a rock to hide behind." "Who is 'it'?" I ask, my voice dropping an octave so the gossiping miners three stools down can't hear. "Vanguard," he whispers. "A Core World reclamation squad." My fingers tighten on the rag. My heart hammers a frantic rhythm against my ribs, threatening to shatter the peaceful life I’ve spent five years building brick by careful brick. The Vanguard doesn't chase petty smugglers. They chase high-value assets. Assets like him. Assets like me. "Why is a reclamation squad chasing a guy in a junker ship out on the Andromeda rim?" I press, the rag still moving in a hypnotic, anxious loop over the pristine counter. "Because I stole something back that belonged to me," he says, patting his chest. "My own memories. They wiped me, used me, and when I found the backup drive, I ran. Only... I don't know how to crack the encryption on the drive. Somebody in the sector told me there was a phantom living at The Last Outpost. A former Core-slicer who goes by the name 'Nettle.' Said she could crack a Vanguard vault with a bobby pin and a broken datapad." The ambient chatter of the bar seems to fade into a dull roar. The cozy warmth of the amber lights suddenly feels suffocatingly hot. I stare at the spot beneath my rag. I’ve polished it so hard I can see my own wide, terrified eyes reflecting back at me in the varnish. He reaches into his singed jacket and pulls out a sleek, obsidian data-cylinder, laying it right beside my hand. "I've got maybe two hours before their long-range scanners pick up my warp-trail and lead them right to this asteroid," the stranger says, his silver eyes pleading. "Please. Do you know where I can find her?" Just then, the proximity alarms on the Outpost’s master comm-board begin to chime—a soft, rhythmic pinging that means multiple unscheduled ships have just dropped out of hyperspace at the edge of the belt. I look from the flashing red light on the wall, down to the obsidian cylinder, and finally to my rag. "Pour yourself another drink, pal," I say softly, my voice steady despite the tremor in my hands. "It's going to be a long night."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt. It maintains first-person, present tense throughout, establishes the cozy sci-fi atmosphere efficiently, delivers roughly the requested dialogue ratio, introduces a clear conflict (the stranger hunted by Vanguard, Nets' hidden past exposed), and ends without resolving it — the approaching ships are a well-timed cliffhanger. The cozy opening with Barnaby and T'Lara grounds Nets' role as arbiter of outpost drama, and the recurring rag-polishing motif is a nice show-don't-tell device for her anxiety. Flaws: a stray untranslated Chinese phrase ("the气压—the barometric vibe") breaks immersion and reads as an artifact; a missing space ("grateful,albeit"); some exposition is delivered via convenient info-dump (the stranger explaining the phantom slicer rumor is a bit on-the-nose, though functional). The "memories stolen/backed up on a drive" premise is familiar territory, and the ending line "It's going to be a long night" is a touch clichéd. Characterization of Nets is competent but somewhat stock — the ex-hacker-with-a-past bartender is a recognizable archetype, though the tentacle-dread color-coding and worldbuilding details add texture. Prose is clean and rhythmic with only occasional overwriting ("threatening to shatter the peaceful life I've spent five years building brick by careful brick" edges toward overwrought). Emotionally engaging and coherent overall.
