Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The guy in the rusted Ford Ranger didn't even slow to a complete stop. He just leaned across the stained bench seat, shoved the passenger door open, and grunted, "End of the line, kid." So here I am. Downtown New Orleans. The air feels like breathing through a hot, wet washcloth, and it smells like a weird mix of deep-fried dough, stale beer, and horse piss. I hike my backpack up, and the stupid left strap immediately slides right back down my shoulder. The plastic buckle cracked somewhere outside of Hattiesburg, and now the whole thing hangs crooked, digging into my collarbone. I’m sixteen, I have forty-three dollars in crumpled ones and fives, and I am officially a runaway. Mr. Miller, my smug-ass guidance counselor with the coffee-stained teeth, is probably having a field day with this. *Concerning behavioral patterns,* he’d told my mom over the phone last month after I set off a smoke bomb in the boys' locker room. Like, sorry I didn't want to quietly rot away in a town whose only cultural landmark is a Sonic Drive-In. Back home, you either die of boredom or you invent some drama. Except two days ago, I didn't invent drama. I sat at the kitchen table, staring at the peeling laminate, and told my parents the truth. That the girl they thought they were raising doesn't exist. Never did. I’m Taylor, and I’m not their daughter. My dad didn't even yell at first. He just looked at me like I was a rabid dog that had wandered into his living room. My mom started crying and praying at the same time. The next forty-eight hours were a blur of slammed doors, threats about a " wilderness camp" in Utah, and this crushing, suffocating panic. So last night, I packed a bag in thirty minutes, climbed out my bedroom window, and headed south. Now, walking down Decatur Street, the panic is starting to curdle into something heavier. My stomach growls, loud and pathetic. The strap slips off my shoulder again, the heavy canvas bag thumping against my hip. I yank it up so hard the frayed nylon burns my palm. "You keep fighting that bag, it's gonna win," a voice says. I freeze, heart hammering against my ribs. Sitting on the steps of a boarded-up storefront is a guy—maybe seventeen or eighteen. He’s wearing a sleeveless denim vest covered in safety pins and faded band patches, and his dark hair is buzzed on one side. He’s peeling an orange with a pocketknife that looks way too big to be legal. "I'm fine," I say, trying to make my voice drop into that lower register I’ve been practicing. It cracks on the last word. Great. Very intimidating. He pops an orange slice into his mouth, dark eyes scanning me from my beat-up Vans to my sleep-deprived face. "You got that fresh-off-the-interstate look. Where you from? Mississippi? Bama?" "Tennessee," I mutter, before I can stop myself. *Stupid. Don't give out details.* "Ah. Running from Jesus or running from the cops?" He holds out a piece of the orange on the flat of the knife blade. I look at the blade, then at his face. There’s a faded bruise yellowing along his jawline, and his knuckles are scabbed over. "Maybe I'm just on vacation." He laughs, a sharp, barking sound, and pulls the knife back, eating the fruit himself. "Yeah, right. With a busted Jansport and yesterday's eyeliner smudged under your eyes. I'm Jude." "Taylor." I shift my weight. The goddamn strap slides down my arm again. I just let it hang from my elbow this time. "Do you know where I can get something cheap to eat? Like, really cheap?" Jude stands up, folding the knife and slipping it into his pocket. He’s taller than me, skinny in a way that looks like he’s missed a lot of meals. "Follow me. And don't look so terrified, Taylor from Tennessee. The vultures down here can smell fresh meat from three blocks away." I know I shouldn't follow a stranger with a knife down an unfamiliar street. Every PSA I’ve ever been forced to watch in health class is screaming at me right now. *Stranger danger. Human trafficking. Murder.* But I'm starving, my feet hurt, and honestly, the way Jude looked at me—like he actually saw *me*, not the freaked-out freak my parents saw—makes me take a step forward. The afternoon stretches out, hot and surreal. Jude leads me through the French Quarter, past tarot card readers setting up their folding tables and brass bands warming up on street corners. He shows me a bakery where, if you go around the back alley and knock twice on the screen door, an old woman in a flour-covered apron will hand you a bag of day-old croissants for two bucks. We sit on a concrete wall near the river, tearing into the flaky bread. The Mississippi is massive here, brown and churning, carrying huge cargo ships that look like floating cities. "So," Jude says, wiping crumbs from his vest. "What’s the real story?" I stare at the water. "I told my parents who I really am. They wanted to send me away to get 'fixed.' So I fixed the problem myself and left." Jude nods slowly, not looking surprised at all. "Parents are a trip. They say they love you unconditionally, right up until you violate the terms and conditions." "What about yours?" I ask. His whole posture changes. The easy, street-smart smirk vanishes, replaced by a hard, blank wall. He reaches into his vest pocket, pulls out a battered flip phone, checks the screen, and snaps it shut. "Dead to me. Or I'm dead to them. Doesn't really matter which." A shadow falls over us. I look up and see a guy in his twenties standing a few feet away. He’s wearing a pristine white tracksuit that looks ridiculous in this heat, and he’s staring dead at Jude. "You're late, man," the tracksuit guy says. His voice is calm, which somehow makes my skin crawl. "Marcus is getting pissed. You got the drop?" Jude stands up fast, stepping slightly in front of me. "Tell Marcus I'm getting it tonight. I had a setback." The guy’s eyes flick to me, cold and assessing. "Who's the kid?" "Nobody," Jude snaps, an edge of panic creeping into his voice. "Just a tourist asking for directions. Tell Marcus I'll be at the warehouse at ten." The guy stares for another agonizing second, then spits on the pavement and walks away. My heart is in my throat. The croissant turns to lead in my stomach. "Jude, what was that? Who is Marcus?" "Nothing. Just some local drama," Jude says, not meeting my eyes. His hands are shaking slightly as he shoves them into his pockets. *Drama.* Right. Back home, drama was spray-painting a dick on the principal’s Prius. Down here, drama wears a tracksuit and looks like it carries a gun. The sun is starting to sink, painting the sky a bruised purple. The streetlights flicker on, and the city's energy shifts into something louder, sharper, and infinitely more dangerous. "Look, you can crash at my squat tonight," Jude says, finally looking at me. He looks younger suddenly. Scared. "It's an abandoned house up in the Bywater. No AC, and you gotta watch for nails in the floorboards, but it's dry." I look at him, really look at him. He's hiding something huge, something that got his jaw bruised and has him answering to guys like Marcus. Trusting him is probably a terrible idea. Then I think about my mom's weeping, my dad's cold fury, and the dark, empty streets of New Orleans stretching out behind me. I yank my backpack strap back up onto my shoulder, holding it in place with my fist so it can't slip again. "Okay," I say. "Lead the way."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt's requirements with notable competence. It maintains first person, mixed tense, and Taylor's sardonic teen voice throughout, with the internal monologue threaded naturally into the action. The opening efficiently re-establishes the backstory (coming out, the counselor, the escape) without dumping it wholesale, and the emotional stakes of the family rejection land with genuine weight. Taylor is a well-drawn protagonist: defensive, wry, self-aware about their own bad decisions ("Stupid. Don't give out details"). The voice practicing a lower register and having it crack is a small, effective characterizing detail. Jude is a solid foil—street-smart but visibly damaged, with the bruised jaw and scabbed knuckles doing quiet work. The tracksuit encounter introduces menace economically, and Jude's panic there is convincing. Weaknesses: the plot machinery is somewhat familiar. The mysterious runaway with a dangerous debt to a shadowy "Marcus" is well-trodden territory, and the tracksuit gangster is a stock figure. The bakery back-door knock is a charming touch, but the "vultures can smell fresh meat" line and the closing "Lead the way" beat are predictable genre moves. Some of the telling ("the city's energy shifts into something louder, sharper, and infinitely more dangerous") leans on summary rather than sensation. The parents' reaction, while painful, is rendered in shorthand ("crying and praying at the same time") that borders on caricature of the Southern religious family. Still, the prose flows well, the dialogue has texture and rhythm, the emotional complexity—terror, hunger, loneliness, the desperate need to be seen—is authentic, and the ending's ambivalence (trusting a stranger because the alternative is worse) is earned rather than sentimental. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Great Unplugging had not gone down the way the cinema had promised. There had been a distinct lack of leather chaps, and far too much queuing for lukewarm cabbage soup before everyone decided to just hit each other with ergonomic keyboards. Now, fifty years later, the world consisted mostly of rust, suspiciously geometric weeds, and Midas. Midas was currently squatting behind a petrified sofa in the ruins of what the Ancients had called a "Strip Mall," though historical consensus was still divided on whether one went there to undress or to be peeled. "We are out of beans," Midas whispered, peering through a pair of binoculars that only had one lens, making them, technically, a monocular with delusions of grandeur. "And the water filter is making a noise like a dying badger. Therefore, we must brave the Vault of Bargains." Beside him, propped against a cinderblock, sat Chewy. Chewy was an animatronic koala from the Before Times. Time and a brief, misunderstood encounter with a mutated terrier had relieved Chewy of his left ear and most of his synthetic eucalyptus-scented fur, exposing the oxidized brass and grey plastic beneath. His left eye was a proud, glowing red LED; his right was a blue trousers button Midas had sewn on for symmetry. Chewy’s jaw clicked twice, a servo whining in his chest, before he spoke in a voice that sounded like a barbershop quartet being dragged backward through a hedge. *"Bazinga!"* Chewy declared to the desolate wasteland. *"Ask your doctor if internal bleeding is right for you!"* "A grim omen, I agree," Midas sighed, adjusting his armor, which was largely composed of flattened license plates and optimism. "The Vault is currently occupied by the Silicon Brotherhood, who worship a broken photocopier, and at least one feral Roomba the size of a Buick. Stealth is our watchword." *"Taste the rainbow, motherf—"* Chewy’s voice box shorted out in a brief shower of sparks, before resetting with a cheerful chime. *"I’m lovin’ it!"* "Right then. Onward." Midas was not a natural survivor. Natural survivors had names like 'Blade' or 'Grit' and knew which mosses were edible. Midas had been named after a mythological king who died of starvation because he didn't understand basic economics, or alternatively, after an ancient muffler repair shop. Either way, Midas possessed a gravitational pull for misfortune so dense it practically bent light. He slung Chewy into his backpack—ears poking out the top—and crept across the cracked asphalt toward the looming, faded blue facade of the Vault of Bargains. The plan was simple: slip through the shattered automatic doors, locate the legendary Aisle Four, acquire tins of food that didn't rattle when shaken, and leave before the local fauna noticed. It was a good plan. It lasted approximately eleven seconds. Midas stepped over a threshold that had once welcomed millions of bargain-hunters and immediately caught his boot on a tangled nest of cassette tape. In attempting to regain his balance, he Windmilled of Death into a towering display of petrified kitty litter. The resulting avalanche sounded like two skeletons having a vigorous disagreement inside a biscuit tin. Silence fell over the cavernous gloom of the superstore. Then, from the direction of the Customer Service desk, came the rhythmic, ominous *thump-thump-squeak* of the Silicon Brotherhood. They wore robes woven from ethernet cables and helmets made from gutted CRT monitors. "Ah," said Midas, flat on his back in a snowdrift of calcified clay. From the backpack came a whirring of gears. Chewy’s head rotated a full two hundred and seventy degrees, his red LED eye sweeping the gloom. *"Have you or a loved one been diagnosed with mesothelioma?"* the koala bellowed at maximum volume. *"Act now! Supplies are limited!"* *"Heresy!"* shrieked the lead cultist, pointing a jagged RAM stick at Midas. *"He speaks the Forbidden Pop-Ups! Format him!"* Midas scrambled to his feet. "No, wait! I have coupons!" he yelled, though he wasn't entirely sure what a coupon was, only that the Ancients believed they could ward off financial ruin. A cultist hurled a brick-sized Nokia phone. It missed Midas’s head by an inch and embedded itself three inches deep into a concrete pillar, entirely undamaged. Midas didn't wait for the reload. He bolted down the nearest aisle, which happened to be Sporting Goods, skidding on a spill of forty-year-old protein powder. Behind him, the cultists chanted in binary, their monitor-helmets bobbing. Ahead of him, something large, round, and furious woke up. The Mega-Roomba had evolved—or rather, been heavily modified by a madman with a welding torch and too much free time—to clean up the apocalypse. It had circular saws for side-brushes and a bumper coated in rusty nails. Its status light turned from a placid green to a homicidal scarlet. It beeped once, a sound full of malice and dust-bunnies, and charged. "Left! Go left!" Midas told himself, and promptly went right, crashing through a decaying drywall partition into Hardware. The Roomba didn't bother with doors. It simply ate the wall. The cultists, seeing the great Dust-Eater awakened, began prostrating themselves in the rubble, offering up prayers and loose toner cartridges. Midas sprinted toward the sunlight of the loading bay, clutching a single, dented can he had swiped blindly from a shelf in passing. The Roomba was gaining, its vacuum turbine roaring like a jet engine with bronchitis. "Chewy, do something!" Midas wheezed. *"Red Bull gives you wings!"* Chewy shrieked, and whether by providence or a loose spring, his left arm detached entirely from its socket and bounced beneath the Roomba’s forward caster wheel. The great machine hit the plastic limb, hydroplaned on a patch of ancient motor oil, and careened violently into a display of cast-iron skillets, trapping itself in a loud, metallic purgatory. Midas didn't look back until they were safely bolted inside their home base—the rusted hulk of an overturned municipal bus. He collapsed onto a mattress stuffed with shredded tax returns, panting, bleeding from three distinct and embarrassing places, and missing the heel of his left boot. He pulled Chewy from the pack and set the one-armed marsupial on an overturned milk crate. "Well," Midas gasped, holding up his singular prize. The label was gone, save for the word *PATE* and a picture of a very smug-looking cat. "It’s protein. Probably." Chewy’s remaining ear twitched. A tiny plume of grey smoke drifted from his left nostril. His jaw unhinged with a tired *clack*. *"Maybe she’s born with it,"* Chewy rasped, his red eye flickering dimly. *"Maybe it’s... low battery."* "Yeah," Midas sighed, reaching for the tin opener and a roll of duct tape. "Me too, buddy. Me too."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a genuinely strong piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's voice with surprising fidelity. The opening line—"The Great Unplugging had not gone down the way the cinema had promised"—immediately establishes the wry, footnote-adjacent tone the prompt requested. The worldbuilding is delivered through dry asides (the Strip Mall etymological debate, the "ergonomic keyboards" as weapons) rather than exposition dumps, which is exactly the Pratchett mode. Chewy is the story's best invention: an animatronic koala whose corrupted advertising voiceboard spits out mangled slogans ("Ask your doctor if internal bleeding is right for you!") functions as both comic relief and accidental oracle. The device is used with discipline—each glitch is a punchline, and the final "Maybe it's... low battery" lands a genuinely bittersweet note that earns the story's closing beat. Midas's name etymology joke (mythological king vs. muffler shop) is a nice touch of self-aware absurdity. The plot follows the requested structure precisely: deliberation at home base, a mission (Aisle Four, the beans), escalating catastrophe (cassette tape trip, Silicon Brotherhood, Mega-Roomba), and a return home battered but intact with a single dented can of cat pâté. The "worse for wear" ending is honored: Midas is bleeding from "three distinct and embarrassing places," Chewy is one-armed, and the prize is dubious. The lightness of the ending is earned by the established tone rather than imposed. Minor criticisms: the humor occasionally leans on familiar internet-era jokes (the indestructible Nokia is a well-worn meme; "Bazinga" is borrowed rather than invented), which slightly dents the originality. The Mega-Roomba resolution—Chewy's arm detaching "whether by providence or a loose spring"—is a touch convenient, though the story lampshades it. Some similes ("jet engine with bronchitis," "barbershop quartet dragged backward through a hedge") are excellent; a few gags (skeletons in a biscuit tin) are near-Pratchett but slightly derivative of his actual cadence. The prose is clean, rhythmically controlled, and never purple. Dialogue is minimal but functional; Chewy's corrupted lines do the heavy lifting and do it well. Coherence is high throughout; the piece never meanders despite packing a full arc into ~1000 words. Emotionally it's primarily comedic, with a light melancholy at the close that is understated rather than complex. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 60.7
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The brass bell above the door of *Caban Llyfrau* didn’t just ring; it panicked, rattling violently against the glass as a tall figure threw himself inside, slamming the heavy oak door shut behind him. Ffion dropped her pricing gun. It clattered onto the counter, breaking the sacred, dusty silence of her Tuesday afternoon. The man pressed his back against the wood, chest heaving. He was wearing a drenched Burberry trench coat, dark sunglasses despite the gloom of the Welsh rain outside, and a look of theatrical martyrdom. Slowly, he peeled the glasses off, revealing a pair of startlingly blue eyes and a jawline that had recently been plastered across the side of every double-decker bus in the UK. Julian Vance. Ffion’s heart did an involuntary, traitorous gymnastics routine against her ribs. She immediately smoothed her expression into one of mild retail irritation, shoving her trembling hands into the pockets of her oversized cardigan. "Tell me," Julian breathed, his voice a rich, gravelly baritone trained at RADA and perfected in Hollywood bedrooms. He flashed a crooked, devastating smile—Number Four in his repertoire, meant to inspire instant maternal forgiveness. "Do you offer sanctuary to the hunted, or are you going to toss me back to the wolves?" Outside, two men with telescopic lenses jogged past the rain-streaked bay window, oblivious. "Depends," Ffion said, her Welsh lilt cool and entirely unimpressed. "Are the wolves paying customers? Because right now, you're just dripping all over my floorboards." Julian’s smile faltered for a microsecond. People didn’t usually talk to him about floorboards. People usually gasped, dropped things, or asked him to sign their chests. He recalibrated, leaning an elbow on a precarious stack of hardbacks and turning the charm up to eleven. "My deepest apologies. I’ll buy you a new floor. The whole shop, if you like, provided it comes with a place to hide for twenty minutes." He extended a hand. "I'm Julian." "I'm aware of who you are, Mr. Vance. Your face is currently blocking the sun on a billboard near the M4," Ffion said, ignoring the hand and gesturing with her chin toward his elbow. "And you’re leaning on a first-edition Dylan Thomas. If you crush the spine, you actually *will* be buying the shop." Julian snatched his arm back as if the books were hot coals. "Right. Sorry." He looked at her closely now, the practiced smoothness slipping just a fraction. She had dark, unruly curls pinned up with a biro, a smudge of ink on her cheek, and fierce, intelligent brown eyes. Why wasn't she swooning? He was very good at making people swoon. He *needed* her to swoon, just a little, to right the axis of his universe. "Not a fan of my work, then?" he asked, tilting his head, injecting a note of boyish vulnerability into his tone. "Was it *Shattered Crown*? Because I assure you, the accent was the director's fault." "I don't watch much cinema," Ffion lied. She had seen *Shattered Crown* twice at the tiny theater in Carmarthen, and had spent a week afterwards annoyed by how much she’d fancied him in chainmail. Her pulse was currently hammering in her throat, so she turned away, busying herself with straightening a display of local history pamphlets. "And if you’re staying, you can’t lurk by the door. Go into the back aisle. The light is terrible, they won't see you through the glass." Julian followed her like an overly eager stray dog. The shop was narrow, smelling of vanilla, old paper, and damp wool. He stopped beside her counter, his eyes catching on a large, glass-topped wooden box sitting next to the antique till. Inside, pinned to velvet, were dozens of moths. Beside the box lay a magnifying lamp, fine-tipped forceps, and a small bottle of clear liquid. "Wait a second," Julian said, the affected actor’s cadence dropping out of his voice entirely. He leaned over the counter, invading her space, smelling impossibly good—like cedarwood and rain. "Is that a setting board? Are you mounting *Lepidoptera*?" Ffion froze, her cheeks warming. People usually found her hobby macabre. "They’re ethically sourced. Found dead in greenhouses or my garden shed." "No, look at the wing span on that Privet Hawk-moth," Julian said, genuine awe overriding his smooth persona. He pointed a long finger at the glass. "You relaxed the joints with hot water? Or do you use ethyl acetate?" Ffion stared at him, her carefully constructed apathy crumbling. "Hot water and a tiny bit of thymol to stop the mold. Wait. How do you know what a Privet Hawk-moth looks like?" Julian looked up, and suddenly, the distance between them felt very small. The movie star was gone; in his place was a man looking a little sheepish, his ego entirely unguarded. "My granddad was a groundskeeper in Sussex," Julian admitted quietly. "Used to set up a white sheet and a mercury vapor lamp in the summer. Only time I ever sat still as a kid was waiting for the Emperor moths to land. I tried bringing a light-trap to a shoot in Prague last year, and my publicist threatened to resign. Said 'bug collecting' wasn't sexy." Ffion’s breath hitched. He was looking at her with such earnest hope—not the arrogant demand for adoration he’d walked in with, but a quiet plea to be understood. It was infinitely more dangerous than his smile. "Your publicist is an idiot," Ffion said softly, her voice losing its sharp edge. "Have they ever seen a Garden Tiger moth? They’re stunning." "Right?" Julian’s face lit up, a real smile breaking across his features, crinkling the corners of his eyes in a way the airbrushed posters always erased. It knocked the wind right out of her. "The orange hindwings! Absolute showstoppers. Though, looking at this—" He tapped the glass above a smaller, muted brown specimen. "—your pinning on the Herald moth is a bit crooked. Left forewing is dragging." Ffion gasped, a laugh bubbling up before she could stop it. "Excuse me! My pinning is immaculate. The specimen was damaged when I found it in the coal scuttle!" "A likely story," Julian murmured. His gaze dropped from her eyes to her mouth, the teasing atmosphere suddenly thickening into something heavy and electric. He leaned in just an inch closer across the counter. "A poor craftsman blames the coal scuttle." Ffion swallowed hard, entirely forgetting to be immune to him. "Well, you’re welcome to show me how it's done, Mr. Vance. If you think your hands are steady enough." Julian looked at the forceps, then back up at her flushed cheeks. His heart gave a strange, unfamiliar lurch. He didn't care if the paparazzi were gone. "Lock the door," he said softly, shrugging off his wet trench coat. "Put the 'Closed' sign up. I'm about to blow your mind."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This scene executes the brief with notable skill. The premise (actor fleeing paparazzi into a Welsh bookstore) is delivered efficiently, and the dynamic requested—rogue with fragile ego meets superficially immune owner—is dramatized rather than merely stated. Julian's need to be liked is shown through his "recalibrating" smiles and internal need for her to swoon; Ffion's flustered interior is rendered via her lie about not watching cinema and her "traitorous" pulse. The moth-collecting shared interest is a genuinely clever device to derail the charm offensive: it strips his persona, reveals vulnerability, and shifts the power balance believably. The dialogue is distinct and lively—his theatrical baritone versus her dry Welsh deflection—and the banter about the Herald moth's crooked pinning lands as playful flirtation with real specificity (thymol, mercury vapor lamps, Privet Hawk-moths—well-researched detail). Weaknesses: the prose occasionally overreaches ("her heart did an involuntary, traitorous gymnastics routine," "perfected in Hollywood bedrooms" is a slightly crass cliché). The ending—"Lock the door... I'm about to blow your mind"—veers into cheesy innuendo that undercuts the otherwise subtle chemistry, and the transformation from wariness to invitation happens a touch fast, though the moth-connection groundwork mostly earns it. Some beats are familiar (the "are you a fan" exchange, the billboard reference), and the paparazzi threat conveniently evaporates from the scene's tension. Still, the piece is coherent, well-paced at ~1000 words, emotionally engaging, and shows rather than tells for the most part. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 77.8
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The heavy iron door yielded not with a shriek of rusted hinges, as Aya had anticipated, but with the greased, silent slide of well-maintained machinery. The air that exhaled from the underhold was thick with the cloying stench of refined whale oil, ozone, and the briny rot of the bilge. Aya stepped across the threshold, her velvet-shod boots making no sound upon the slick flagstones. Behind her, Katra’s hand rested on the grip of a brass-platedpepperbox pistol, while Simeon brought up the rear, his breath shallow. In the suffocating quiet, the intricate clockwork pocket watch nestled in Simeon’s brocade waistcoat seemed to amplify, its steady *tick-tick-tick* counting down the seconds of their audacity. In the center of the subterranean vault, bathed in the sickly, greenish luminescence of spermaceti lamps, rested the Scythan artifact. It was a monolith of petrified Leviathan bone, etched with non-Euclidean geometries that made Aya’s eyes water and the dark *immateria* beneath her skin hum with a ravenous, phantom itch. Before she could summon a tendril of the void to unpick the arcane wards, the shadows detached themselves from the vaulted pillars. *Click-clack.* The unmistakable sound of heavy harpoon-rifles being cocked echoed through the chamber. A dozen burly figures stepped into the green light, their faces obscured by brass-goggled gas masks, the glass canisters on their backs bubbling with pressurized oil. And then, a slow, rhythmic clapping. "A bold play, Little Wraith," a voice purred, gravelly as coal dust and twice as suffocating. "Truly. I almost admire the gall." Aya froze. The blood in her veins turned to glacial slush. Stepping from behind the Scythan plinth was Vespera, the Matriarch of the Morska. She was decidedly un-incarcerated. Her oilskin duster was immaculate, and the twin whale-bone pistols at her hips were leveled squarely at Aya’s chest. "Bloody hells," Katra hissed, her fingers twitching over her weapon. "The broadsheets said the Magistracy had you in the Iron Hulks by dawn." "And you believed the broadsheets?" Vespera chuckled, a wet, rattling sound. "Drop the iron, Katra. If my boys pull these triggers, there won’t be enough of you left to chum the harbor." *Think,* Aya commanded herself, her mind racing through the thermodynamic probabilities of the room. *Summon a shade. Rip the veil.* Yet, as she reached for the cold dark of the *immateria*, she saw the runes etched into the floorboards at her feet. Salt-silver and scrimshawed wards. A dead-zone. Vespera hadn't just anticipated a coup; she had prepared for *her*. *Tick-tick-tick,* went Simeon’s watch. "Simeon, Katra, stand down," Aya said, her voice muffled by the porcelain visor of her mask. "We are outmaneuvered." With a curse, Katra let her pistol clatter to the stones. Two of Vespera’s brutes surged forward, their whale-leather coats creaking. Aya didn’t resist as rough, calloused hands wrenched her arms behind her back, snapping cold iron manacles around her wrists. Beside her, Simeon whimpered as a rifle butt drove him to his knees, and Katra was forced down beside him. "I fed the Constabulary a decoy and a purse of sovereigns," Vespera explained, sauntering toward them. The amber lenses of her spectacles caught the green lamplight. "Nothing smokes out ambitious rats quite like the scent of an empty throne. Especially rats who dabble in the dark arts." Vespera stopped before Aya. "Now, let us see the face of the terror who has been summoning nightmares from the abyss to do her lockpicking." Vespera’s leather-gloved hand shot out, seizing the porcelain edge of Aya’s mask. With a brutal yank, the ribbon snapped. The cold, dank air of the underhold hit Aya’s flushed cheeks. For a moment, nobody breathed. Only Simeon’s watch dared to speak. *Tick-tick-tick.* Vespera blinked, leaning in close. The Matriarch’s lip curled, first in confusion, and then in wicked, triumphant comprehension. "Well, strike me blind," Vespera whispered. "Lady Aya Vance. The Earl of Ashbourne’s porcelain doll." She threw her head back and laughed, a harsh bark that bounced off the damp stone. "An aristocrat! Slumming it in the gutters with the cutthroats!" "Aya?" Katra’s voice was a jagged shard of betrayal. She stared up at Aya’s high cheekbones and braided raven hair. "You're a bleeding *peer*?" Aya kept her chin raised, though her stomach plummeted into the abyss. The disgrace of the Morska was one thing; the discovery of her bloodline’s cursed affinity was another. She saw, with terrifying clarity, the silhouette of her mother swinging from the gallows at Tyburn Wharf, her neck snapped for the crime of whispering to the *immateria*. If the Magistracy learned Lady Vance was a practitioner, the Earl’s title wouldn't save her from the noose. "A dead peer, soon enough," Vespera sneered, raising a pistol and pressing the cold, oily barrel directly between Aya’s eyes. "I don't tolerate traitors, highborn or otherwise." *Tick-tick-tick.* The watch was a frantic heartbeat now. "Pull that trigger, Vespera, and you shoot away a king's ransom," Aya said. Her voice was remarkably steady, honing the haughty, clipped cadence of the drawing rooms she despised. "I am the sole heiress to the Vance Leviathan Yards. My father controls a third of the city's refined oil." Vespera paused, her finger resting heavy on the brass trigger. "Go on." "My corpse is a liability that will bring the High Constabulary and my father’s private militia down upon this underhold like the wrath of God," Aya pressed, her eyes locked onto Vespera’s. "Alive, however... I am leverage. I am shipping manifests. I am pardons signed in my father’s hand. I am worth more to you breathing than bleeding on your floor." "You think your daddy will pay to keep your little secret?" Vespera tilted her head, the barrel indenting Aya’s skin. "That his precious daughter is a witch? A vessel for the Void?" *He might let me hang just to scrub the stain from the family crest,* Aya thought darkly, the gothic horror of her reality closing in like a coffin lid. *But Vespera doesn't know that.* "He values the Vance name above all else," Aya lied smoothly. "He will emptied his vaults to ensure it is not dragged into the muck of a public execution. Kill my companions, and the deal is off. Keep us alive, and you own the House of Vance." Simeon’s watch ticked into the suffocating silence. One second. Two. Three. Slowly, Vespera lowered the hammer of the pistol with her thumb. She smiled, revealing teeth stained yellow from pipe-weed. "Lock them in the brine-cells," Vespera ordered her men. "It seems the Morska has just gone into the kidnapping business."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response is a strong execution of the prompt. It hits every required story beat: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the un-incarcerated guild leader (Vespera), is captured without a fight scene, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates for her life as a hostage while grappling internally with the exposure of both her aristocratic identity and her outlawed magickal heritage. The whalepunk/steampunk-Victorian aesthetic is consistently rendered—spermaceti lamps, whale-bone pistols, harpoon-rifles, oilskin dusters, the Leviathan Yards—and the gothic horror register is present in the non-Euclidean artifact, the dead-zone wards, and Aya's recurring vision of her mother's gallows. Third person past tense with internal monologue: check. Dialogue is period-flavored and character-distinct (Vespera's gravelly menace, Katra's betrayal, Aya's drawing-room diction as armor). Weaknesses: a few typographical/editing slips ("brass-platedpepperbox," "He will emptied his vaults") slightly undermine polish. Some imagery is stock or over-familiar for the genre ("blood turned to glacial slush," "the wrath of God," "racing through thermodynamic probabilities" is a nice touch though). The ticking watch motif is effective but borders on formulaic suspense shorthand. Vespera's capitulation to Aya's argument is a touch convenient—she folds quickly after one speech—but it is plausibly motivated by greed and the logic of leverage, so it mostly earns its place. The ending ("kidnapping business") lands with appropriate grim wit rather than false positivity. Prose is generally elegant with occasional overwrought flourishes ("gravelly as coal dust and twice as suffocating" works; "the gothic horror of her reality closing in like a coffin lid" is a bit on-the-nose meta-labeling). Emotionally, the piece engages via Aya's dual terror—social ruin and death—though Katra and Simeon remain thin, functional figures. Overall a competent, atmospheric, well-structured scene with minor craft blemishes. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 76.3
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The ceiling fan in the Rusty Anchor doesn’t so much circulate the air as it chops the humidity into thick, breathable slices. It smells like stale beer, cheap bleach, and the kind of desperation that only festers in port towns. Spike Spiegel sits at the sticky mahogany bar, nursing a warm gin and tonic. His stomach growls, a hollow, familiar ache reminding him that the last thing he ate was a questionable synthesized protein bar thirty-six hours ago. He pulls a crumpled pack of cigarettes from his blue suit jacket, straightens a bent filter with his lips, and flicks his Zippo. A ring of rust on Spike’s lighter suggests it’s been dropped in water more than once, a souvenir from a dozen bad days. The flame catches, illuminating his mismatched eyes—one looking at the present, the other forever stuck in the past. The heavy wooden door slams open, rattling the bottles behind the bar. She walks in like she owns the oxygen in the room. Cut-off denim shorts, a black crop top that leaves little to the imagination, and twin leather holsters slung across her shoulders like a second skin. A tribal dragon tattoo snakes up her right arm, flexing as she shoves a drunk sailor out of her path. "Bacardi," she barks at the bartender, dropping onto the stool two seats down from Spike. "Leave the bottle. And if it’s watered down, I’ll use your kneecaps for target practice." Spike exhales a long plume of gray smoke, watching her out of the corner of his good eye. "Rough night?" Revy turns her head slowly, her dark eyes narrowing as she takes in the lanky guy with the ridiculous fluffy hair and the relaxed slouch. She pulls a cigarette from her own pack, sticking it between her teeth. "Mind your own fucking business, beanpole. Unless you’re volunteering to be the target." Spike just smiles, lazy and entirely unbothered. He slides his rusted Zippo across the polished wood. It stops right in front of her. "Just making conversation. Waiting on a guy. Figured you might be waiting on the same one." Revy stares at the lighter, then at Spike. She snatches it, flicks it open, and lights her smoke, inhaling deeply before tossing the metal casing back at his chest. He catches it with fluid, effortless grace. "Mateo Cruz," she says, her voice dropping an octave, thick with gravel and nicotine. "Five million woolongs. Or fifty grand in US paper, depending on who’s paying. And he’s mine." "Funny," Spike murmurs, swirling the melted ice in his glass. "My partner told me he was ours. And I really need the beef with bell peppers tonight." Revy barks out a harsh, humorless laugh, pouring herself a brimming shot of rum and throwing it back. "Too bad, cowboy. I don't split checks, and I don't share bounties." Before Spike can offer a philosophical quip, the back booth explodes into motion. Mateo Cruz—a grease-slicked cartel runner with more nerve than brains—kicks his table over, his four bodyguards drawing submachine guns in a chorus of metallic clicks. "Shit," Spike sighs, already sliding off his stool like water spilling from a glass. Revy grins, a feral, terrifying expression that transforms her entire face. "Finally!" The bar erupts in a deafening symphony of muzzle flashes and shattering glass. Revy doesn't even bother with cover. She vaults over the bar as bullets chew up the wood behind her, drawing her twin custom Berettas—the Sword Cutlasses—in a blur of silver. She pops back up, firing both pistols simultaneously with terrifying, rhythmic precision. Two guards drop instantly, red blossoms painting their chests. Spike moves differently. He flows. A guard rushes him with a combat knife; Spike pivots, deflecting the blade with a loose, open palm in a textbook Jeet Kune Do intercept, following through with a snapping high kick that shatters the man's jaw. In the same fluid motion, he draws his Jericho 941 from beneath his jacket and puts two rounds through the last bodyguard’s shoulder, spinning him into the jukebox. The music dies in a shower of sparks. Smoke hangs heavy in the sudden silence, smelling sharply of cordite and spilled liquor. Mateo is gone, the back door swinging on broken hinges. Revy vaults back over the counter, her boots crunching on broken glass. Her chest is heaving, skin slick with sweat, eyes bright with the high of the gunfight. She looks at the downed men, then locks eyes with Spike. There’s a sudden, electric current between them—an unspoken recognition of a fellow apex predator. "Not bad, suit," she pants, licking her lower lip. "You move like a freak, though." "Whatever happens, happens," Spike says, holstering the Jericho. He nods toward the back door. "He’s heading for the motel across the alley." *** Ten minutes later, the door to Room 104 splinters inward under Revy’s boot. The room is empty, save for an open window with the curtains billowing in the humid night breeze, and a duffel bag spilled across the cheap floral bedspread. Mateo didn't have a bounty on him for stealing cash; he was hunted for stealing from his bosses. The bag is empty. Mateo is in the wind, probably already on a speedboat out of the harbor. "Mother*fucker*!" Revy roars, kicking a rickety wooden chair so hard it shatters against the peeling wallpaper. Spike steps into the room, closing the broken door behind him as best he can. The single neon sign outside flashes red, then blue, casting stark, shifting shadows across the cramped space. "Looks like nobody’s eating tonight." Revy whirls on him, her frustration boiling over. In a flash, both silver Berettas are up, one aimed squarely between Spike’s eyes. Simultaneously, the cold black barrel of Spike’s Jericho presses firmly beneath her chin, tilting her head back slightly. They freeze. The distance between them is less than an arm's length. Spike can smell the rum on her breath, mixed with gun oil and cheap soap. Revy stares down the length of his arm, taking in the absolute stillness of his posture. He isn't afraid. Worse, he looks almost bored, like a man waiting for a train that’s already derailed. "You think you're fast enough?" she whispers, her finger tightening fractionally on the trigger. Her pulse is hammering in her throat, right against the muzzle of his gun. It isn't fear; it's an intoxicating, violent thrill. "I'll blow your fucking head off before your finger twitches." "Maybe," Spike says, his voice a low rumble in the dark. His good eye drops to her parted lips, then back up to her fierce, damaged gaze. "I’ve already died once. Wouldn't be much of a surprise." "Bullshit artist," she scoffs, though she doesn't pull the trigger. Instead, she steps *into* his space, forcing the barrel of the Jericho to slide down her throat until it rests between her collarbones. Her other gun comes up, pressing into his ribs. "You're just another dead man walking. I know the look." "Takes one to know one, Two Hands," Spike murmurs. His free hand comes up, not to disarm her, but to pluck the half-smoked cigarette from her lips. He puts it between his own, takes a drag, and blows the smoke over her shoulder. The sheer audacity of it makes her breath hitch. Revy’s eyes darken. With a sudden, aggressive surge, she grabs the lapel of his blue jacket, yanking him down until their noses are practically brushing. The metal of their guns clicks together between their bodies, a lethal cage of their own making. "I'm not a good person, not a bad person," she breathes against his mouth, a warning and an invitation tangled together. "I'm just here. And right now, you're in my way." Spike looks at her—really looks at her—and sees the jagged edges, the bottomless anger, the complete lack of a tomorrow. She’s the exact opposite of Julia, yet entirely the same: a fatal attraction wrapped in gunpowder. He lowers his gun a fraction of an inch, the tension in the room coiling so tight it feels ready to snap and level the whole building. "Then shoot me," he whispers, tilting his head to close the final millimeter between them. "Or put the toys away." In the flashing red light of the motel sign, nobody pulls a trigger, and nobody backs down.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a competent, atmospheric crossover that hits most of the prompt's beats: the seedy bar, the shared bounty, drinking, gunplay, and the motel room standoff with unresolved tension. The prose is generally strong—present tense is maintained, the setting is vivid without being overwrought, and the action choreography is clear and kinetic. Both characters' canonical details are woven in well: Spike's hunger, his lighter, his "already died once" fatalism, his Jeet Kune Do fluidity; Revy's Cutlasses, her dragon tattoo, her profanity, her famous quote repurposed as dialogue. Strengths: The action sequence is well-staged, with distinct fighting styles for each character (Revy's aggressive dual-wielding vs. Spike's flowing interception). The cigarette-sharing moment is a nice character beat—Spike plucking the smoke from her lips is exactly the kind of casual audacity that fits him. The mutual recognition of "fellow apex predators" lands. The ending withholds resolution appropriately, matching the prompt's request for unresolved tension. Weaknesses: The piece leans on familiar noir/crossover tropes without subverting them—the bar fight, the escaped bounty, the standoff are all predictable beats. Some lines are over-explanatory ("an unspoken recognition of a fellow apex predator" tells us what the scene should show). The Julia comparison ("She's the exact opposite of Julia, yet entirely the same") is a bit on-the-nose. Revy's dialogue occasionally slips into generic tough-girl register rather than her specific voice, though it's serviceable. The bounty escaping via speedboat is a convenient plot device to force the motel confrontation. The emotional complexity is present but somewhat surface-level—both characters stay in their archetypes without much genuine vulnerability or surprise. The word count is roughly on target. Minor purple moments ("chops the humidity into thick, breathable slices") are mostly controlled. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
It is easy, from the distance of thirty years, to blame the boredom. In the autumn of 1995, my father’s forestry job dragged us from our bright apartment in Stockholm to a decaying timber house in Västerbotten. At fifteen, the silence of the northern woods felt like a physical weight. When Astrid offered me an escape, I took it without asking where it led. Astrid smelled of cloves and woodsmoke. She wore combat boots and her grandfather’s oversized flannel shirts, and she possessed a local’s casual contempt for the vast, suffocating forest. By October, she had already introduced me to what she called the midnight games. We had melted lead into cold water to see the initials of the boys we’d marry, and we had buried a lock of Sofie Lindqvist’s hair under a rotting birch log to make her fail math. When Sofie actually failed, we laughed until our ribs hurt, drunk on the coincidence and the illicit thrill of our own cruelty. Then came the Friday Astrid suggested *Útiseta*. "Sitting out," she explained as we trudged up the logging road past the edge of the village. My Walkman was shoved deep into the pocket of my denim jacket, the battery long dead. "Farmor told me how the old people did it. You sit on a *hög*—a grave mound—from midnight until the spirits come to answer your questions. Tonight, we’re going to find out what Marcus really did in the gym locker room." "It’s freezing, Astrid," I complained, my breath pluming white in the beam of my flashlight. "And sitting on a grave is gross." "It’s not a graveyard grave," she said, rolling her eyes. "It’s the Bronze Age cairn up by the ridge. Just a pile of stones and moss. Nobody’s cried over those bones in three thousand years. Besides, if we do it right, they have to give us knowledge. That’s the law." We left the gravel road and pushed through the dense spruce forest. The ground was spongy with frost-bitten moss and rotting pine needles. Finally, the trees thinned, revealing a clearing dominated by a low, swelling hillock of earth and lichen-crusted boulders. In the pale wash of the quarter moon, it looked like the spine of a sleeping beast. Astrid became brisk, shedding her teenage slouch for something terribly focused. "Take off your watch," she ordered, stripping off her silver rings. "No iron, no steel, no ticking things. Give me your house keys." I handed them over, my fingers stiff with cold. She tossed our metal belongings into a hollow beneath a pine root, well away from the mound. From her backpack, she pulled an old, stiff reindeer hide that smelled faintly of damp dog and iron. She spread it over the crown of the mound. "We sit back-to-back on the skin," she said, her voice dropping to a businesslike murmur. "Hold this." She pressed a crooked twig of rowan wood into my palm. "Once I say the words, we cannot speak. Not a whisper. And whatever you hear, whatever you think you see, you cannot look behind you, and you cannot step off the hide. If you step off before I tap your shoulder three times, you’ll go mad." "You made that part up," I said, trying to force a laugh. Astrid looked at me, her pale eyes catching the moonlight. "Farmor didn't make things up, Linnea. Sit." We climbed the mound. The stones shifted beneath the moss with a hollow, grinding sound that set my teeth on edge. We sat on the hide, our spine bones pressing together through our heavy coats. Astrid’s back was a warm anchor against the biting chill. She cleared her throat, spat to the left, and spoke a few guttural phrases in a dialect so thick and archaic I couldn't catch a single word. Then, she went entirely still. I stared out at the wall of black pines. The silence of the north rushed in to fill the space left by Astrid’s voice. For the first twenty minutes, I only felt ridiculous. My tailbone ached from the rocks beneath the hide. My nose was running, and I wanted my Walkman. I thought about Stockholm, about streetlights and the rumble of the metro. Then the wind rose. It moved through the high crowns of the pine trees, a dry, sibilant rustling that sounded almost like faint whispers. I shivered, gripping the rowan twig harder. As my eyes adjusted to the gloom, the forest lost its familiarity. The trunks seemed to shift, leaning inward like tall, gaunt men crowding the edge of the clearing. The temperature dropped sharply. The whispers in the pines grew distinct, overlapping like a crowd murmuring in a dark theater. I told myself it was an auditory hallucination—the brain’s desperate attempt to find patterns in white noise. Yet, beneath the wind, I heard a rhythmic crunching, slow and heavy, circling the base of the mound. Someone was walking on the frozen moss. Against my spine, I felt Astrid tremble. She wasn't laughing now. Her breathing was shallow, rapid, and terrified. A smell drifted across the clearing, cutting through the sharp scent of pine. It was the odor of stagnant bog water, wet wool, and old, turned earth. *Ask,* a voice seemed to sigh, right at the edge of my hearing, woven into the creaking of the branches. *Ask us.* I squeezed my eyes shut. We were just two stupid girls playing a game in the dark. We wanted to know about a boy from school. We had brought petty, adolescent static to a place that was deep, hungry, and ancient, and something had actually picked up the receiver. A freezing draft brushed the side of my neck, as intimate as dead fingers lifting my hair. Behind me, Astrid let out a tiny, choked whimper. I didn't wait for the three taps. Blind with panic, I scrambled off the reindeer hide, kicking stones loose as I tumbled down the mound, tearing my jeans and screaming Astrid’s name into the whispering dark.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the brief. It hits the required length (~1000 words), maintains first-person past-tense recollection with the "thirty years later" framing kept largely transparent, and delivers the single midnight excursion with ritual preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions mixing teen pettiness with specific traditional elements (rowan twig, reindeer hide, no iron, spitting left, archaic dialect), and escalating ambiguity. The folk horror texture is convincing: the Bronze Age cairn, the Västerbotten setting, the "midnight games" backstory with Sofie Lindqvist's failed math test establishing the dangerous trivialization of old practices. Strengths: The prose is controlled and evocative without tipping into purple. Astrid is well-drawn—her shift from eye-rolling teen to "terribly focused" ritualist is one of the chapter's best beats. The ambiguity is handled well: whispers in pines explained as auditory hallucination, then undercut by Astrid's genuine terror felt through her spine. The ending—Linnea breaking the taboo by fleeing before the three taps—is a satisfying, ominous close that leaves consequences implied rather than stated. Weaknesses: The voice occasionally slips into adult-essayist register ("the illicit thrill of our own cruelty," "adolescent static... something had actually picked up the receiver")—the receiver metaphor is clever but slightly anachronistic-cute for the moment of terror. The "spine of a sleeping beast" simile is a touch stock. The motive (learning what Marcus did in the locker room) is thin, though plausibly teenage. Some tension beats (temperature drop, smell of bog water) are familiar folk-horror furniture, mildly unsurprising. Dialogue is functional and mostly believable, though Astrid's exposition is a bit neat. The psychological-vs-supernatural balance is maintained, and the darkness is earned through the buildup. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The vinyl of the treatment table sticks to the backs of my thighs, cold until my body heat turns it clammy. Above me, the fluorescent lights hum, washing out the clinical white walls where framed anatomical charts hang like verdicts. "Lie supine," Julian says, not looking up from his clipboard. "Let’s see what the scar tissue is doing today." I resent the authority in his voice almost as much as I resent the insurance mandate that forces me into this room three times a week. Mostly, I resent that Julian is standing there, whole and thriving, wearing a crisp polo shirt pushed up to reveal those ridiculous neon-geometric compression sleeves on his forearms—the exact pair he used to wear when we ran the 400-meter hurdles together in Eugene. Back when we had the same dream, before my right acetabular labrum shredded and took my identity with it. I lower myself onto my back, staring at the ceiling tiles. He sets the clipboard down. When he approaches the right side of the table, the familiar scent of him—cedarwood soap and the faint, sharp tang of wintergreen rub—cuts through the sterile air. My stomach tightens, an involuntary traitor. "Relax your rectus femoris, Maya," he murmurs, his voice dropping an octave into that focused register he used to save for the starting blocks. "You’re guarding before I’ve even touched you." "I'm not guarding," I lie. His hands make contact. His left hand settles firmly over my left anterior superior iliac spine, pinning my pelvis to the table so my hips can't hike or rotate to cheat the stretch. The heat of his palm burns right through the thin nylon of my running shorts. With his right hand, he cradles my right calcaneus, his fingers wrapping around my heel while my calf rests along the neon-patterned Lycra of his forearm. He begins to lift my right leg, flexing both my hip and my knee simultaneously. At ninety degrees, the movement is fine. At a hundred, the deep, fibrotic pinch begins in the crease of my groin. "Breathe through it," Julian says. He leans over me to use his bodyweight, guiding my knee toward my chest. Now his chest is inches from my knee, his face hovering just above my torso. I can see the faint silver scar on his jawline, the dark sweep of his lashes as he watches the angle of my femur, entirely professional, entirely detached—except for the way his jaw muscles clench when I let out a sharp, hitched breath. My hamstring quivers against his forearm. The pain is a hot wire threading through the capsule of my hip, but it’s braided so tightly with the sensation of his hands on me that my nervous system can’t separate the two. My fingers dig into the vinyl edges of the table. "Right there," I grit out. "That’s the wall." "That’s just tissue resistance, not the bone block," he replies softly. His left thumb shifts slightly, pressing into the crease of my hip flexor to palpate the tendon of the iliopsoas. The touch is clinical, precise, and devastatingly intimate. My abdominal muscles flutter beneath my shirt. His eyes flick up, catching mine for a fraction of a second. The clinical mask slips; his pupils are wide, dark, and fixed on my mouth. The air between us goes thick, charged with the memory of hotel rooms in Zurich and Doha, of a tension we never resolved because the track always came first. He looks away first, clearing his throat. "Hold here. Contract against my forearm. Push your thigh back down toward the table. Twenty percent effort." It’s a proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation stretch—contract-relax. I drive the back of my thigh into his neon-sleeved forearm, engaging my glute and hamstring. His bicep swells as he matches my force, keeping my leg completely static in an isometric hold. Sweat breaks out along my collarbone. Pushing against him feels primal, a muted wrestling match where neither of us is allowed to move an inch. "Five, four, three, two... release," he whispers. "Exhale." I let the breath out in a shuddering sigh, forcing my muscles to go slack. Immediately, before my myotatic reflex can kick back in, Julian leans forward, sinking his weight down to push my knee an extra two inches toward my right shoulder. A sharp, electric ache flares deep in the socket, radiating down to my adductor magnus. A sound escapes my throat—half groan, half gasp—and my left hand flies up by reflex, latching onto his right bicep. Beneath my fingers, his muscle is rock-hard, trembling slightly with the effort of controlling my limb. He freezes. We stay locked in that geometry: my hip pushed to its absolute anatomical end-range, the dull fire of stretching scar tissue blooming in my groin, and his chest rising and falling against the shin of my bent leg. I can feel the rapid thud of his pulse through the skin of his inner arm. "Too much?" he asks. His voice is rough, stripped of its textbook neutrality. His thumb is still pressed into the hollow of my hip, right beside the hem of my shorts, his skin scorching against mine. "No," I whisper, though my eyes are watering from the deep, bruised ache in the joint. I don't let go of his arm. If I let go, we go back to being the broken athlete and the successful clinician. As long as the pain is there, he has to hold me. "Don't stop." Julian’s nostrils flare as he inhales slowly. Gently, deliberately, he shifts his grip, sliding his hand from my heel up to wrap around the proximal end of my tibia, just below my knee. To abduct the hip, he has to step in closer, wedging his own hip against the edge of the treatment table to stabilize himself. He draws my knee outward, away from the midline of my body, while simultaneously applying a downward traction force toward the foot of the table to create space in the joint capsule. The head of my femur glides inside the socket. The sensation is dizzying—a sudden, hollow relief followed by the burning stretch of my inner thigh muscles, the gracilis and pectineus pulling taut like violin strings. My back arches slightly off the table. Julian’s left hand slides from my pelvic bone to flatten squarely across my lower ribs, pressing me back down. His palm is wide and heavy, trapping the frantic beat of my heart beneath my sternum. "Stay with me, Maya," he murmurs, looking down at me, his face shadowed against the fluorescent glare. His thumb brushes the bare skin where my shirt has ridden up, a millimeter of contact that has nothing to do with physical therapy and everything to do with the tremor in his fingers. "Don't fight it." I force my spine flat into the vinyl, surrendering to the traction, hating that he is the one putting me back together, and terrified of the moment the timer will beep and he will finally let me go.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a tightly controlled, physically literate scene that delivers most of what the prompt asks for: a former athlete's resentment, a former training partner turned clinician, and sustained erotic tension braided into legitimate therapeutic technique. The anatomical specificity (ASIS stabilization, contract-relax PNF stretching, joint traction, myotatic reflex timing) is genuinely accurate and gives the prose authority—this is rare in writing about bodywork. The tension is well-modulated through involuntary responses: the quivering hamstring, the reflexive grip on his bicep, the pulse felt through skin. The central psychological insight—"As long as the pain is there, he has to hold me"—is the piece's best line and earns the emotional stakes. Weaknesses: The prompt specifies a female physiotherapist attracted to a male protagonist; the response inverts the genders (Julian treating Maya). This is a clear deviation from instructions, though the dynamic itself is preserved. The Zurich/Doha hotel-room backstory is delivered as a single tell-heavy sentence rather than dramatized. Some phrases edge toward stock ("the air between us goes thick," "his voice dropping an octave"). The ending is effective but arrives quickly—the scene is a single continuous escalation without much variation in rhythm. Dialogue is functional and mostly credible, occasionally expository ("That's just tissue resistance, not the bone block" works; "Stay with me, Maya" is a touch romantic-clinical cliché). Prose is clean, sensory, and disciplined; only light purple tendencies (violin-string muscles, "charts hang like verdicts"—the latter is actually good). No meandering; the piece is economical and coherent throughout.
