+ Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The humidity of the Pearl River pressed against my woollen uniform, heavy as a sodden blanket. At the anchorage of Whampoa, the *HMS Vengeance* sat bloated in the brown water, her rigging slack in the heat. I was meant to be tallying the midshipmen’s sightings before noon, yet my marrow had already begun to ache—a dull, hollow thrumming that only one fragrance in Canton could quiet. As I stepped toward the gangway, a violent spasm seized my chest. I doubled over, barking into a linen handkerchief. When I pulled the cloth away, my mouth was thick with the bright, sharp taste of copper. "Rough sound to that, Mr. Merrick," Commander Vance noted, pausing by the quarterdeck rail. His eyes, pale and sharp as salt-scrubbed holystone, lingered on my trembling collar. "You look remarkably peaked." "Nothing to trouble the surgeon with, sir," I replied, tucking the speckled linen safely out of sight. "Merely the damp off the flats. This cursed sea air gets into the bellows." "See that it doesn't rot them entirely," Vance said, turning back to his glass. "Captain wants the Lintin patrol rosters on his desk by four bells." "Aye, sir. I am only going ashore to settle an account with the compradors regarding our fresh water casks. A matter of two hours." It was a lie so well-worn it slipped from my tongue like grease. Ten minutes later, a hired sampan was skulling me past the towering East Indiamen and into the chaotic, sewage-choked arteries near the Thirteen Factories. The smell of rotting cabbage, bilge, and roasting duck fat rose from the mud flats. I stripped off my gold-braided coat in the boat, leaving me in my waistcoat and damp linen shirt, though any eye along Hog Lane could still spot a King’s officer by his boots. I found Jeremiah Finch in the back room of a chandlery that smelled predominantly of tar and salted fish. Finch was a supercargo cast out by the Company for skimming tea duties, now making a fatter living in the illicit coastal trade. He didn't look up from his ledger as I entered. "You're early, Lieutenant," Finch muttered, his quill scratching against the parchment. "And sweating through your linen." "I have the rotation for the inner bar," I said, dropping a rolled slip of Admiralty foolscap onto his desk. "The cutter *Bramble* is stripping her copper at Macao until Tuesday. The revenue boats are blind on the east channel." Finch unrolled the paper, his jaundiced eyes scanning my cramped handwriting. A chest rattled in my ribs, and I coughed again—a wet, tearing sound that brought the metallic tang of blood back to the root of my tongue. Finch grimaced, waving a hand in front of his nose. "God’s teeth, Merrick. You sound like a consumptive cur." "It is the river mist," I rasped, wiping my lips with the back of my hand. "Nothing more. My fee, Finch. The silver." "Half now," he said, sliding three clipped Spanish dollars across the scarred wood. They were worn thin, greasy from a thousand palms. "The rest if the clippers get the Malwa chests through the Bogue without your fellows boarding us." "The agreement was six dollars upon delivery of the chart." "The agreement," Finch said, finally looking up with a dead, flat smile, "was made with an officer who didn't look as though he’d sell his King’s commission for a pipe of mud. Take the three, James. Before I decide I don't need the Navy’s blind eye after all." My fingers twitched toward the spot where my dirk usually hung, but the shivering in my calves betrayed me. I swept the three coins into my palm and left him in the gloom. Outside, the afternoon rain had begun—a warm, relentless drizzle that turned the unpaved alleys beyond the foreign quarter into troughs of black mire. I navigated the labyrinth by scent alone, passing beneath bamboo scaffolding and tattered silk banners until the stench of nightsoil gave way to something heavier. Sweet. Roasted. Like burnt treacle and dead flowers. I ducked through a low doorway hung with greasy hemp curtains. The air inside was blue and stagnant, lit only by the pinprick glow of peanut-oil lamps. Around the perimeter, figures lay curled on woven reed mats like dried shrimp. Old Leung sat behind a low rosewood table, his fingernails curving like horn as he weighed black, tarry globules of Bengal opium on a bone-beam scale. "Three dollars," I said, dropping Finch's clipped silver onto the tray. "Give me the Patna. Not the dross you scraped from the bowls yesterday." Leung didn't touch the coins immediately. He peered at me through the gloom, the oil lamp reflecting in his cataracts. "Three dollars buys very little Patna today, Captain. The Mandarin’s men burned two crab-boats at Whampoa this morning. Prices have gone up." "I know every junk on that river, Leung, and nothing burned today," I said, leaning over the table until my knuckles went white against the wood. Another cough tore through me, so violent the little brass weights on his table danced. The copper taste flooded my throat, warm and slick. Leung watched me recover, entirely unmoved. "You have the marsh-rot in your chest, foreigner." "The sea air disagrees with me," I panted, gripping the edge of his table to keep my knees from buckling. "Weigh the paste, old man. Before I bring a file of Marines down this alley to turn your pots over." "If you brought Marines, where would you sleep at noon?" Leung asked softly. Yet he took a brass needle, speared a dark brown bead from a porcelain jar, and held it over the lamp. It began to bubble, swelling and spitting as it roasted. That first ribbon of smoke curled upward, catching my nostrils, and the knot in my belly instantly began to loosen. I collapsed onto the nearest reed mat, my boots sticking out into the narrow walkway, mud drying on the Hessian leather. Leung handed me the long bamboo stem. My teeth clicked against the ivory mouthpiece as I drew the heavy, sweet vapour deep into the bottom of my lungs, burying the taste of blood beneath the warm, obliterating dark.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-researched piece of historical fiction that fulfills the brief with considerable skill. The prose is disciplined and sensory-rich without tipping into excess: "the humidity of the Pearl River pressed against my woollen uniform, heavy as a sodden blanket" sets the tone economically, and the sensory palette throughout—tar, salted fish, burnt treacle, nightsoil, peanut-oil lamps—is specific to time and place rather than generic. The structure follows the prompt faithfully: a single day, dialogue-forward, moving from ship to compradore to dealer, with the opium-seeking drive clearly established through physical withdrawal symptoms (the marrow ache, the cough, the blood). The coughing blood is an effective device—it gives the addiction a physical cost and gives Finch and Leung leverage over Merrick, showing how his deterioration erodes his negotiating position. The dialogue is the piece's strongest asset. Vance's "See that it doesn't rot them entirely" is nicely dry; Finch's "The agreement was made with an officer who didn't look as though he'd sell his King's commission for a pipe of mud" is a sharp, characterful threat; Leung's "If you brought Marines, where would you sleep at noon?" is the best line in the piece—soft, knowing, and devastating, exposing the emptiness of Merrick's bluster in a single stroke. Each speaker has a distinct register. The moral texture is well handled. Merrick isn't romanticized—he's selling patrol rosters and revenue intelligence, actively betraying his King's commission, and the piece doesn't flinch from this. The "lie so well-worn it slipped from my tongue like grease" is a good self-aware beat. The ending—burying "the taste of blood beneath the warm, obliterating dark"—earns its darkness honestly rather than reaching for false redemption. Minor criticisms: the coughing-blood motif is deployed three times and edges toward repetition; the "dragon" of the prompt is never invoked, though the addiction is vividly rendered regardless; Leung's price dispute resolves a touch too easily; and the piece is essentially a single unbroken descent with no variation in rhythm, which is faithful to the brief but makes the final third slightly predictable in trajectory. The period detail (holystone, foolscap, Patna vs. Malwa opium, the Thirteen Factories, clipped Spanish dollars) is convincing, though occasionally it feels curated—details deployed to signal authenticity rather than always doing narrative work. These are small quibbles against a piece that is coherent, atmospheric, tonally consistent, and genuinely engaging. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The cosmology of the Underworld was largely designed by committee, which explains why there is so much bare rock and nowhere decent to sit. On the south face of the Hill of Eternal Futility, Sisyphus leaned his shoulder into five tons of granite, dug his heels into the scree, and exhaled. Beside him, perched on a jutting shelf of shale with an inkwell wedged between two stones, a large, slightly ragged crow held a quill in its beak. "Read the next one, would you, Crow?" Sisyphus said. His voice had the pleasant, gravelly rumble of two millstones getting along rather well. "We’ve got a good forty yards before the incline gets properly vertical." Crow shifted his weight, pinned a scrap of parchment down with one scaly yellow foot, and cleared his throat. It sounded like a rusty hinge. *Dear Sisyphus,* *My husband of twelve years has recently taken up artisanal cheese-making. I want to be supportive, I really do, but the airing cupboard smells like a badger died in it, and he’s started referring to the cellar as ‘the caves.’ Worse, when I tried to initiate some bedroom festivities last Tuesday, he told me he couldn't lose focus because his Brie was at a critical juncture. How do I compete with dairy?* *Yours,* *Curdled in Corinth* Sisyphus grunted, shifting his grip to a familiar groove on the boulder’s left flank. He’d worn that groove smooth around the time the Assyrians were getting ideas above their station. "Take this down," Sisyphus said, leaning into the granite. *Dear Curdled,* *First of all, never try to compete with a new hobby during its honeymoon phase. A man who has just discovered he can turn milk into something solid by leaving it in the dark is briefly drunk on his own godlike power. Let him have it.* *However, you have a boundary issue, and it’s currently living in your airing cupboard. Tell him that while you admire his passion, warm linen and fermenting dairy are poor bedfellows, and so are the two of you if he doesn't wash the rennet off his hands before nine o'clock. Don't make it an ultimatum. Just buy a very nice loaf of crusty bread, a bottle of the heavy red from the vineyard by the blacksmith's, and meet him at the cellar door wearing that tunic he likes. If he still chooses the Brie, lock him in 'the caves' until he remembers he married a woman and not a goat.* "Got that?" Sisyphus asked, pausing to wipe his brow with the back of a forearm that looked like knotted oak. "Married a goat," Crow muttered around the quill, scratching furiously. "Right. Next one’s on scented vellum. Smells like lavender and poor decisions." *Dear Sisyphus,* *I am a clerk in the Department of Weights and Measures. Every day I weigh things, I measure things, I write the numbers in a ledger, and then the ledger is filed in a basement that floods every spring, washing the ink away. What is the point of anything? Why do we bother getting out of bed when the universe is clearly just a giant mill grinding us into dust?* *Existentially Exhausted* Sisyphus smiled warmly. He braced his calves, took the weight of the stone on his thighs, and pushed it over a tricky ridge of quartz. *Dear Exhausted,* *You’re looking at the ledger, and you ought to be looking at the sandwiches.* *People get terribly worked up about 'legacy' and 'purpose,' which is mostly just vanity wearing a philosophical toga. Of course the ink washes away. Everything washes away eventually. The trick isn't to find a job that echoes through eternity; eternity is overrated and the acoustics are dreadful. The trick is to pack a really good lunch.* *Put some of that pickled cabbage you like on thick bread. Talk to the girl at the desk next to yours—the one who draws little cartoons in the margins of the grain tariffs. Notice the way the light hits the dust motes at three in the afternoon. The universe isn't grinding you into dust; it's just giving you something to do with your hands while you figure out who you are. Now go buy some better ink, and stop brooding. It ruins the digestion.* The air beside the path shimmered with the oily, ligeramente-off-purple light that usually heralded bureaucracy. Phobetor, Under-Secretary for Minor Torments and Nightmares Involving Teeth Falling Out, materialized on a flat rock. He was carrying a clipboard made of pressed bone. "I’m not sure about this at all," Phobetor said, adjusting his pince-nez. "It’s irregular." "Morning, Phobetor," Sisyphus said cheerfully, keeping his shoulder wedged firmly against the boulder so it wouldn't roll over his toes. "How’s the sciatica?" "Never mind my sciatica. I’ve been reviewing your file." Phobetor tapped the clipboard. "The punishment is 'Eternal Toil and Crushing Despair.' I’m seeing the toil, yes, very nice form on the calves, by the way, very classical—but there is a distinct lack of despair. You’re running an agony column, Sisyphus. You’re supposed to be in agony, not *writing* to it." "I'm multitasking," Sisyphus said pleasantly. "Doesn't interfere with the quotas. Look, we’re nearly at the crest." "It’s the tone of the thing," Phobetor complained, peering down his nose at Crow, who hissed softly and covered the inkwell with a wing. "If the shades see you being well-adjusted, they'll all want to be well-adjusted. Next thing you know, Tantalus will be starting a podcast about intermittent fasting. It makes the Department look soft." "Tell you what," Sisyphus said, giving a mighty heave that brought him within three feet of the summit. "When it rolls back down in a minute, I'll pull a really tragic face. Proper wailing and gnashing. How's that?" Phobetor sighed, the sound of dry leaves skittering across a crypt. "Just try to look a bit more alienated, would you? Hades has the auditors in next week." With a faint *pop* of displaced sulfur, he was gone. "Right," Sisyphus said, reaching the very top of the hill. The boulder teetered on the apex, balanced on a knife-edge of gravity. "Squeeze one more in before the drop?" Crow flipped a small, hastily folded note open with his beak. *Dear Sisyphus,* *My brother-in-law has been staying on our couch for four months. He eats all the olives, critiques my pottery, and claims he is 'waiting for the muses to align' before he looks for work. How do I get him to leave without upsetting my sister?* *Crowded in Crete* Just as Crow finished reading, the boulder’s center of gravity shifted. It hung for a fraction of a second, then plunged back down the slope, bouncing over the rocks with a series of deafening *cracks* before settling in a cloud of dust at the very bottom. Sisyphus stood at the summit, stretching his lower back until it popped. He looked down the long, familiar hill, the warm breeze of Tartarus ruffling his beard. *Dear Crowded,* he dictated, beginning the long walk down. *Tell your sister you’ve decided to take up the bagpipes. Tell your brother-in-law that the muses spoke to you in a dream, and they said they’re currently aligning in a quarry about forty miles east of here. Give him a packed lunch and a shovel. Some things in life just need a gentle push, and then you let gravity do the rest.* *Warmest regards,* *Sisyphus.* He reached the bottom of the hill, spat on his hands, and placed them against the warm, rough stone. "Right then, Crow," Sisyphus said, leaning in. "Who's next?"
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of Pratchett pastiche that hits most of its brief with confidence and craft. The opening line ("designed by committee, which explains why there is so much bare rock and nowhere decent to sit") immediately establishes the right comic-cosmological register, and the prose throughout maintains the dry, digressive-but-controlled Pratchett cadence — "the pleasant, gravelly rumble of two millstones getting along rather well" is a genuinely good joke in the right voice. The epistolary structure works well. The letters are varied in tone (domestic comedy, existential despair, freeloading relatives), and the replies are the piece's greatest strength: the advice is specific, practical, and warm rather than sententious. "You're looking at the ledger, and you ought to be looking at the sandwiches" is exactly the kind of grounded, anti-stoic wisdom the prompt demanded. The single sanctioned boulder metaphor ("a gentle push, and then you let gravity do the rest") is smuggled in subtly, as instructed. Sisyphus is shown as contented and competent rather than told — his ease emerges through action, pacing, and his banter with Phobetor. The Phobetor interlude is a smart addition: a bureaucratic antagonist gives the piece dramatic shape and lets the comedy of "insufficient despair" carry the theme without lecturing. His dialogue ("Tantalus will be starting a podcast about intermittent fasting") is a highlight. Flaws: the word "ligeramente" — a Spanish artifact — appears mid-description ("the oily, ligeramente-off-purple light"), an obvious editing slip that briefly breaks the spell. The prompt requested "several" letters including risque material; the piece delivers three letters, none especially risque, so coverage is slightly thinner than specified. The final letter's answer arrives after the boulder has already rolled down, which slightly muddles the "dictate while pushing" mechanic, though it's handled gracefully. The ending is pleasant but a touch abrupt — a fourth letter or a closing beat with Phobetor's auditors might have rounded it off. Some jokes ("married a woman and not a goat") flirt with the forced rather than the understated. These are minor quibbles against a piece that is coherent, funny, well-voiced, and faithful to nearly every constraint. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The neon canyon of Den Den Town hummed with a chaotic symphony of pachinko parlors, megaphone-wielding maids, and 8-bit chiptunes. Hana kept her head down, clutching a brown paper bag containing a vintage Roland patch cable to her chest like a shield. She was just looking for a quiet exit to the subway when a sudden, blistering cascade of notes cut through the humid Osaka air. It was an electric guitar, overdriven and ferocious. Drawn by an invisible tether, Hana drifted toward the glowing entrance of the Taito Station arcade. A small crowd had gathered around a girl who looked to be about eighteen. She had bleached, choppy hair tucked beneath a backwards cap, ripped jeans, and a battered seafoam-green Fender Stratocaster slung low over her hip. Her fingers flew across the fretboard, tearing through a heavy-metal arrangement of "Cruel Angel’s Thesis." The song ended on a screaming harmonic. The small crowd clapped politely before dispersing into the night. Hana remained frozen by a row of gachapon machines, staring at the girl’s pedalboard. The guitarist wiped her brow with the back of her hand, caught Hana staring, and flashed a crooked, shark-like grin. "You’ve been staring at my rig for three minutes straight," the girl called out, her voice cutting cleanly over the arcade’s ambient noise. "Either you want to steal my pedals, or you’re a gearhead. Which is it?" Hana flinched, her gaze snapping up. "I—neither! I mean, not the stealing part." She swallowed hard, her throat suddenly dry. "Um. Your pitch-shifter. You’re routing it *after* the fuzz pedal, right? Most people put it at the start of the chain." The girl’s eyebrows shot up. She clicked off her battery-powered amp and leaned on her guitar like a shovel. "Look at the big brains on you. Yeah, I do. Gives the octave-up a really nasty, synthetic tracking glitch. You play?" "Not guitar," Hana mumbled, looking down at her scuffs on her sneakers. "Keys. Mostly synthesizers. You, um, dropped the third beat in the bridge, by the way. On purpose, I think. Turning it into a 7/8 time signature for two bars?" The guitarist laughed, a bright, barking sound that made Hana’s ears burn. "Okay, now I’m officially intimidated. Who are you, the ghost of Ryuichi Sakamoto? Most people just throw a hundred-yen coin in the case and ask if I know any RADWIMPS." "I'm Hana," she whispered, fumbling in her pocket. "Oh. Sorry. I didn't throw a coin—" "Keep your money, Hana. Critique that specific is worth at least five hundred yen." The girl began unstrapping her guitar, tossing it into a sticker-plastered gig bag with terrifying carelessness. "I’m Ren. And I am starving. Playing that tapping solo on an empty stomach is a human rights violation. Come on." "Come on... where?" "Kura Sushi is two blocks down. You like conveyor belt sushi, right? Of course you do, you're human. Help me carry my amp?" Before Hana could formulate a polite excuse about her mom expecting her home, or her general fear of spontaneous social interaction, Ren had already shoved the small Roland Cube amp into her hands. Ten minutes later, they were wedged into a plastic booth under the harsh fluorescent lights of the kaitenzushi restaurant. Plates of salmon, yellowtail, and miniature pudding cups glided past them on a mechanical track. Hana sat stiffly, her hands folded in her lap, while Ren immediately snatched three plates of spicy tuna from the belt. "Eat," Ren commanded around a mouthful of rice. "You look like you’re awaiting sentencing." "I'm just... not used to doing things like this," Hana admitted, hesitantly pulling a plate of tamago off the line. "Talking to people on the street." "Well, I don't usually kidnap girls outside Taito Station, so we’re both breaking routine." Ren poured powdered green tea into two cups and blasted them with hot water from the table’s tap. She slid one toward Hana. "So, synths, huh? What’s in the bag? Looked like you were guarding the nuclear codes earlier." Hana’s shoulders dropped a fraction of an inch. "It's just an old MIDI sync cable. For a Korg MS-20 Mini. I found it in a junk bin at a retro audio shop on the backstreets." "An MS-20? Man, the filters on those things are filthy. I love it." Ren leaned her elbows on the table, resting her chin in her hands. "What kind of stuff do you make? Wait, let me guess. Ambient noisescapes about the crushing loneliness of the modern metropolis?" A surprised laugh escaped Hana’s lips. She quickly covered her mouth, then lowered her hand, smiling shyly. "Close. Mostly retro-futuristic stuff. Like old 80s and 90s OVA soundtracks." "Hold on." Ren held up a chopstick like a weapon. "Define 'old.' Are we talking *Akira*?" "No, more electronic. Like, um... have you ever seen *Key the Metal Idol*? Or *Serial Experiments Lain*?" Ren’s jaw dropped. She slammed her hands on the table, rattling the soy sauce dispenser. "Shut up. Do *not* tell me you’re into Nakaido Reichi’s *Lain* Cyberia Mixes. Nobody under the age of forty knows about that." Hana’s eyes widened, the residual shyness evaporating in the sudden warmth of shared obsession. "I have the bootleg cassette! The way they used the Roland TB-303 basslines with the distorted breakbeats—Wait, you know the track 'Antidepressant044'?" "Know it? I spent a whole weekend last month trying to replicate that creepy, detuned arpeggio on my delay pedal!" Ren grinned, a genuine, massive smile that reached the corners of her dark eyes. "I failed miserably, obviously. Because I don't have a synth player." Hana paused, a piece of egg sushi halfway to her mouth. "You... you tried to play a step-sequenced analog synth line on a six-string guitar?" "Hey, I’m ambitious, okay? And clearly in need of adult supervision." Ren grabbed another plate off the belt—fried shrimp this time—and pointed it at Hana. "You got a studio setup?" "Just my bedroom," Hana said, her voice finally steady, matching the rhythm of the clattering plates around them. "My closet is full of patch cables instead of clothes. My mom hates it." "Moms never appreciate sonic genius," Ren said solemnly. She pulled her phone from her pocket, unlocked it, and slid it across the table, right between the pickled ginger and the wasabi. "Put your LINE info in there, synth-wizard." Hana looked at the phone, then up at Ren. The older girl was watching her with an expression that was entirely open, devoid of the mockery Hana usually braced for at school. "Why?" Hana asked softly. "Because my guitar sounds lonely," Ren said, taking a bite of shrimp. "And your Korg needs to get out of the closet. Come on, type it in. I'm thinking we do a heavy synth-metal cover of the *Lain* opening next Friday. Right outside the arcade. We'll melt their faces off." Hana picked up the phone. Her thumbs hovered over the screen for a second, her heart doing a strange, syncopated polyrhythm against her ribs. Then, smiling, she began to type.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This scene is a confident, well-executed piece of slice-of-life writing that hits nearly every beat of the prompt. The two central requirements—dialogue-forward construction and distinct character voices—are handled skillfully. Hana's speech is appropriately halting and technical ("I—neither! I mean, not the stealing part"), while Ren's voice crackles with playful, fast-moving confidence ("You like conveyor belt sushi, right? Of course you do, you're human"). The voices are distinguishable even without dialogue tags. The technical music detail is the piece's greatest strength. The pitch-shifter-after-fuzz signal chain, the 7/8 time signature observation, the Korg MS-20, the Serial Experiments Lain Cyberia Mix references—these are specific, accurate, and character-revealing rather than decorative. The gear-talk functions as the mechanism of connection, which makes the emotional turn earned: Hana's shyness doesn't evaporate by authorial fiat, it dissolves in the warmth of shared obsession, and the text explicitly stages this ("the residual shyness evaporating in the sudden warmth of shared obsession"—slightly tell-y, but earned by the dialogue preceding it). The transition from street to sushi restaurant is handled economically, with the amp-carrying beat giving Hana a plausible reason to be swept along. The ending—exchanging LINE info and planning a collab—is a satisfying, low-stakes coming-of-age beat that stays true to the "first connection" premise. Weaknesses: a few lines flirt with cliché ("her heart doing a strange, syncopated polyrhythm against her ribs" is a bit precious, though thematically apt). Ren is somewhat archetypal—the confident manic-pixie-ish busker—and her instant warmth is slightly convenient, though the prompt requests exactly this dynamic. Some of Hana's interiority is told rather than shown ("her general fear of spontaneous social interaction"). The prose is clean but occasionally workmanlike ("terrifying carelessness" is a nice touch, though). The piece is not surprising in structure—it follows the prompt's beats almost mechanically—but executes them with genuine charm and verisimilitude. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I never should have bought a smartwatch from a guy selling electronics out of a velvet-lined suitcase behind the bowling alley. I know, I know. Stupid, right? My best friend Chloe told me it was probably cursed. Or stolen. Or both. "Look at it, Leo," she had said, poking the bulky black dial on my wrist. "It doesn't even have a brand name. Just an hourglass." "It's vintage-futuristic," I’d argued. And for the first twenty-four hours, it was the greatest ten bucks I’d ever spent. I figured out the trick during third-period gym. Coach Davis had us playing dodgeball. Naturally, Brad Miller—a seventh-grader the size of a vending machine—launched a rubber ball directly at my face. Instinctively, I threw my hands up to shield myself, accidentally twisting the metal bezel of the watch counter-clockwise. *BZZZZT.* A cold zap shot up my arm. The gym blurred into streaks of nauseating neon. Sound stretched out like a dying cassette tape, then snapped back. Suddenly, Brad was holding the ball again. I was standing five feet to the left. I ducked. The ball whistled past my ear and slammed into the bleachers. I had rewound time. Once I realized what the watch could do, I went a little crazy. Okay, a *lot* crazy. Dropped my lunch tray? *Twist. Zap.* Saved the lasagna. Guessed wrong on a pop quiz in Mr. Harrison’s history class? *Twist. Zap.* Instant A-plus. Said something completely humiliating to Chloe about how her braces looked cool in the fluorescent light? *Twist. Zap.* Kept my big mouth shut. I probably used it twenty times by Tuesday afternoon. Every time I twisted the bezel back, the glowing green numbers on the digital face would flicker. For a split second, the normal time would vanish, replaced by a red countdown: *68... 67... 66...* I figured it was the battery percentage. By fifth period, though, I started feeling weird. My knees ached with a dull, throbbing pain, like I’d just run ten miles. My shoes felt like vices crushing my toes. And my hoodie sleeves—which usually hung past my knuckles—were suddenly riding up my forearms. "Hey, man, do you have the notes for chapter four?" a kid asked, tapping my shoulder in the hallway. "Yeah, sure," I said. Or tried to say. My voice cracked so hard it sounded like a goose getting stepped on, before dropping into a deep, gravelly baritone I didn't recognize. I clapped a hand over my throat. What was *that*? I ducked into the boys' bathroom and gripped the edge of the sink. When I looked into the mirror, my heart did a triple-backflip into my stomach. Staring back at me wasn't a scrawny twelve-year-old. My face had stretched out, my jawline suddenly sharp and covered in patchy, dark stubble. A cluster of angry red zits dotted my forehead. I was taller—way taller. I looked down at my wrist. The black strap of the smartwatch was digging painfully into thicker skin, and the watch face flickered rapidly. *52... 51...* It wasn't a battery percentage. And I wasn't rewinding *my* time. I was only rewinding the world around me, while my own body fast-forwarded through the rewinds. Every five-minute jump was costing me months, maybe *years* of my life! Panic clawed at my chest. I splashed cold water on my face, scrubbing at the stubble as if it were dirt. I shuffled out of the bathroom, keeping my head down. "Excuse me!" Ms. Gable, the hall monitor, barked at me. "High schoolers aren't allowed in the middle school wing during class hours! Let me see your hall pass, young man!" "I—I'm Leo!" I croaked in my new, booming voice. "Seventh grade!" Ms. Gable narrowed her eyes, reaching for her walkie-talkie. I bolted. I burst through the heavy double doors to the front of the school, just as the final bell rang. Kids flooded out onto the sidewalk. I spotted Chloe near the crosswalk, her nose buried in her phone as she stepped off the curb. Then I heard the roar of an engine. A rusty blue pickup truck was barreling down Oak Street, the driver looking down at his lap. He wasn't slowing for the blinking yellow lights. "Chloe!" I screamed. She looked up. Instead of seeing her best friend, she saw a terrifying, lanky teenager in a too-small hoodie sprinting toward her, yelling her name. She froze in fear, stepping backward—right into the path of the truck. Wait. *No.* In the original timeline, before I got held up by Ms. Gable, I always walked out *with* Chloe. I always pulled her back from the curb because she never looked up from her phone. Because I was older, because I was late, because I scared her, I had ruined the timeline! Tires screeched. Kids screamed. A sickening *THUD* echoed down the street. Chloe’s backpack went flying into the air, papers scattering like white birds. "NO!" I dropped to my knees on the concrete, tears blurring my vision. My chest heaved. I looked down at my wrist. The watch face flickered wildly, the glass hot against my skin. *14... 13... 12...* I didn't know what those numbers meant anymore. Years left? Rewinds left? If I twisted this bezel back five minutes to save her, how old would I get? Thirty? Eighty? Would I turn to dust right here on the sidewalk? Sirens wailed in the distance. Ahead of me, the crowd was gathering around the front of the truck. I gripped the metal bezel. My knuckles were thick, hairy, and trembling. "Hold on, Chloe," I whispered, my voice raspy and ancient. I closed my eyes and twisted the dial all the way to the left. *BZZZZT.* The world dissolved into neon, and the red numbers flashed one last time in the dark: *01... 00...*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, well-executed teen horror chapter that hits every beat of the prompt: the mysterious smartwatch, the time-rewind mechanic, the protagonist's obliviousness to the aging cost, the physical transformation (accelerated puberty), people treating him differently (hall monitor scene), and the timeline disaster with Chloe that can only be fixed by rewinding again — left on a cliffhanger, very Goosebumps-appropriate. The voice is pitch-perfect for middle-grade horror: first-person, wry, self-deprecating ("greatest ten bucks I'd ever spent"), short punchy sentences, and escalating dread. The opening line (buying a watch from a guy with a velvet-lined suitcase behind a bowling alley) is a great hook that establishes tone immediately. The montage of small rewinds (lasagna, pop quiz, braces comment) efficiently shows escalating use before consequences kick in. The mechanics are cleverly handled: the red countdown numbers misread as "battery percentage" is a nice bit of dramatic irony, and the ambiguity of what the numbers mean (years left? rewinds left?) at the end is exactly the right kind of unresolved dread for the genre. The twist that his aged appearance is what causes Chloe's accident — that he ruined the timeline by being late and unrecognizable — is a genuinely well-constructed causal loop, not a random disaster. The transformation is shown well: aching knees, tight shoes, sleeves riding up, voice cracking into a baritone, stubble, zits. The mirror scene is a classic but effective beat. The ending "01... 00..." is a strong cliffhanger, though it does leave the "maybe rectified" ambiguity the prompt requested — appropriate here. Minor criticisms: some elements are stock (dodgeball bully, truck driver texting, mirror reveal). Chloe is thin as a character — mostly a plot device. The prose occasionally leans on familiar formulations ("heart did a triple-backflip into my stomach," "papers scattering like white birds"). The internal explanation paragraph ("It wasn't a battery percentage...") spells out the mechanics a bit tell-y, though acceptable for the age band. The prose is clean and readable but not especially elegant — it's functional genre prose, which suits it. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 76.6
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on, casting a bruised, electric glow against the fading violet of the Atlantic sky. *His locks.* The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else—dangerously compelling—quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger—the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn’t even know his name. The air was thick with the brine of the ocean and the scorched-sugar scent of spun cotton candy. The smell hit the back of her throat, sharp and cloying, tugging at a childhood memory that refused to fully surface. Something about a torn white dress, the dizzying blur of a carousel, and a hand gripping her wrist a little too tightly in the dark. Was it fear she had felt then, or the first intoxicating thrum of disobedience? She couldn't place it, and the inability to remember made her skin prickle beneath her silk blouse. "You’re late," a voice murmured, low and smooth as poured whiskey, right beside her ear. "Or perhaps you were just trying to decide if you had the stomach for it." Clara didn't jump, though her pulse fractured into a violent rhythm. She turned slowly. He was leaning against the striped awning pole of the shooting gallery, the flickering yellow bulbs catching the sharp angles of his cheekbones. A dark lock of hair fell over his forehead, nearly brushing the bruised-looking shadows beneath his eyes. He wore no hat, a deliberate rebellion in a sea of straw boaters and fedoras, and his dark suit was tailored with a precision that suggested money acquired by questionable means. "I wasn't aware we had a strict appointment," she replied, keeping her chin tilted up, grateful that the humid breeze masked the sudden flush in her cheeks. "And I have the stomach for plenty, Mr...?" "Just Julian," he said, pushing off the pole. He didn't offer his hand. Instead, he stepped into her space, close enough that the scent of spun sugar was entirely eclipsed by his clove cigarettes and expensive, cedar-heavy cologne. "Last names are for business ledgers and tombstones, Clara. Tonight is neither." *He remembered my name,* she thought, though she had only whispered it once, in a moment of weakness when he’d caught her stumbling off the Wonder Wheel the night before. The way he said it now felt less like an address and more like a claim. A sensible woman from Manhattan’s Upper East Side would turn on her heel, take the BMT line back to safety, and forget the way his mouth curved when he looked at her. Sensible women did not loiter by the Coney Island rifle racks with men who looked like fallen angels with bruised knuckles. "So, what is tonight, then?" she asked, her gaze dropping briefly to his hands. He was rolling a silver half-dollar across his knuckles with hypnotic dexterity. "An assessment," Julian said softly. He turned slightly, gesturing toward the counter of the shooting gallery, where a row of battered .22 caliber rifles lay chained to the wood. Tin ducks and painted iron stars moved along a rusted track at the back of the booth, clanking in time with the distant roar of the Cyclone. "Let’s see how steady your hands really are." He tossed the silver coin to the barker, a toothless man who took one look at Julian’s eyes and wisely decided to move to the far end of the counter. Julian picked up a rifle, the chain rattling like a shackle, and held it out to her. "I don't shoot," Clara said, though her fingers twitched against the clasp of her handbag. "Liar," he whispered, a dark, knowing smile ghosting across his lips. "You’ve been looking for a reason to pull a trigger since the moment I found you yesterday. Take it." It wasn't a request. The edge in his voice sent a illicit shiver down her spine, pooling heavy and warm in her stomach. She stepped up to the counter, taking the warm metal from his hands. Their fingers brushed—his skin was calloused, burning hot—and the contact felt dangerously close to a surrender. "Too loose," he murmured, moving directly behind her. Before she could protest, his chest was pressed against her back. He reached around her, his left hand covering hers on the fore-end of the stock, his right guiding her fingers to the trigger guard. She was trapped between the hard wood of the counter and the harder line of his body. She could feel the steady, rhythmic rise and fall of his chest, entirely unaffected, while her own breath came in shallow, traitorous gasps. "You’re holding it like it might bite you," Julian said, his lips brushing the shell of her ear as he spoke. "It won't. It only does what you tell it to do. There’s a lesson in that, darling." "And what if I don't like taking lessons?" she breathed, leaning back just a fraction, testing the boundary, feeling the sudden rigid tension in his frame as her shoulder blades pressed into his lapels. "Oh, I think you do," he countered, his grip tightening over her knuckles, bruisingly firm, commanding her complete stillness. "I think you’re exhausted from being the one in charge of your neat, suffocating little life. Look down the sight." She forced her eyes open, hadn't even realized they had fluttered shut. The iron ducks blurred beneath the glowing neon. That childhood scent of burnt sugar washed over her again—*let go, just let go*—and suddenly she didn't care about the consequences. "Breathe in," Julian commanded softly, his thumb stroking the inside of her wrist where her pulse hammered frantically. "And give in." Clara exhaled, and pulled the trigger. The crack of the rifle was sharp, instantly swallowed by the roar of the boardwalk crowd, the metallic *clang* of a tin star flipping backward lost in the symphony of the night. Julian didn't step back. If anything, his hold on her tightened, his breath hot against her neck. "Good girl," he murmured, the praise laced with a dark, possessive promise that terrified and thrilled her in equal measure. "Now, walk with me into the dark, and tell me what else you're willing to do."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt: a 1937 Coney Island scene blending romantic allure with menace, told from Clara's feminine perspective. It honors the seed text, integrates it smoothly, and builds tension through the shooting gallery conceit—a rifle lesson as seduction/power exchange, which is thematically apt (control, surrender, "it only does what you tell it to do"). Strengths: The dialogue is generally sharp and period-appropriate ("Last names are for business ledgers and tombstones"), with good power dynamics and subtext. The barker's wary retreat is an economical show-don't-tell beat establishing Julian's menace. Sensory grounding is consistent (burnt sugar, clove cigarettes, cedar cologne, the Cyclone's roar). The childhood memory fragment adds psychological depth and ambiguity—fear vs. the "first intoxicating thrum of disobedience"—giving Clara an interior life beyond the scene. Prose rhythm is controlled, sentences flow well, and the ending lands on an ominous, tension-preserving note rather than resolving anything prematurely. Weaknesses: Some imagery is stock—voice "smooth as poured whiskey," "fallen angels," "bruised knuckles," "Good girl" as possessive praise are all well-worn romance-novel furniture. The physical escalation (his chest against her back, hand over hers) is effective but borders on the formulaic dominant-alpha template; a critic could call it 50 Shades cosplay with period dress, though the prompt explicitly invited that register. A few phrases strain: "a illicit shiver" (grammatical slip), "pulse fractured into a violent rhythm," "bruised-looking shadows." The transformation of Clara from hesitant to trigger-pulling is earned via the memory motif, but the speed of her capitulation ("suddenly she didn't care about the consequences") is slightly convenient. Minor typos ("a illicit") and the repeated "bruised" motif suggest light editing lapses. Nothing meanders; pacing is tight and the ~50% dialogue target is roughly met. Overall this is confident, atmospheric genre writing with genuine tension, held back from excellence mainly by its reliance on familiar dark-romance tropes and occasional overwrought phrasing. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The smell of the butcher shed was always the same: copper, wet hide, and the sharp, piney tang of turpentine. Usually, by the second night, the shed was a place of loud, bragging camaraderie, his father and Mike passing a bottle of Wild Turkey back and forth while Gilles, their local guide, worked the skinning knife with the effortless grace of a surgeon. Tonight, the only sound was the wet *shhhk-shhhk* of the blade and the frantic buzzing of a late-autumn blowfly trapped against the bare lightbulb. JT leaned against the doorframe, his hands shoved deep into the pockets of his Mackinaw jacket. He was nursing a warm Busch, the aluminum can sweating against his palm. He hadn't drunk much of it, just enough to wash away the dry, metallic taste that had been coating his tongue since the clearing. *Since the buck.* Or since he’d hallucinated the buck. Because that was the alternative, wasn't it? Either his steel-spined old man had tried to pet a wild bull caribou like a backyard golden retriever, or JT’s own wiring was coming loose. He watched Gilles work. The old Cree guide had taken them out every October since JT was twelve. Gilles was normally a fountain of dirty jokes and terrifying stories about bush-mad trappers. This trip, the man had barely spoken ten words. He kept his chin tucked into the collar of his stained flannel, his movements jerky, almost frantic. He wasn't savoring the work tonight. He was rushing it. "You're cutting too deep on the flank, Gilles," JT’s father said. His voice didn't sound right. It lacked its usual booming authority. He was sitting on an upturned five-gallon bucket, staring blankly at the concrete floor between his boots. Gilles didn't look up. *Shhhk-shhhk.* "Meat's fine, Mr. Miller." "Looks bruised," Mike muttered. He was leaning against the workbench, methodically clicking the safety of his Remington on and off. *Click-clack. Click-clack.* His eyes were fixed on the hanging carcass—the first one they’d shot, the one that had just stood there waiting to die. "Looks dark." Gilles stopped. The knife hovered an inch from the pale fascia of the caribou’s ribs. Slowly, the old man wiped his blade on his jeans and slid it into his belt sheath. He looked at the carcass, then at JT’s father, and finally, his dark, rheumy eyes locked onto JT. There was a terrifying lucidity in Gilles’s gaze. It was the look of a man smelling smoke in a crowded theater. "I'm done for the night," Gilles said, his voice a dry rattle. He walked toward the door, forcing JT to step aside into the ankle-deep weeds outside. "Hold on," JT’s father called out, standing up slowly, as if his joints were rusted. "We haven't quartered it yet." "Leave it hang," Gilles said, already moving toward his battered F-150 parked at the edge of the gravel turnaround. JT followed him, the cold night air hitting his lungs like ice water. Above the jagged black teeth of the spruce trees, the moon was rising—a bloated, gibbous thing, just a sliver shy of full. It cast a milky, dead light over the clearing. "Gilles, wait up," JT said, jogging to catch him. The guide wrenched open his truck door. The dome light didn't work, leaving his face in shadow as he climbed into the cab. JT grabbed the top of the door before Gilles could pull it shut. "What's going on, man?" JT whispered, glancing back toward the yellow square of light spilling from the shed. "You've been spooked since we got here." Gilles gripped the steering wheel. His knuckles were white. "You got your own truck, JT. Keys are on the peg by the stove." "Yeah, I know where the keys are. We're here till Sunday." "Full moon's tomorrow night," Gilles said. He looked straight ahead through the cracked windshield, staring into the wall of dark timber. "Pack your gear in the morning. Don't wait for the sun to get high. Just pack the truck and drive south." A cold prickle started at the base of JT’s skull, radiating down his spine. "Why? Is it poachers? Bears?" Gilles finally looked at him. In the pale moonlight, the deep lines of the old man's face looked like cracks in dry mud. "The herd's wrong this year, boy. They aren't running. You saw it. They're coming *in*." "Coming in to what?" "Just leave before the moon fills out," Gilles whispered. "Once it's full, the woods close up. You tell your dad—" Gilles stopped, his gaze flicking past JT’s shoulder toward the shed. His jaw tightened. "No. Don't tell him nothing. You just get in that truck and drive, JT. Even if you got to drive it alone." The engine turned over with a violent roar, drowning out JT’s next question. Gilles yanked the door shut, threw the truck into reverse, and spat gravel against JT's shins as he wheeled around and tore down the narrow dirt track, his taillights swallowed instantly by the brooding trees. JT stood alone in the sudden, suffocating silence. *Even if you got to drive it alone.* What the hell was that supposed to mean? He turned back toward the lodge. The light in the butcher shed was out. "Dad?" JT called. His voice sounded small, swallowed up by the thick, heavy air. "Mike?" No answer. JT walked back toward the shed, his boots crunching loudly on the frost-stiffened grass. The door was swung wide open. Inside, it was pitch black, smelling heavily of raw meat and that strange, sweet musk he’d smelled in the clearing earlier. He reached in and fumbled for the string of the overhead bulb, pulling it. The light snapped on. The shed was empty. His father and brother were gone. Hanging from the gambrel hook, swaying almost imperceptibly, was the skinned carcass of the caribou. JT stared at it, his breath hitching in his throat. Gilles had taken the head off hours ago, tossing it into the gut bucket in the corner. JT had *watched* him do it. Yet, as JT stood frozen under the buzzing forty-watt bulb, he could hear the distinct, rhythmic sound of heavy breathing coming from the meat. *In. Out.* The ribcage, stripped red and bare, expanded slightly, then fell. JT backed out of the shed, his mind screaming that it was a trick of the light, a spasm of cooling nerves, too much cheap beer on an empty stomach. He stumbled backward, his heel catching on a root, and went down hard on his ass in the dirt. He scrambled up, frantic now, his eyes darting toward the main cabin. The porch light was on, casting a long, distorted shadow across the yard. His father and Mike were standing at the very edge of the treeline, fifty yards away. Their backs were to him. They had left their rifles in the shed. They stood shoulder to shoulder, utterly motionless, their heads tilted slightly back as they stared into the impenetrable black of the spruce forest. And there, just beyond them in the dark, catching the pale spill of the porch light, were dozens of pairs of flat, dark eyes, staring back. Waiting.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The continuation successfully maintains the King-inspired register: grounded, masculine detail (Busch beer, Mackinaw jacket, Remington, Wild Turkey) anchoring escalating surreal dread. The chapter adds a new character, Gilles, whose panic provides an effective exposition vehicle without over-explaining—the "full moon" and "the herd's coming in" is a nice, ominous fragment of lore. Dialogue is functional and character-appropriate, though Gilles's warnings flirt with genre cliché ("Leave before the moon fills out," "the woods close up"). The pacing is tight: shed scene, guide's flight, discovery of the empty shed, breathing carcass, and the final image of father and brother standing at the treeline among waiting eyes. That final tableau is a strong, cinematic payoff that pays off the seed's "build tension towards a payoff" instruction. The unreliable-narrator ambiguity is preserved—JT rationalizes the breathing carcass as "a trick of the light, a spasm of cooling nerves"—which honors the psychological ambiguity requirement. Character actions are believable: Gilles's flight is motivated by observed wrongness; JT's hesitation and self-doubt are consistent with his established passivity. Weaknesses: some familiar horror furniture (gibbous "bloated" moon, white knuckles, "cracks in dry mud" face). Gilles is somewhat stock—a wise Indigenous guide who knows the land's secrets edges toward trope. The exposition dump, while atmospheric, is slightly convenient. Prose is competent and controlled rather than exceptional; a few phrases ("brooding trees," "spine-cold") are stock. Emotional complexity is somewhat limited—JT's fear dominates, with only a flicker of shame/isolation carried over. Still, the piece is coherent, well-paced at ~1000 words, avoids meandering, and ends darkly, congruent with genre. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 78.4
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Morning in the Seventh Circle always smelled faintly of burnt toast and broken promises. Lucifer Morningstar sat at the edge of his obsidian breakfast bar, nursing a mug of black coffee that was, quite literally, boiling. Before him lay a stack of parchment thick enough to choke a Leviathan. He signed an order authorizing a ten-percent increase in the swarm density of the Locust Pits, rejected a requisition for ergonomic pitchforks from the Third Circle Union of Tormentors, and sighed. The sigh melted the frost on the inside of his kitchen window—a window he had installed purely so he could frost it, just to feel something other than ambient heat. It was a Tuesday. Tuesdays were unbearable. Since Lilith had moved her things out three centuries ago—taking the good blender and a third of the minor demonic legions—the palace had felt entirely too large. The echoing screams of the damned just didn’t fill a room the way her judgmental silences used to. The heavy mahogany doors of his study blew inward, splintering slightly off their hinges. A lesser imp, who had been attempting to dust the baseboards, was vaporized by the sheer kinetic arrogance of the entrance. "You didn't latch the deadbolt," Lilith said, stepping over the tiny pile of imp-ash. She looked devastating, as usual, dressed in something woven from midnight shadows and spite. Slung over her shoulder was her favorite handbag: a massive, scorched leather purse that looked as though it had survived a dragon attack, largely because it had. "I left it unlocked in case the postman came," Lucifer lied smoothly, setting his quill down. "Are you here to assassinate me, darling? Because if so, you’re early. I have you penciled in for a blood-feud on Thursday." "Thursday doesn't work for me. I’m inciting a revolution in the mortal realm," she said, dropping the scorched purse onto his meticulously organized desk. It landed with a heavy, metallic thud, crushing a scale model of the newly proposed Sloth Expressway. "Anyway, I was in the neighborhood. You left your cufflinks in my lair in the wastes of Edom. Back in 1884." She began to rummage through the purse. Lucifer watched, entirely transfixed, as she pulled items from its seemingly bottomless depths to clear a path. First came a petrified human spleen. Then, a pristine 1997 Tamagotchi, beeping frantically for food. Next, a bundle of stolen Vatican parking passes, and finally, a half-eaten sleeve of Fig Newtons. "Are those mortal biscuits?" Lucifer asked, raising an immaculate eyebrow. "They were on sale in Purgatory," she muttered. "Aha." She extracted a pair of diamond cufflinks—the ones shaped like weeping cherubs—and tossed them onto his blotter. Then, instead of leaving, she pulled up a chair upholstered in the finest hypocritical politicians and sat down. "You look terrible, Samael," she observed, using his old name just to irritate him. "I’m the Prince of Darkness. I’m supposed to look brooding and tragic." "You look like a middle-management accountant who hasn't been laid since the Renaissance," she corrected, popping a Fig Newton into her mouth. "Have you been eating? Or are you just brooding on the balcony and throwing thunderbolts at the Lake of Fire again?" "I don't throw thunderbolts when I'm sad," Lucifer said defensively. "It was a lightning storm. A natural atmospheric phenomenon." "Down here, *you* are the atmosphere." Silence stretched between them, punctuated only by the distant, rhythmic chanting of a thousand damned souls pushing boulders up a hill, and the pathetic *beep-beep* of the Tamagotchi on the desk. Lucifer reached out, tapped a button on the little plastic egg to clean up its digital droppings, and slid it back toward her. "Thank you," she said softly. "I stole it from a warlock in Seattle. If it dies, I lose a bet with Hecate." "How is Hecate?" "Still three-faced. Still owes me twenty bucks." Lilith leaned back, crossing her legs. "Beelzebub tells me you’ve been delegating the flaying." Lucifer winced. "Beelzebub is a gossip. And I haven't been delegating *all* of it. It's just… once you’ve seen one corrupt senator turned inside out, you’ve really seen them all. The spark is gone, Lil. The pageantry." Lilith looked at him, her dark eyes softening by a fraction of a degree—just enough to lower the room's temperature from *incinerating* to *mildly blistering*. Over the last few decades, her visits had shifted. First, she had stopped by to throw curses at his head. Then, she had stopped by to mock his interior decorating. Last month, she had brought him a severed head just because it looked like a guy they both hated in Mesopotamia. In demonology, this was practically couples therapy. "The problem with you," Lilith said, sweeping the spleen and the Vatican passes back into her scorched leather bag, "is that you treat apocalypse like a nine-to-five. You need a hobby. Or a companion." "I tried getting a hellhound," Lucifer admitted, staring into his boiling coffee. "Cerberus ate it. Then he ate the rug." "I wasn't talking about a dog, you idiot." She stood up, slinging the heavy purse over her shoulder. She walked around the desk, her fingers trailing over the ruined model of the Sloth Expressway. When she reached him, she didn't stab him with a concealed dagger of bone, which was her usual farewell. Instead, she reached down and adjusted the lapel of his velvet smoking jacket, smoothing out an imaginary wrinkle. "I have a gallery opening in Paris tonight," she said, her voice dropping to a low purr that smelled of ozone and pomegranate. "An artist sold his soul for the ability to paint with existential dread. It’s going to be wonderfully pretentious. Lots of crying." Lucifer looked up at her, a slow, dangerous smile finally breaking across his face. The frost on the kitchen window vanished entirely. "That sounds atrocious." "It will be," she agreed. "Pick me up at eight. And wear the cufflinks. If you show up in that ratty tunic you wore during the Black Plague, I’ll flay you myself." She turned and strode out through the broken doors. Lucifer sat alone for a moment in the quiet of his study. Then, whistling a cheerful, minor-key tune that had once driven a monastery to madness, he picked up his quill. He had a lot of tortures to cancel if he was going to be ready by eight.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed piece of dark domestic comedy that hits nearly every note the prompt requested. The central conceit—bureaucratic hell administration juxtaposed with a stalled romance—lands immediately ("rejected a requisition for ergonomic pitchforks from the Third Circle Union of Tormentors") and is sustained throughout without wearing thin. The Gaiman influence is evident in the dry, matter-of-fact treatment of the supernatural: the Tamagotchi in the bottomless purse, the cufflinks left in Edom in 1884, the offhand "I stole it from a warlock in Seattle." These details do the worldbuilding work through specificity rather than exposition, which is exactly the understated irony the prompt called for. The purse inventory scene is the strongest comedic set piece—it's absurd, but each item reveals character (Lilith's pettiness, her longevity, her strange sentimentality). The relationship dynamics are genuinely nuanced. Lilith's visits escalating from "throwing curses at his head" to "mocking his interior decorating" to the severed-head gift is a lovely compression of the reconciliation arc, and the line "In demonology, this was practically couples therapy" is the piece's best joke—wry, economical, and thematically load-bearing. Lucifer's loneliness is shown rather than told: the frosted window installed "just to feel something," the delegating of flayings, the eaten hellhound. The temperature shift when her eyes soften is a nice physical register for emotional change. The dialogue is sharp and character-distinct throughout. Lilith's "you look like a middle-management accountant who hasn't been laid since the Renaissance" is a highlight, and the Hecate exchange ("Still three-faced. Still owes me twenty bucks") has the right throwaway rhythm. Weaknesses: the piece occasionally over-eggs a joke. "Kinetic arrogance of the entrance" and "chair upholstered in the finest hypocritical politicians" are good, but the density of modifiers sometimes tips toward the ornamental. The ending—canceling tortures to make his date—is a satisfying button, but the reconciliation happens slightly fast; the "on again" turn is telegraphed rather than fully earned, though the prompt itself specifies the cycle "may be coming around," which mitigates this. A few jokes (Fig Newtons/Purgatory sale) are more cute than funny. The prose is occasionally a touch pleased with itself, and the piece stays in one emotional register—amused melancholy—without ever risking real darkness or real pain, which keeps it from being truly exceptional. Still, this is polished, coherent, tonally consistent work with genuine wit and a clear authorial voice. It fulfills the brief almost exactly. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
The afternoon heat pressed down on the Ludus Magnus like a bronze shield, trapping the stench of a hundred sweating men, stale olive oil, and the sour tang of fermented fish sauce drifting from the kitchens. Beyond the high brick walls of our training school, the monster that was the Flavian Amphitheater loomed against a bruised Roman sky. Even from the courtyard, we could hear it breathing—a low, vibrating hum of fifty thousand citizens gathering to watch us bleed. I sat on a rough-hewn bench in the shade of the portico, a wooden strigil in my hand. Slowly, methodically, I scraped the mixture of sand, sweat, and oil from my forearms. The gritty paste fell in gray ribbons onto the packed dirt between my sandals. My muscles ached with a dull, familiar throb from the morning’s drills against the *palus*, the six-foot wooden post that had been my only enemy for the last three weeks. Tomorrow, the wood would be replaced by flesh and iron. Across the yard, the *lanista*, Batiatus’s successor, a greasy freedman named Cornelius Lentulus, was entertaining a senator. I didn't know the politician's name, only the thick purple stripe on his blindingly white toga and the way he held a scented handkerchief to his nose. They were haggling over the price of blood. "The plebs are restless, Lentulus," the senator’s voice carried over the rhythmic clack-clack of wooden swords. "The grain ships from Alexandria are delayed again. If the dole is short next week, there will be riots in the Subura. The Emperor wants a distraction. He wants a spectacle that will make them forget their bellies are empty." "And he shall have it, Senator," Lentulus oiled back, bowing slightly. "My Thracians are starved for glory, and the murmillo there—Crixus—has survived seven sands. The crowd loves him. Women buy vials of his sweat outside the gates as an aphrodisiac." I paused my scraping, my jaw tightening until my teeth creaked. *A distraction.* That was all we were. Rome sat at the zenith of the world, its borders stretching from the mists of Britannia to the burning sands of Parthia, gorging itself on the wealth of conquered nations. Yet its own people were starving in the alleyways, pacified only by free bread and the sight of enslaved men butchering one another. I remembered the rolling green hills of my homeland in Dacia, the smell of pine needles and cold mountain streams, before Trajan’s legions burned my village and put me in chains. Here, the air tasted only of dust, woodsmoke, and copper. "Staring at the purple won't make you free, Dacian," a deep voice rumbled beside me. Atticus, a towering *retiarius* from the provinces of Gaul, dropped onto the bench, the wooden frame groaning under his weight. He was mending his net, his thick fingers surprisingly nimble as he knotted the hemp cord. A jagged scar ran from the corner of his left eye down to his collarbone—a souvenir from a secutor’s blade two summers ago. "I was just wondering how softly he bleeds," I murmured, my eyes still fixed on the senator, who was now pinching the bicep of a young Germanic recruit as if checking the ripeness of a melon. "Like any other pig," Atticus spat into the dirt. "Don't waste your anger on them, brother. Save it for the sand. Word from the armorers is that they are pairing us tomorrow." My stomach dropped, a cold stone sinking into my gut. I looked at Atticus. In the arena, the *murmillo*—the heavily armored fish-man, which was my discipline—was traditionally pitted against the lightly clad net-fighter, the *retiarius*. We were natural enemies by the design of the games. Yet, in the cramped cells of the ludus, Atticus had been the one to hold me down when the physician sewed my thigh without poppy juice. We had shared sour wine and stories of the women we had loved before Rome swallowed us whole. "Is it true?" I asked, my voice barely a whisper. Atticus didn't look up from his net. "Lentulus promised the senator a match of veterans. No mercy. *Sine missione*." To the death. The words hung between us, heavier than the stifling August heat. The cries of the *doctores* barking orders at the new recruits faded into a dull buzz in my ears. If I survived tomorrow, it meant Atticus would be dragged out through the Libitinian Gate on a meat hook. A horn blew, signaling the evening meal. The yard began to empty as the men shuffled toward the mess hall for their *puls*—the thick barley and bean mash that packed fat over our muscles so we could take shallow cuts without dying, bleeding dramatically for the howling mob while keeping our vitals intact. "Go eat," I told Atticus, standing up. "I have something to do." He looked at me then, his dark eyes hollow, already mourning one of us. He nodded once and walked away, his net slung over his bare shoulder. I retreated into the cool, damp bowels of the ludus, down the narrow corridor lined with our cells. The smell here was different—moldering straw, urine, and the sharp, metallic scent of fear that never quite washed out of the stone. I ducked into my cell, a space barely wide enough for me to lie down. From beneath my straw pallet, I pried loose a cracked floor tile and pulled out a small leather pouch. Inside were the tools of my ritual, a superstition I had kept secret from the guards since my very first fight in the provincial rings of Capua. I knelt on the cold stone. First, I took a pinch of dried earth—not the yellow sand of the arena, which was soaked in the grease of dead men, but dark, rich soil I had scraped from the roots of an olive tree outside the city walls during a transport three years ago. It didn't smell like Dacia, not truly, but it smelled of things that grew rather than things that died. I rubbed the dirt into the calloused palm of my sword hand, whispering the names of my father and my brothers in my native tongue, a language I was slowly forgetting. Next, I pulled out a small, flattened lead coin, its face worn completely smooth. Before every bout, I placed this coin beneath my tongue, holding it there until the gates opened. It was a mockery of the Roman custom of paying Charon, the ferryman of the dead. By holding the coin in my mouth *before* the fight, I told the gods that I was already dead. And a dead man cannot be killed. As I pressed the cold, bitter metal against my tongue, the distant roar of the city seemed to penetrate the thick stone walls. Tomorrow, the Emperor would sit in his shaded box, the senators would fan themselves, and the starving mob would scream for blood, blind to the chains they wore themselves. I spat the coin back into my dirt-stained palm and closed my fingers tightly around it. I didn't know if the gods of my homeland could hear me beneath the weight of so much Roman stone. I only knew that tomorrow, when the iron gates rose and the blinding sun hit my eyes, I would have to look across the sand at my only friend, and remember how to be a monster.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, well-crafted historical fiction piece that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements: first person, past tense, non-combat slice-of-life, rich sensory detail, interiority, political/social context, and a clear sense of a larger story. The prose is confident and controlled, with vivid sensory grounding (the strigil scraping gray ribbons of paste, the smell of fermented fish sauce, the "metallic scent of fear" in the stone). The political dimension is woven in naturally through the senator's dialogue about grain dole and distraction, and the narrator's Dacian backstory personalizes imperial conquest. The central conflict—being paired against his only friend, sine missione—is a classic gladiator trope, arguably bordering on predictable, but it's executed with enough specificity (the Charon coin ritual, the soil from the olive tree) to feel earned rather than generic. The pre-fight ritual is the piece's strongest original element, giving the character genuine interiority and cultural texture. Weaknesses: some phrases strain slightly ("oiled back" as a verb is a nice touch, but "the monster that was the Flavian Amphitheater... we could hear it breathing" is a familiar image). The senator's dialogue is a bit expository—"The Emperor wants a distraction" is on-the-nose, though functional. The ending lands well with the "remember how to be a monster" line, though the friend-vs-friend setup is the most obvious route the prompt could take. Minor anachronism risk (Batiatus reference, Trajan-era Dacian wars) is handled plausibly. Emotionally complex, coherent, well-paced, no meandering.
